title: Apology for Raimond Sebond
paragraphs: Learning is, indeed, a very great and very substantial accomplishment, and those who despise it betray their own lack of understanding well enough. But I do not prize it at the inflated rate some others do — as Herillus the philosopher did, for one, who placed the sovereign good in it and maintained that "it alone can make us wise and contented," which I do not believe. No more do I believe what others have said: that learning is the mother of all virtue, and all vice proceeds from ignorance — which, if true, would require a very long explanation. My house has long been open to men of knowledge, and is well known to them. For my father, who governed it for fifty years and more, fired by the new ardour with which Francis the First embraced letters and brought them into esteem, hunted after the acquaintance of learned men with great diligence and expense, receiving them into his house as persons sacred and touched with some particular inspiration of divine wisdom. He collected their sayings and sentences as so many oracles, with all the more reverence and religious devotion as he was the less able to judge of them, for he had no learning, any more than his predecessors. For my part I love such men, but I do not adore them. Among others, Peter Bunel, a man of great reputation for knowledge in his time, having spent some days at Montaigne in my father's company along with others of his sort, presented him at his departure with a book entitled _Theologia naturalis; sive Liber Creaturarum, magistri Raimondi de Sebonde._ Since Italian and Spanish were familiar to my father, and this book was written in a kind of jargon — Spanish with Latin endings — he hoped that with a little help he might be able to understand it, and so he recommended it as a very useful book, and one suited to the time in which he gave it to him. That was when Luther's new doctrines were beginning to come into vogue, and in many places to shake our ancient belief — wherein he was very well advised, foreseeing wisely, by his own reason, that the beginning of this disorder would easily slide into an abominable atheism. For the common people, lacking the faculty of judging things for themselves, allow themselves to be carried away by chance and appearance. Once they have been emboldened to despise and challenge opinions they had previously held in extreme reverence — those on which their salvation depends — and once some articles of their religion have been brought into doubt and dispute, they soon throw all the other parts of their belief into the same uncertainty. They had no other authority or foundation than the ones they have already disturbed, and they shake off every impression they had received from the authority of the laws or the reverence of ancient custom as if it were a tyrannical yoke:
Nam cupide conculcatur nimis ante metutum;
["For with most eagerness they spurn the law / By which they were before most kept in awe"]
— resolving to admit nothing in future to which they have not first applied their own decrees and given their particular consent.

It happened that my father, a little before his death, having accidentally come upon this book under a heap of other neglected papers, ordered me to translate it for him into French. Authors of this kind are worth translating, where it is mostly the matter that needs to be carried over; but works where grace of language and elegance of style are the point are dangerous to attempt, especially when a man is turning them into a weaker idiom. It was a strange and a new undertaking for me, but having by chance nothing else to do at the time, and being unable to refuse the command of the best father that ever was, I did it as well as I could. He was so well pleased with it that he ordered it to be printed, which, after his death, was done.

I found this author's ideas exceedingly fine, the structure of his work well followed, and his design full of piety. And because many people enjoy reading it, particularly the ladies — to whom we owe the most service — I have often thought to help them clear the book of two principal objections that have been raised against it. His design is bold and daring, for he undertakes, by human and natural reasons, to establish and make good every article of the Christian religion against the atheists. To tell the truth, he is so firm and so successful at it that I do not think the subject can be handled better; I believe he has been equalled by no one. The work seemed to me so beautiful and so rich, for an author whose name is so little known — all we know of him is that he was a Spaniard, practising medicine at Toulouse about two hundred years ago — that I asked Adrian Turnebus, who knew everything, what he thought of that book. He answered that he thought it was some abstract drawn from St Thomas Aquinas, since in truth only a mind so full of infinite erudition and admirable subtlety was capable of such thoughts. Whatever the case, and whoever the author and inventor (and it is not reasonable, without greater certainty, to deprive Sebond of that title), he was a man of great judgment and most admirable parts.

The first thing they criticize in his work is this: that Christians are wrong to rest their belief on human reason, since belief is grasped only by faith and the particular inspiration of divine grace. There appears to be something of zealous piety in this objection, and we must therefore try to satisfy those who raise it with all the more mildness and respect. This task would suit a man well read in divinity better than it suits me, who know nothing of it. Nevertheless, I conceive that in a thing so divine, so high, so far above all human intelligence as that truth with which the bounty of God has been pleased to enlighten us, it is very necessary that he should also lend us his assistance, as a quite extraordinary favour and privilege, to conceive it and imprint it on our understanding. And I do not believe that purely human means are in any sort capable of doing it: for if they were, so many rare and excellent souls, so abundantly furnished with natural strength in former ages, could not have failed by their reason to arrive at this knowledge. It is faith alone that vividly and certainly grasps the deep mysteries of our religion. And yet I do not say that it is not a worthy and very laudable attempt to put the natural, human tools with which God has endowed us to the service of our faith. There is no doubt that this is the most noble use we can put them to, and that there is no design more noble in a Christian than to make it the aim and end of all his studies to extend and amplify the truth of his belief. We do not content ourselves with serving God with soul and understanding alone — we owe and offer him a bodily reverence as well, applying our limbs, motions, and external things to his honour. Here we must do the same, and accompany our faith with all the reason we have, but always with this reservation: not to imagine that faith depends on us, nor that our arguments and efforts can reach so supernatural and divine a knowledge. If it does not enter us by an extraordinary infusion, if it enters by reason alone and by merely human ways, it is not in us in its true dignity and splendour. And yet I am afraid we have it only by this latter way.

If we held on to God by the mediation of a living faith, if we held on to God through him and not through ourselves, if we had a divine basis and foundation, human accidents would not have the power to shake us as they do; our fortress would not surrender to so weak a battery; the love of novelty, the constraint of princes, the success of a faction, the rash and chance change of our opinions, would not have the power to stagger and alter our belief. We should not then leave it at the mercy of every new argument, nor abandon it to all the rhetoric in the world; we should withstand the fury of those waves with immovable, unyielding constancy:
As a great rock repels the rolling tides,
That foam and bark about her marble sides, / From its strong bulk.

If we were even touched with this ray of divinity, it would show through everywhere; not only our words but our works would carry its brightness and lustre. Everything that came from us would be seen lit by this noble light. We ought to be ashamed that, in all human sects, there has never been a partisan who did not in some measure conform his life and behaviour to it — whereas this divine and heavenly institution distinguishes Christians by the name only. Do you want the proof? Compare our manners to those of a Muslim or a pagan: you will still find that we fall very

short — and that, out of regard for the reputation and advantage of our religion, we ought to shine in excellence at a vast distance beyond all others, so that it should be said of us, "Are they so just, so charitable, so good? Then they are Christians." All other signs are common to every religion: hope, trust, events, ceremonies, penance,

martyrdom. The peculiar mark of our truth ought to be our virtue, since it is also the most heavenly and difficult, and the most worthy product of truth. In this our good Saint Louis was in the right when, the Tartar king having become Christian and planning to come to Lyon to kiss the Pope's feet and there witness with his own eyes the sanctity he hoped to find in our customs, immediately turned him from his purpose — for fear lest our disorderly way of living should, on the contrary, put him off so holy a belief. And yet it happened quite the other way with that later visitor who, going to Rome for the same purpose and there seeing the dissoluteness of the prelates and the people of that time, settled himself all the more firmly in our religion, considering how great must necessarily be the force and divinity of a religion that could maintain its dignity and splendour amid so much corruption, and in such vicious hands. If we had but a single grain of faith, we should move mountains from their places, says the sacred Word; our actions, then directed and accompanied by divinity, would not be merely human — they would have in them something of the miraculous, just as our belief would: _Brevis est institutio vitæ honestæ beataeque, si credas._ ["Believe, and the way to happiness and virtue is a short one."] Some people impose on the world that they believe what they do not; others, more numerous, make themselves believe that they believe, though they cannot get to the bottom of what believing actually is. We think it strange if, in the civil war that now troubles our state, we see events drift and vary in a common and ordinary fashion — but this is because we bring nothing to it but ourselves. Justice, which is on one side, is there only as ornament and palliation; it is alleged, indeed, but it is not really received, settled, and embraced. It is in the war as in the mouth of an advocate, not in the heart and affection of the party. God owes his extraordinary assistance to faith and religion, not to our passions. Men are the conductors here, using religion to serve their ends, whereas it ought to be the other way round. Observe whether it isn't with our own hands that we guide and train it, and pull it like wax into so many contrary figures, from a rule in itself so direct and firm. When and where was this more obvious than in France in our day? Those who took it on the left, those who took it on the right; those who call it black, those who call it white — all alike use it for their violent and ambitious designs, conducting it with a progress so similar in riot and injustice that they render doubtful and hard to credit the diversity they claim in their opinions on a thing on which the conduct and rule of our life depends. Did anyone ever see, coming from the same school and discipline, manners more uniform and more identical? Observe with what shocking impudence we toss divine arguments back and forth, and how irreligiously we have both rejected and retrieved them, according as fortune has shifted our places in these domestic storms.

This very solemn question — whether it is lawful for a subject to rebel and take up arms against his prince in defence of his religion — do you remember in whose mouths, only last year, the affirmative was the prop of one party and the negative the pillar of another? And listen now from which quarter the voice and instruction of each side now comes, and whether the arms make any less noise and rattle for this cause than for that. We condemn to the fire those who say that truth must be made to bear the yoke of our necessity — and how much worse does France do than say it? Let us confess the truth: whoever should pull out of the army (even the one raised by the king) those who take up arms out of pure zeal for religion, and also those who do so only to protect the laws of their country or to serve their prince, could hardly out of both put together make a single complete company of gendarmes. Where does it come from that there are so few who have maintained the same will and the same course in our civil commotions, and that we see them at one moment moving at a foot-pace and at the next running at full speed? — that the same men one moment damage our affairs by their violent heat and fierceness, and at the next by their coldness, gentleness, and slowness? — except that they are pushed on by particular and incidental considerations, varying with the directions in which they move?
I see clearly enough that we are willing to grant devotion only those offices that suit our own passions.

There is no hostility so remarkable as the Christian. Our zeal performs wonders when it seconds our inclinations to hatred, cruelty, ambition, avarice, slander, and rebellion; but when it moves against the grain, towards kindness, gentleness, and temperance — unless by some miracle a rare and virtuous disposition prompts us — we don't stir hand or foot. Our religion is meant to root out vices; instead it shields, nourishes, and incites them. We must not mock God. If we believed in him — I do not say by faith, but with a simple belief; that is to say (and I say it to our great shame), if we believed in him and recognized him as we do any other story, or as we would one of our companions — we should love him above all other things for the infinite goodness and beauty that shines in him. At the very least he would go equal in our affection with riches, pleasure, glory, and our friends. The best of us is not so afraid to outrage him as he is afraid to injure his neighbour, his kinsman, or his master. Is there any understanding so weak that, having on one side the object of one of our vicious pleasures and on the other (in equal knowledge and persuasion) the prospect of immortal glory, would trade the first for the second? And yet we often renounce it out of mere contempt: for what lust tempts us to blaspheme, if not, perhaps, the very desire to give offence? The philosopher Antisthenes, as he was being initiated into the mysteries of Orpheus, when the priest told him "that those who professed themselves of that religion were certain to receive perfect and eternal felicity after death," answered, "If you believe that, why don't you die yourself?" Diogenes, more bluntly in his usual manner and farther from our purpose, said to a priest who similarly preached to him to take up his religion in order to obtain the happiness of the other world, "What! you'd have me believe that Agesilaus and Epaminondas, who were so great, will be miserable, while you, who are nothing but a calf and can do nothing to the point, will be happy because you are a priest?" If we received these great promises of eternal blessedness with the same reverence and respect as we do a philosophical discourse, we should not hold death in such horror:
Non jam se moriens dissolvi conquereretur; / Sed magis ire foras, vestemque relinquere ut anguis, / Gauderet, prælonga senex aut cornua cervus.

["We should not on a deathbed grieve to be / Dissolved, but rather launch out cheerfully / From our old hut, and with the snake, be glad / To cast off the corrupted slough we had; / Or with the old stag rejoice to be now clear / From the large horns, too ponderous grown to bear."]

"I desire to be dissolved," we should say, "and to be with Jesus Christ." The force of Plato's arguments about the immortality of the soul drove some of his disciples to seek a premature grave, so that they might the sooner enjoy what he had given them to hope for.

All this is a very clear sign that we receive our religion only after our own fashion, by our own hands, no differently than other religions are received. Either we happen to live in the country where it is practised, or we revere the antiquity of it, or the authority of the men who have maintained it, or we fear the threats it hurls against unbelievers, or we are drawn by its promises. These considerations should indeed bear on our belief, but only as auxiliaries — they are human obligations. Another religion, other witnesses, similar promises and threats, might by the same path imprint quite the opposite belief. We are Christians by the same title as we are Périgordians or Germans. And what Plato says — that few men are so obstinate in their atheism that a pressing danger will not reduce them to an acknowledgment of the divine power — does not concern a true Christian: it belongs to mortal and human religions to be received by human recommendation. What sort of faith is it that cowardice and lack of courage establish in us? A pretty faith, that believes what it believes only for want of courage to disbelieve! Can a vicious passion such as inconstancy and panic produce any orderly result in our souls? "They are confident in their judgment," he says, "that what is said of hell and future torments is all made up. But when occasion arises to put their conviction to the test — when old age or disease brings them to the brink of the grave — the terror of death, through dread of that future condition, inspires them with a new belief." And because such impressions render them timorous, he forbids in his _Laws_ all such threatening doctrines, and all persuasion that any ill can come from the gods, except for our great good when it does, and for some medicinal effect. They say of Bion that, infected with the atheism of Theodorus, he had long held religious men in great scorn and contempt — but when death surprised him, he gave himself up to the most extreme superstition, as if the gods came and went according to Bion's needs. Plato and these examples would conclude that we are brought to belief in God either by reason or by force. Atheism being a proposition as unnatural as it is monstrous, also difficult and hard to establish in the human understanding however arrogant, men enough are seen — out of vanity and pride — to be the authors of extraordinary and reforming opinions, and to put on the outward profession of them; who, however foolish they may be, nevertheless have not the power to plant them in their own conscience. Still they will not fail to lift up their hands towards heaven if you give them a good thrust in the chest with a sword, and once fear or illness has cooled and dulled the licentious fury of that giddy humour, they will easily come round, and quite discreetly suffer themselves to be reconciled to the public faith and example. A doctrine seriously digested is one thing; those superficial impressions are another, which, springing from the disorder of an unhinged understanding, float at random in the mind with great uncertainty. Miserable and senseless men, who strive to be worse than they can.

The error of paganism and the ignorance of our sacred truth made this great soul of Plato — great only in human greatness — fall also into this other mistake, that children and old men are most susceptible to religion, as if it sprang up and drew its credit from our weakness. The knot that ought to bind judgment and will, that ought to restrain the soul and join it to its creator, should be a knot that draws its folds and strength not from our considerations, our reasons and passions, but from a divine and supernatural compulsion, having one form, one face, one lustre only, which is the authority of God and his divine grace. Now the heart and soul being governed and commanded by faith, it is only reasonable that they should marshal all our other faculties, according to their ability, to the service and assistance of faith's design. Nor is it to be imagined that all this machine has no marks imprinted on it by the hand of the mighty architect, and that there is not in the things of this world some image that in some measure resembles the workman who has built and formed them. In his stupendous works he has left the stamp of his divinity, and it is our own weakness alone that prevents us from seeing it. It is what he himself is pleased to tell us — that he manifests his invisible operations to us by those that are visible. Sebond set himself to this praiseworthy and noble study, and shows us that there is not a part or member of the world that disclaims its maker or derogates from him. It would do wrong to the divine goodness if the universe did not concur with our belief. The heavens, the earth, the elements, our bodies and our souls — all things contribute to it. We have only to find the way to use them; they instruct us, if we are capable of being instructed. For this world is a sacred temple, into which man is introduced, there to contemplate statues — not the works of a mortal hand, but such as the divine purpose has made the objects of sense: the sun, the stars, the water, the earth — to represent those things that are intelligible to us. "The invisible things of God," says Saint Paul, "appear by the creation of the world, his eternal wisdom and divinity being understood from his works."

And God himself envies not men the grace / Of seeing and admiring heaven's face; / But, rolling it about, he still anew / Presents its varied splendour to our view, / And on our minds himself inculcates, so / That we the Almighty mover well may know: / Instructing us by seeing him the cause / Of all, to reverence and obey his laws.

Now our prayers and human discourses are like raw and undigested matter. The grace of God is the form; it is what gives them fashion and value. As the virtuous actions of Socrates and Cato remain vain and fruitless for not having had the love and obedience of the true creator of all things, so it is with our imaginings and discourses: they have a kind of body, but it is a shapeless mass, without form and without light, if faith and grace are not added. Faith, coming to tint and illuminate Sebond's arguments, makes them firm and solid — so much so that they can serve as guidance, and as first guides to an elementary Christian, to put him on the path to this knowledge. They form him to some degree and render him capable of God's grace, by which means he afterwards completes and perfects himself in the true belief. I know a man of authority, brought up to letters, who has confessed to me that he was brought back from the errors of unbelief by Sebond's arguments. And should they be stripped of this ornament and of the support and approval of faith, and looked on as mere fancies only — to fight those who are thrown into the dreadful and horrible darkness of irreligion — they will even there be found as solid and firm as any others of the same sort that can be opposed to them, so that we shall be ready to say to our opponents:
Si melius quid habes, arcesse; vel imperium fer:
["If you have arguments more fit, / Produce them, or to these submit."]

— let them admit the force of our reasons, or let them show us others, on some other subject, better woven and of finer thread. I find myself, without meaning to, already half engaged in the second objection that I proposed to answer on Sebond's behalf. Some say his arguments are weak and unable to make good what he intends, and they take it on themselves, with great ease, to refute them. These need to be handled a little more roughly, for they are more dangerous and malicious than the first. Men willingly twist the sayings of others to favour their own prejudices. To an atheist, all writings tend to atheism: he corrupts the most innocent matter with his own venom. These people have judgments so preoccupied that they cannot relish Sebond's reasoning. For the rest, they think we give them fair play in giving them the liberty of fighting our religion with merely human weapons — religion which, in its majesty, full of authority and command, they would not dare attack. The means I shall use, and that I think most proper to subdue this madness, is to crush and trample underfoot pride and human arrogance; to make them feel the inanity, vanity, and worthlessness of man; to wrest the wretched weapons of their reason out of their hands; to make them bow down and bite the ground under the authority and reverence of the divine majesty. To that alone do knowledge and wisdom belong; that alone can make a true estimate of itself, and from it we filch whatever we pride ourselves on: [Greek] "God permits not any being but himself to be truly wise." Let us subdue this presumption, the first foundation of the tyranny of the evil spirit: _Deus superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam._ ["God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble."] "Understanding is in the gods," says Plato, "and not at all, or very little, in men." Now it is meanwhile a great consolation to a Christian to see our frail and mortal parts so well fitted to our holy and divine faith that, when we employ them on subjects of their own mortal and frail nature, they are not even there more fittingly or more firmly adjusted. Let us see, then, whether man has in his power any reasons more forcible and convincing than Sebond's — that is to say, whether it is in him to arrive at any certainty by argument and reason. For Saint Augustine, disputing with these people, had good cause to reproach them with injustice in maintaining that the part of our belief our reason cannot establish is false. And to show that many things may be — and have been — of which our nature could not sound out the reason and causes, he proposes to them certain known and undoubted experiments in which men confess they see nothing; and he does this, as he does everything, with curious and ingenious inquiry. We must do more than this, and make them know that, to demonstrate the weakness of their reason, there is no need to cull uncommon examples: that it is so defective and so blind that no subject is clear enough for it; that the easy and the hard are all one to it; that every subject equally, and nature in general, disclaims its authority and rejects its mediation.

What does truth mean when she preaches to us to flee worldly philosophy, when she so often urges on us that our wisdom is but folly in the sight of God; that the vainest of all vanities is man; that the man who presumes upon his wisdom does not yet know what wisdom is; and that man, who is nothing, deceives and seduces himself if he thinks he is anything? These sentences of the Holy Spirit so clearly and vividly express what I would maintain that I should need no other proof against men who would submit to his authority with all humility and obedience. But these men will have to be whipped at their own expense, and will not let a man oppose their reason except by itself.

Let us, then, for once consider a man alone, without foreign assistance, armed only with his own weapons, and stripped of the divine grace and wisdom that are all his honour, his strength, and the foundation of his being. Let us see how he stands in this fine equipment. Let him make me understand, by the force of his reason, on what foundations he has built the great advantages he thinks he has over other creatures. Who has made him believe that this admirable motion of the celestial arch, the eternal light of those luminaries that roll so high over his head, the wondrous and fearful motions of that infinite ocean, were established and continued so many ages for his service and convenience? Can anything be imagined so ridiculous as that this miserable and wretched creature, who is not even master of himself, but subject to the injuries of all things, should call himself master and emperor of the world, of which he has no power to know the least part, much less to command the whole? And as for the privilege he claims of being the only creature in this vast structure who has the understanding to discover the beauty and parts of it — the only one who can return thanks to the architect and keep the accounts of the world — I wonder who sealed him this patent. Let us see his commission for this great employment. Was it granted in favour of the wise alone? Few people will be concerned in it. Are fools and wicked persons worthy of so extraordinary a favour, and, being the worst part of the world, to be preferred to the rest? Shall we believe this man? "For whose sake, then, shall we conclude that the world was made? For those who have the use of reason: these are gods and men, than whom nothing certainly can be better." We can never sufficiently decry the impudence of this pairing. But, wretched creature, what does he have in himself worthy of such an advantage? Consider the incorruptible existence of the heavenly bodies, their beauty, magnitude, and continual revolution by so exact a rule;
Cum suspicimus magni cælestia mundi / Templa super, stellisque micantibus æthera fixum, / Et venit in mentem lunæ solisque viarum.
["When we the heavenly arch above behold, / And the vast sky adorned with stars of gold, / And mark the regular courses that the sun / And moon in their alternate progress run."]
Consider the dominion and influence those bodies have, not only over our lives and fortunes,
Facta etenim et vitas hominum suspendit ab astris;
["Men's lives and actions on the stars depend."]
but even over our inclinations, our thoughts and wills, which they govern, incite, and stir at the mercy of their influences, as our reason teaches us;

["Contemplating the stars he finds that they / Rule by a secret and a silent sway; / And that the enamelled spheres which roll above / Do ever by alternate causes move. / And, studying these, he can also foresee, / By certain signs, the turns of destiny."]
seeing that not only a man, not only kings, but monarchies, empires, and all this lower world follow the influence of the celestial motions,
["How great a change a little motion brings! / So great this kingdom is that governs kings."]

If our virtues, our vices, our knowledge, and even this very discourse we are now upon, of the power of the stars and the comparison we are making between them and us, proceed (as our reason supposes) from their favour;

["One mad in love may cross the raging main, / To level lofty Ilium with the plain; / Another's fate inclines him more by far / To study laws and statutes for the bar. / Sons kill their fathers, fathers kill their sons, / And one armed brother against another runs. / This war's not theirs, but fate's, that spurs them on / To shed the blood which, shed, they must bemoan; / And I ascribe it to the will of fate / That on this theme I now expatiate."]

if we derive this little portion of reason we have from the bounty of heaven, how is it possible for reason ever to make us equal to it? How can we subject its essence and condition to our knowledge? Whatever we see in those bodies astonishes us: _Quæ molitio, quæ ferramenta, qui vectes, quæ machinæ, qui ministri tanti operis fuerunt?_ ["What contrivance, what tools, what materials, what engines, were employed about so stupendous a work?"] Why do we deprive them of soul, life, and reason? Have we discovered in them any immovable or insensible stupidity — we who have no commerce with them but obedience? Shall we say that we have discovered the use of a reasonable soul in no other creature than man? What! have we seen anything like the sun? Does he cease to be because we have seen nothing like him? And do his motions cease because there are no other like them? If whatever we have not seen does not exist, our knowledge is marvellously contracted: _Quæ sunt tantæ animi angustiæ!_ ["How narrow are our understandings!"] Aren't they dreams of human vanity to make the moon into a celestial earth — to imagine mountains and valleys there, as Anaxagoras did; to fix habitations and human dwellings there, and plant colonies for our convenience, as Plato and Plutarch have done; and to make our own earth into a luminous and resplendent star? "Among the other inconveniences of mortality, this is one: that darkness of the understanding that leads men astray, not so much from a necessity of erring as from a love of error. The corruptible body stupefies the soul, and the earthly habitation dulls the faculties of the imagination."

Presumption is our natural and original disease. The most wretched and frail of all creatures is man, and also the proudest. He feels and sees himself lodged here in the dirt and filth of the world, nailed and riveted to the worst, deadest part of the universe, in the lowest storey of the house, the most remote from the heavenly arch, with animals of the worst condition of the three; and yet, in his imagination, he places himself above the circle of the moon and brings the heavens under his feet. By the same vanity of imagination he equals himself to God, attributes divine qualities to himself, withdraws and separates himself from the crowd of other creatures, parcels out the portions of the animals (his fellows and companions), and distributes to them portions of faculty and force as he himself thinks fit. How does he know, by the strength of his understanding, the secret and inner motions of animals? From what comparison between them and us does he conclude the stupidity he attributes to them? When I play with my cat, who knows whether I am not more her sport than she is mine? We mutually entertain each other with our play. If I have my hour to begin or to refuse, she has hers too. Plato, in his picture of the golden age under Saturn, lists among the chief advantages a man then had his communication with the beasts, from whom, asking and learning, he knew the true qualities and differences of them all, and by this acquired a very perfect intelligence and prudence, and led his life more happily than we can do. Do we need any better proof to condemn human impudence in the matter of beasts? This great author was of the opinion that nature, in the bodily form she gave them, had for the most part only had regard to the use of the prognostics derived from them in his time. The defect that hinders communication between them and us — why may it not be on our side as well as on theirs? It is still to be determined where the fault lies that we do not understand each other — for we understand them no more than they understand us; and by the same reasoning they may think us beasts as we think them. It is no great wonder if we do not understand them, when we do not understand a Basque or a Troglodyte. And yet some have boasted that they understood them — Apollonius of Tyana, Melampus, Tiresias, Thales, and others. And seeing, as cosmographers report, that there are nations who have a dog for their king, they must necessarily be able to interpret his voice and motions. We must observe the parity between us, have some tolerable understanding of their meaning, and let beasts have some of ours — about the same. They caress us, threaten us, and beg of us, and we do the same to them.

For the rest, we plainly see that they have a full and absolute communication among themselves, and that they perfectly understand one another — not only those of the same species, but of different kinds:

["The tamer herds, and wilder sort of brutes, / Though we of higher race conclude them mutes, / Yet utter dissonant and various notes, / From gentler lungs or more distended throats, / As fear, or grief, or anger, do them move, / Or as they do approach the joys of love."]

In one kind of barking of a dog the horse knows there is anger; another sort of bark does not frighten him. Even in the very beasts that have no voice at all, we easily conclude, from the network of offices we observe among them, that there is some other kind of communication: their very motions show it.
["As infants who, for want of words, devise / Expressive motions with their hands and eyes."]

And why not, as well as our dumb people, dispute, argue, and tell stories by signs? I have seen some so skilled and active in this by practice that in fact they lacked nothing of the perfection of making themselves understood. Lovers are angry, are reconciled, entreat, thank, make appointments, in short say everything by their eyes:
["Even silence in a lover / Love and passion can discover."]

What about the hands? We request, promise, call, dismiss, threaten, pray, supplicate, deny, refuse, question, marvel, count, confess, repent, fear, express confusion, doubt, instruct, command, urge, encourage, swear, testify, accuse, condemn, absolve, abuse, despise, defy, provoke, flatter, applaud, bless, submit, mock, reconcile, recommend, exalt, entertain, congratulate, complain, grieve, despair, wonder, exclaim — what not! And all this with a variety and multiplicity that rivals speech. With the head we invite, dismiss, confess, deny, give the lie, welcome, honour, revere, disdain, demand, rejoice, lament, refuse, caress, rebuke, submit, swagger, encourage, threaten, assure, and inquire. What of the eyebrows? What of the shoulders? There is not a motion that does not speak, and in an intelligible language without instruction, a public language that everyone understands — from which it should follow, considering the variety and use that distinguishes them from other gestures, that these rather should be judged the property of human nature. I leave out what necessity in particular suddenly suggests to those in need: alphabets traced on fingers, grammars in gesture, and the sciences that are exercised and expressed only through them, and the nations which Pliny reports have no other language. An ambassador of the city of Abdera, after a long conference with Agis, King of Sparta, asked him, "Well, sir, what answer am I to take back to my fellow citizens?" "That I have given you leave," he said, "to say what you would, and as much as you would, without ever speaking a word." Is this not a silent speech, and very easy to understand?

For the rest, what is there in us that we do not see in the operations of animals? Is there a polity better ordered, the offices better distributed and more inviolably observed and maintained, than that of bees? Can we imagine that such an orderly distribution of employments could be carried out without reasoning and deliberation?
["Hence to the bee some sages have assigned / Some portion of the god and heavenly wind."]

The swallows we see at the return of spring, searching every corner of our houses for the most suitable places to build their nest — do they seek without judgment, and out of a thousand choose the most proper for their purpose without discretion? And in the elegant and admirable structure of their buildings, can birds choose a square figure rather than a round, an obtuse angle rather than a right one, without knowing the properties and effects? Do they bring water, then clay, without knowing that clay's hardness softens when wetted? Do they line their palace with moss or down without foreseeing that their tender young will lie there more safely and easily? Do they shelter themselves from the wet and rainy winds, placing their lodgings against the east, without knowing the different qualities of the winds and considering that one is more wholesome than another? Why does the spider make her web tighter in one place and slacker in another? why now make one sort of knot, then another, if she has no deliberation, thought, and conclusion? We sufficiently see in most of their works how much animals excel us, and how incapable our art is of imitating them. We see, nevertheless, in our cruder performances, that we employ all our faculties and apply the utmost power of our souls. Why do we not conclude the same of them?

Why should we attribute to I know not what natural and servile inclination the works that surpass all we can do by nature and art? In doing so, without realizing it, we give them a huge advantage over us — making nature, with maternal gentleness and love, accompany and lead them, as it were by the hand, to all the actions and conveniences of their lives, while she leaves us to chance and fortune, to seek by art the things necessary for our survival, while at the same time denying us the means of being able, by any instruction or effort of the understanding, to reach the natural sufficiency of beasts. Their brutish stupidity thus surpasses in every convenience all that our divine intelligence can do. Really, at this rate, we might with great reason call her an unjust stepmother. But it isn't so; our polity is not so irregular and unformed.

Nature has cared universally for all her creatures, and there is not one she has not amply furnished with all the means necessary for the preservation of its being. As to the common complaints I hear men make (since the licence of their opinions one moment lifts them up above the clouds and then again pushes them down to the antipodes) — that we are the only animal abandoned naked on the bare earth, tied and bound, having nothing to arm or clothe ourselves but by the spoils of others, whereas nature has covered every other creature with shells, husks, bark, hair, wool, prickles, leather, down, feathers, scales, or silk, according to the needs of their being; has armed them with claws, teeth, or horns for assault and defence; and has herself taught them what is most proper for them — to swim, to run, to fly, and to sing — whereas man does not know how to walk, speak, eat, or do anything but weep without being taught:

["Like to the wretched mariner, when tossed / By raging seas upon the desert coast, / The tender babe lies naked on the earth, / Of all supports of life stripped by his birth; / When nature first presents him to the day, / Freed from the cell wherein before he lay, / He fills the ambient air with doleful cries, / Foretelling thus life's future miseries; / But beasts, both wild and tame, greater and less, / Do of themselves in strength and bulk increase; / They need no rattle, nor the broken chat / By which the nurse first teaches boys to prate; / They look not out for different robes to wear, / According to the seasons of the year; / And need no arms nor walls their goods to save, / Since earth and liberal nature ever have, / And will, in all abundance, still produce / All things whereof they can have need or use."]

— these complaints are false. There is in the polity of the world a greater equality, and a more uniform relation. Our skins are as well able to defend us from the injuries of the weather as theirs — witness several nations that still do not know the use of clothes. Our ancient Gauls were but lightly clad, and so are the Irish our neighbours, though in so cold a climate. But we can judge better of this by ourselves: all the parts we choose to expose to the air are found very able to endure it — face, feet, hands, arms, head, depending on the customary dress; if there is a tender part about us that would seem to be in danger from the cold, it should be the stomach where digestion happens, and yet our forefathers always went open there, and our ladies, as delicate and tender as they are, sometimes go half-bare as low as the navel. The binding and swaddling of infants is no more necessary either — and the Lacedaemonian mothers brought theirs up in all liberty of motion of their limbs, with no swaddling at all. Our crying is shared with most other animals; there are few creatures that are not observed to groan and lament for a long time after coming into the world, since it is a behaviour suited to the weakness in which they find themselves. As for the habit of eating, it is in us, as in them, natural, and without instruction:
["For everyone soon finds his natural force, / Which he may better or worse employ."]

Who doubts that an infant, once it has reached strength enough to feed itself, can manage to find something to eat? The earth produces and offers him what he needs, without other cultivation or artifice; and if not at all times, no more does she do for the beasts — witness the provision we see ants and other creatures hoard up against the dead seasons of the year. The recently discovered nations, so abundantly furnished with natural food and drink, without effort or cookery, may give us to understand that bread is not our only food, and that, without tillage, our mother nature has provided us with all we need — indeed, more fully and plentifully than she does at present, now that we have added our own industry:

["The earth did first spontaneously afford / Choice fruits and wines to furnish out the board; / With herbs and flow'rs unsown in verdant fields. / But scarce by art so good a harvest yields; / Though men and oxen mutually have strove, / With all their utmost force the soil to improve."]
— the debauchery and irregularity of our appetites outpaces all the inventions we can contrive to satisfy them.

As for arms, we have more natural ones than most other animals: more various motions of limbs, and, naturally and without lesson, get more service from them. Those who are trained to fight naked are seen to throw themselves into the same hazards we do. If some beasts surpass us in this advantage, we surpass many others. And the practice of fortifying the body and covering it by acquired means — don't we have it by instinct and natural precept? That it is so the elephant shows: he sharpens and whets the teeth he uses in war (for he has particular ones for that service which he spares, never employing them for any other use). When bulls go to fight, they toss and throw the dust about them; boars whet their tusks; the ichneumon, when about to engage with the crocodile, fortifies his body and covers and crusts it all over with close-wrought, well-tempered slime, as with a cuirass. Why shall we not say it is also natural for us to arm ourselves with wood and iron?

As for speech, it is certain that if it is not natural, it is not necessary. Nevertheless, I believe that a child brought up in absolute solitude, remote from all society of men (which would be an experiment very hard to make), would have some kind of speech to express his meaning. And it is not to be supposed that nature should have denied to us what she has given to several other animals — for what is this faculty we observe in them, of complaining, rejoicing, calling to one another for help, and inviting each other to love, which they do with the voice, other than speech? And why should they not speak to one another? They speak to us, and we to them. In how many various ways do we speak to our dogs, and they answer us? We converse with them in another sort of language and use other names than we do with birds, hogs, oxen, horses; and we alter the idiom according to the kind.
["Thus from one swarm of ants some sally out, / To spy another's stock or mark its rout."]

Lactantius seems to attribute to beasts not only speech but laughter too. And the difference of language found among us, according to the difference of countries, is also observed in animals of the same kind. Aristotle, by way of proof, cites the various calls of partridges, according to the situation of places:
["And various birds do from their warbling throats / At various times utter quite different notes, / And some their hoarse songs with the seasons change."]

But it is still to be known what language this child would speak; and what is said about it is so much guesswork that it has no great show. If anyone alleges against my opinion that those who are naturally deaf do not speak, I answer that this is not only because they could not receive the instruction of speech by ear, but rather because the sense of hearing, of which they are deprived, is connected to the sense of speech, and the two hold together by a natural and inseparable tie — so that what we speak we must first speak to ourselves within, and make it sound in our own ears, before we can utter it to others.

All this I have said to prove the resemblance there is in human things, and to bring us back and rejoin us to the crowd. We are neither above nor below the rest. Everything under heaven, says the sage, runs by one law and one fate:
["All things remain / Bound and entangled in one fatal chain."]
There is, indeed, some difference — there are several orders and degrees; but it is under the aspect of one and the same nature:
["All things by their own rites proceed, and draw / Towards their ends, by nature's certain law."]

Man must be compelled and restrained within the bounds of this polity. Miserable creature! he is not really in any condition to step over the rail. He is fettered and circumscribed, he is subject to the same necessity that the other creatures of his rank and order are, and his condition is a very modest one, without any prerogative of true and real pre-eminence. What he attributes to himself, by vain fancy and opinion, has neither body nor taste. And if it is so that he alone, of all the animals, has this freedom of imagination and irregularity of thought — representing to himself what is, what is not, what he would have, the false and the true — it is an advantage dearly bought, and one of which he has very little reason to be proud, for from it springs the principal and original source of all the evils that befall him: sin, sickness, irresolution, affliction, despair. To return to my subject, I say there is no plausible reason to make a man believe that beasts should, by a natural and forced inclination, do the same things that we do by our choice and industry. From like effects we should conclude like faculties, and from greater effects greater faculties, and consequently confess that the same reasoning, and the same procedures by which we operate, are common to them — or that they have others that are better. Why should we imagine in them this natural constraint, when we experience no such effect in ourselves? Add that it is more honourable to be guided and obliged to act regularly by a natural and inevitable condition, and to be more closely akin to divinity, than to act regularly by a reckless and chance liberty; and that it is safer to entrust the reins of our conduct to the hand of nature than to our own. The vanity of our presumption makes us prefer to owe our sufficiency to our own exertions rather than to her bounty, and to enrich the other animals with natural goods and renounce them in their favour, in order to honour and ennoble ourselves with acquired goods — very foolishly in my opinion, for I should value just as much parts and virtues that were naturally and purely my own as those I had begged and obtained from education. It is not in our power to obtain a nobler reputation than to be favoured of God and nature.

For instance, take the fox the people of Thrace use when they want to cross the ice of some frozen river. They send him out before them for that purpose; when we see him lay his ear on the bank of the river, down to the ice, listening to hear whether the noise of the running water comes from farther or nearer, and according to what he hears determining the ice to be thicker or thinner, in order to retreat or advance — have we not reason to believe that the same rational thoughts pass through his head that would pass through ours on the like occasion? And that it is a reasoning, drawn by inference from natural sense — that whatever makes a noise runs, whatever runs is not frozen, whatever is not frozen is liquid, and whatever is liquid yields to weight? To attribute this to a mere keenness of hearing, without reason and inference, is a chimera that cannot enter the imagination. We should think the same of the many kinds of subtleties and inventions by which beasts protect themselves from, and frustrate, the schemes we plot against them.

And if we take advantage of the fact that it is in our power to seize them, to put them to our service, and to use them at our pleasure, it is still only the same advantage we have over one another. We have our slaves on these terms. The Climacides — were they not women in Syria who, squatting on all fours, served as a ladder or footstool for the ladies to mount their coaches? And the majority of free persons surrender, for very trivial conveniences, their life and being into the power of another. The wives and concubines of the Thracians fought over who should be chosen to be slain on their husband's tomb. Have tyrants ever lacked men devoted enough to their service? Some of them moreover added this requirement, that their followers accompany them in death as well as in life. Whole armies have bound themselves in this way to their captains. The form of the oath in the harsh school of gladiators ran in these words: "We swear to suffer ourselves to be chained, burnt, wounded, and killed with the sword, and to endure all that true gladiators suffer from their master, engaging both body and soul religiously in his service."
Ure meum, si vis, flamma caput, et pete ferro / Corpus, et intorto verbere terga seca.
["Wound me with steel, or burn my head with fire, / Or scourge my shoulders with well-twisted wire."]

This was an obligation indeed, and yet in one year ten thousand entered into it, to their destruction. When the Scythians buried their king they strangled, on top of his body, the most beloved of his concubines, his cup-bearer, the master of his horse, his chamberlain, the usher of his chamber, and his cook. And on the anniversary of the burial they killed fifty horses, mounted by fifty pages whom they had impaled up the spine to the throat, and left them fixed in triumph around his tomb. The men who serve us do it more cheaply, and for less careful and favourable treatment than what we give our hawks, horses, and dogs. To what trouble do we not put ourselves for the conveniences of these? I do not believe that servants of the most abject condition would willingly do for their masters what princes are pleased to do for their beasts. Diogenes, seeing his relatives anxious to redeem him from servitude, said, "They are fools; it is the man who keeps and feeds me who really serves me." And those who maintain beasts ought rather to be said to serve them than to be served by them. And withal in this the beasts have something more generous, in that no lion has ever submitted to another lion, nor one horse to another, for want of courage. As we hunt beasts, so tigers and lions hunt men, and do the same execution on one another — dogs on hares, pikes on tench, swallows on grasshoppers, sparrow-hawks on blackbirds and larks:

["The stork with snakes and lizards from the wood / And pathless wilds supports her callow brood, / While Jove's own eagle, bird of noble blood, / Scours the wide country for undaunted food; / Sweeps the swift hare or swifter fawn away, / And feeds her nestlings with the generous prey."]

We divide the quarry, as well as the labour of the chase, with our hawks and hounds. And around Amphipolis in Thrace, hawkers and wild falcons divide the prey in equal halves. As also along Lake Maeotis, if the fisherman does not honestly leave the wolves an equal share of what he has caught, they go at once and tear his nets to pieces. And as we have a way of hunting carried on more by subtlety than by force — flushing hares, angling with line and hook — so there is the like among other animals. Aristotle says the cuttlefish casts a gut out of her throat as long as a line, which she extends and draws back at pleasure; and as she perceives some little fish approaching, she lets it nibble at the end of this gut, while she lies hidden in the sand or mud, and little by little draws it in until the little fish is so near her that with one spring she catches it.

As for strength, no creature in the world is exposed to so many injuries as man. We don't need a whale, an elephant, a crocodile, or any such animal — any one of which is enough to dispatch a great number of men — to do our business: lice are enough to vacate Sylla's dictatorship, and the heart and life of a great and triumphant emperor is the breakfast of a little contemptible worm.

Why should we say that only man, by knowledge built up through art and meditation, can distinguish things useful to his being and proper for the cure of his diseases from those which are not — that only he can know the virtues of rhubarb and polypody? When we see the goats of Candia, when wounded with an arrow, choose dittany out of a million of plants for their cure; the tortoise, when she has eaten a viper, immediately go out to look for origanum to purge herself; the dragon to rub and clear his eyes with fennel; the storks to give themselves enemas of seawater; the elephants to draw the darts and javelins thrown at them in battle not only out of their own bodies, and out of the bodies of their companions, but even out of the bodies of their masters (witness the elephant of King Porus whom Alexander defeated), and to do so with such dexterity that we ourselves could not do it with so little pain to the patient — why do we not say that this too is knowledge and reason? To allege, to their disparagement, that it is by the sole instruction and dictate of nature that they know all this is not to take away from them the dignity of knowledge and reason, but with greater force to attribute it to them than to us, for the honour of so infallible a mistress. Chrysippus, though in other respects as scornful a judge of the condition of animals as any other philosopher whatsoever, considering the movements of a dog who comes to a place where three roads meet — whether hunting for his lost master, or in pursuit of some game that flies before him — sniffing first one of the ways, then another, and after having made sure of two without finding the trace of what he seeks, dashing into the third without examination, was forced to confess that this reasoning was in the dog: "I have traced my master to this place; he must of necessity have gone one of these three ways; he is not gone this way nor that, he must then infallibly be gone this other." And assuring himself by this conclusion, he makes no use of his nose in the third way, nor ever lays it to the ground, but lets himself be carried on by the force of reason. This piece of pure logic — this use of propositions divided and joined, this proper enumeration of parts — is it not every bit as good that the dog should know all this of himself as from Trapezuntius?

Animals are not incapable of being instructed in our method, however. We teach blackbirds, ravens, magpies, and parrots to speak; and the ease with which we see them lend us their voices, and render their breath and tongue so supple and pliable as to be formed and confined within a certain number of letters and syllables, proves that they have a reason within them that makes them so docile and willing to learn. Everyone, I believe, is sick of the various tricks tumblers teach their dogs — the dances, where they miss not a single cadence of the sound they hear; the various motions and leaps they make them perform at the command of a word. But I observe with the greatest admiration this effect, which is in any case very common, in the dogs that lead the blind, both in the country and in the cities. I have noticed how they stop at certain doors where they are accustomed to receive alms; how they avoid the path of coaches and carts, even where they have room enough to pass; I have seen them, by the trench of a town, abandon a plain and even path and take a worse one, only to keep their masters further from the ditch. How could a man have made this dog understand that it was his office to look after his master's safety only, and to despise his own convenience to serve him? And how did he know that a path was wide enough for him that was not so for a blind man? Can all this be understood without reasoning?

I must not omit what Plutarch says he saw of a dog at Rome, with the Emperor Vespasian the father, at the theatre of Marcellus. This dog was the assistant of a player who was performing a farce of several parts and characters, in which the dog had his part. Among other things, he had to pretend, for some time, to be dead from a certain drug he was supposed to have eaten. After he had swallowed a piece of bread that passed for the drug, he began after a while to tremble and stagger, as if taken giddy; at last, stretching himself out stiff as if dead, he suffered himself to be drawn and dragged from place to place, as was his role; and afterwards, when he sensed that it was time, he began first to stir gently, as if waking out of a profound sleep, and lifting up his head looked about him in such a way that astonished all the spectators.

The oxen used in the royal gardens of Susa, to water them and turn certain great wheels for that purpose, to which buckets were fastened (such as one sees in many places in Languedoc) — being ordered to draw a hundred turns each a day — were so accustomed to this number that no force could make them draw one turn more; their task done, they would suddenly stop and stand still. We are nearly grown men before we can count to a hundred, and have lately discovered nations that have no notion of numbers at all.

More understanding is required in the teaching of others than in being taught. Now, setting aside what Democritus held and proved — that most of the arts we have were taught us by other animals (weaving and sewing by the spider; building by the swallow; music by the swan and nightingale; and the making of medicines by various animals) — Aristotle is of opinion that nightingales teach their young to sing, and spend much time and care doing so; whence it happens that those we bring up in cages, and which have not had time to learn from their parents, lack much of the grace of their singing. We may judge by this that they improve by discipline and study; and even among the wild, it is not the case that all alike — each has learned to do better or worse, according to his capacity. And they are so jealous of each other while learning that they compete with rivalry, and with such a vigorous competition that sometimes the loser falls dead on the spot, the breath failing sooner than the voice. The younger ones ruminate pensively and begin to mutter some broken notes; the pupil listens to the master's lesson, and gives the best account he is able; they fall silent by turns; one hears faults corrected, and may observe certain rebukes from the teacher. "I once saw," says Arrian, "an elephant with a cymbal hung at each leg, and another fastened to his trunk, at the sound of which all the others danced round about him, rising and bending at certain cadences as they were guided by the instrument; and it was delightful to hear this harmony." In the spectacles of Rome elephants were commonly seen taught to move and dance to the sound of the voice, in dances with several changes and cadences very hard to learn. And some have been known to be so intent on their lesson as to practise it privately by themselves, so as not to be scolded or beaten by their masters.

But this other story about the magpie — for which we have Plutarch himself as warrant — is very strange. She lived in a barber's shop in Rome, and did wonders in imitating with her voice whatever she heard. It happened one day that some trumpeters stood a good while sounding in front of the shop. After that, and all the next day, the magpie was pensive, silent, and melancholy, at which everyone wondered, supposing the noise of the trumpets had so stunned and astonished her that her voice was gone along with her hearing. But it turned out at last that this was a profound meditation, a turning inwards, her thoughts working and preparing her voice to imitate the sound of those trumpets — so that the first voice she uttered was a perfect imitation of their strains, stops, and changes, having by this new lesson dropped and held in disdain all she had learned before.

I will not leave out this other example of a dog, also from Plutarch (I am muddling all order, but I do not aim at arrangement here any more than anywhere else throughout my book). Plutarch says he saw it aboard a ship. This dog, being puzzled how to get the oil at the bottom of a jar, which he could not reach with his tongue because of the narrow mouth of the vessel, went and fetched stones and dropped them into the jar until he made the oil rise high enough for him to reach it. What is this but the effect of a very subtle capacity? It is said the ravens of Barbary do the same when the water they would drink is too low. This action is somewhat akin to what Juba, a king of their nation, reports of elephants: that when, by the cunning of the hunter, one of them is trapped in certain deep pits prepared for them and covered over with brush to deceive them, all the rest bring in great diligence many stones and logs of wood to raise the bottom so he may get out. But this animal in several other effects approaches so close to human capacity that, if I were to recount all that experience has shown of them, I should easily get granted what I usually maintain: that there is more difference between this man and that than between this beast and this man. The keeper of an elephant in a private house in Syria robbed him at every meal of half his ration. One day his master came to feed him himself, and poured the full measure of barley that he had ordered for his allowance into his manger; the elephant, casting an angry look at the keeper, separated the one half from the other with his trunk and pushed it aside, declaring in this way the wrong done him. And another elephant, whose keeper mixed stones in with his corn to make up the measure, went to the pot where the keeper was boiling meat for his own dinner and filled it with ashes. These are particular cases. But what all the world has seen, and all the world knows, is that in all the armies of the Levant one of the greatest forces consisted in elephants, with which they did, without comparison, far greater execution than we do now with our artillery — which roughly takes their place on a day of battle (as may easily be supposed by those well read in ancient history);

["The sires of these huge animals were wont / The Carthaginian Hannibal to mount; / Our leaders also did these beasts bestride, / And mounted thus Pyrrhus his foes defied; / Nay, more, upon their backs they used to bear / Castles with armed cohorts to the war."]

They must necessarily have placed great confidence in the fidelity and understanding of these beasts when they entrusted them with the vanguard of a battle, where the least stop they should make, on account of the bulk and weight of their bodies, and the least fright that might have turned them on their own people, would have been enough to spoil everything; and there are few examples of their having fallen on their own troops, whereas we ourselves break into our own battalions and rout one another. They were charged not with a single simple movement only, but with several different things to be performed in battle — as the Spaniards did with their dogs in their new conquest of the Indies, to whom they gave pay and allowed them a share in the spoil; and those animals showed as much dexterity and judgment in pursuing victory and breaking off pursuit, in charging and retreating as occasion required, and in telling friends from enemies, as they did ardour and ferocity.

We marvel at and value things more when they are rare and strange than those of ordinary observation. I would not else have dwelt so long on these examples, for I believe whoever shall observe carefully what we usually see among the animals we have at home may find as wonderful effects as those we seek in remote countries and ages. It is one and the same nature that runs her course, and whoever has sufficiently considered the present state of things might certainly conclude as to both future and past. I have at times seen men brought here by sea from very distant countries, whose language we did not understand, and whose appearance, expression, and dress were quite different from ours; which of us did not consider them savages and brutes? Who did not attribute it to stupidity and lack of common sense to see them mute, ignorant of French, ignorant of our greetings and bows, our bearing and behaviour — from which all human nature must take its pattern and example? Everything that seems strange to us, and that we do not understand, we condemn. The same thing happens in the judgments we make about beasts. They have several conditions like ours; from these, by comparison, we may draw some conjecture; but by the qualities particular to themselves, how do we know what to make of them? Horses, dogs, oxen, sheep, birds, and most of the animals that live among us know our voices, and let themselves be governed by them. So did Crassus's lamprey, which came when he called it; so do the eels found in Lake Arethusa; and I have seen several ponds where the fish come to eat at a certain call from those who feed them.
["They every one have names, and one and all / Straightway appear at their own master's call."]

We may judge that. We may also say that elephants have some participation in religion, since after various washings and purifications they are observed to lift up their trunks like arms, and, fixing their eyes towards the rising sun, continue long in meditation and contemplation, at certain hours of the day, of their own motion, without instruction or precept. But because we do not see any such signs in other animals, we cannot for that reason conclude that they are without religion, nor make any judgment about what is concealed from us. As we discern something in this action that the philosopher Cleanthes took note of, because it somewhat resembles our own. He saw, he says, "Ants going from their anthill carrying the dead body of an ant towards another anthill, from which several other ants came out to meet them, as if to confer with them; where, after they had been together a while, the last ants returned to consult (one may suppose) with their fellow citizens, and so made two or three journeys, on account of the difficulty of the negotiation. In the end, the last comers brought to the first a worm out of their burrow, as if for the ransom of the dead one, which the first laid upon their backs and carried home, leaving the dead body to the others." This was the interpretation Cleanthes gave of this transaction, giving us to understand by it that those creatures that have no voice are nevertheless not without intercourse and mutual communication — that it is through our own defect that we don't share in it, and that for that reason we foolishly take it on ourselves to pass our censure on them. But they produce effects far beyond our capacity, which we are so far from being able to arrive at by imitation that we cannot even conceive them by imitation. Many are of the opinion that in the great and last naval engagement that Antony lost to Augustus, his flagship galley was stopped in mid-course by the little fish the Latins call _remora_, because of its property of stopping all sorts of vessels to which it attaches itself. And the Emperor Caligula, sailing with a great navy along the coast of Romania, had his galley alone suddenly stopped by the same fish, which he caused to be taken, fastened as it was to the keel of his ship, very angry that such a little animal could resist the sea, the wind, and the force of all his oars, by being only fastened by the beak to his galley (for it is a shellfish); and was moreover, not without good reason, astonished that, being brought to him in the vessel, it no longer had the strength it had outside. A citizen of Cyzicus once acquired the reputation of a good mathematician for having learned the quality of the hedgehog: it has its burrow open in different places and to several winds, and, foreseeing the wind that is to come, stops the hole on that side. That citizen, observing this, gave the city certain predictions of the wind that was presently to blow. The chameleon takes its colour from the place on which it lies; but the polypus gives himself whatever colour he pleases, as occasion serves, either to conceal himself from what he fears or from what he plans to seize: in the chameleon it is a passive change, but in the polypus it is an active one. We have some changes of colour, as in fear, anger, shame, and other passions, that alter our complexions; but it is by the effect of being acted upon, as with the chameleon. It is in the power of jaundice, indeed, to make us turn yellow, but not in the power of our own will. Now these effects we discover in other animals, much greater than ours, suggest some more excellent faculty in them, unknown to us — as it is to be presumed there are several other qualities and abilities of theirs, of which no signs have reached us.

Among all the predictions of earlier times, the most ancient and the most certain were those taken from the flight of birds. We have nothing certain like it, nor anything to be so much admired. That rule and order of the moving of the wing, from which they drew consequences as to future things, must necessarily be guided by some excellent means, to so noble an operation; for to attribute this great effect to some natural disposition, without the intelligence, consent, and meditation of the agent producing it, is an opinion plainly false. That it is so, the cramp-fish has this quality: not only does it numb all the members that touch her, but even through the nets transmits a heavy dullness to the hands of those who move and handle them; and it is further said that if one pours water on her, the numbness will be felt climbing up the water to the hand, and stupefying the feeling through the water. This is a marvellous force; but it is not useless to the cramp-fish — she knows it, and uses it; for, to catch the prey she desires, she will bury herself in the mud, so that other fish swimming over her, struck and benumbed by her coldness, may fall into her power. Cranes, swallows, and other birds of passage, by shifting their abode according to the seasons, sufficiently show the knowledge they have of their divinatory faculty, and put it to use. Huntsmen assure us that to choose, from among many puppies, the one that should be kept as the best, the best way is to refer the choice to the mother: thus, take them and carry them out of the kennel, and the first she brings back will certainly be the best; or if you make as if you would surround the kennel with fire, the one she first snatches up to save. From this it appears that they have a sort of prognostic that we lack — or that they have some other virtue in judging their offspring, more certain than any we have.

The manner of coming into the world, of generating, of nourishing, of acting, moving, living, and dying of the beasts is so close to ours that whatever we subtract from the causes that move them, and add to our own condition above theirs, can in no way proceed from any meditation of our own reason. For the regulation of our health, physicians propose to us the example of the animals' habits and way of life; for this saying (from Plutarch) has at all times been in the mouth of these people: "Keep your feet and head warm; for the rest, live like a beast."

The chief of all natural actions is generation; we have a certain disposition of members that is the most proper to that end; and yet Lucretius orders us to conform to the gesture and posture of the brutes as the most effective:
More ferarum, / Quadrupedumque magis ritu, plerumque putantur / Concipere uxores: quia sic loca sumere possunt, / Pectoribus positis, sublatis semina lumbis;

and the same authority condemns, as harmful, those indiscreet and shameless motions that the women have added of their own invention, to whom it proposes the more temperate and modest pattern and practice of the beasts of their own sex:

Nam mulier prohibet se concipere atque repugnat, / Clunibus ipsa viri Venerem si læta retractet, / Atque exossato ciet omni pectore fluctus. / Ejicit enim sulci recta regione viaque / Vomerem, atque locis avertit seminis ictum.

If it is justice to give everyone his due, the beasts that serve, love, and defend their benefactors, and pursue and fall on strangers and those who offend them, represent in this something of our justice; as also in observing a very equitable equality in the distribution of what they have to their young. And as for friendship, they have it incomparably more lively and constant than men do. King Lysimachus's dog, Hyrcanus, his master being dead, lay on his bed, stubbornly refusing either to eat or drink; and on the day his body was burned, he took a run and leaped into the fire, where he was consumed. So did the dog of one Pyrrhus, for he would not stir from his master's bed from the time he died; and when they carried his master away, he let himself be carried with him, and at last leaped into the pile where they burned his master's body. There are inclinations of affection that sometimes spring up in us, without consulting reason, by a fortuitous impulse that others call sympathy; beasts are as capable of this as we are. We see horses take such an acquaintance with one another that we have great difficulty making them eat or travel when separated. We observe them to favour a particular colour in those of their own kind, and where they meet it, they run to it with great joy and demonstrations of goodwill, and have a dislike and hatred for some other colour. Animals have choice, as we do, in their loves, and pick out their mistresses; neither are they exempt from our jealousies and implacable malice.

Desires are either natural and necessary, like eating and drinking; or natural and not necessary, like the coupling with females; or neither natural nor necessary — of which last sort are almost all the desires of men, all superfluous and artificial. For it is marvellous how little will satisfy nature, how little she has left us to desire; our stews and fancy dishes are not of her ordering. The Stoics say that a man may live on an olive a day. The delicacy of our wines is no part of her instruction, nor are the refinements we introduce into the indulgence of our amorous appetites:
Neque illa / Magno prognatum deposcit consule cunnum.
["Nature, in her pursuit of love, disclaims / The pride of titles, and the pomp of names."]

These irregular desires that ignorance of the good, and false opinion, have infused into us are so many that they almost shut out all natural ones — just as if there were such a number of strangers in a city as to push out the natural inhabitants, or, usurping their ancient rights and privileges, to extinguish their authority and introduce new laws and customs of their own. Animals are much more regular than we, and keep themselves with greater moderation within the limits nature has prescribed; but yet not so exactly that they have not at times an analogy with our debauches.
