And as there have been furious desires that have driven men to the love of beasts, so there have been examples of beasts that have fallen in love with us, and have conceived monstrous affections across kinds: witness the elephant who was rival to Aristophanes the grammarian in the love of a young herb-girl in the city of Alexandria, who did not lag behind him in any office of a very passionate suitor — for, passing through the market where they sold fruit, he would take some in his trunk and carry it to her. He would keep her as much as possible always in his sight, and would sometimes put his trunk under her handkerchief into her bosom to feel her breasts. They also tell of a dragon in love with a girl; of a goose enamoured of a child; of a ram who was suitor to the minstrel Glaucia, in the town of Asopus; and we see, not infrequently, baboons furiously in love with women. We also see certain male animals who are fond of the males of their own kind. Oppian and others give us some examples of the reverence beasts have for their own kindred in copulation; but experience often shows us the opposite:
Nec habetur turpe juvencæ / Ferre patrem tergo; fit equo sua filia conjux; / Quasque creavit, init pecudes caper; ipsaque cujus / Semine concepta est, ex illo concipit ales.

["The heifer thinks it not a shame to take / Her lusty sire upon her willing back: / The horse his daughter leaps, goats scruple not / To increase the herd by those they have begot; / And birds of all sorts do in common live, / And by the seed they have conceived conceive."]

And for subtle cunning, can there be a more telling example than the philosopher Thales's mule? Fording a river, loaded with salt, and stumbling there by accident so that the sacks he carried were all wet, he perceived that the melting of the salt made his burden somewhat lighter. From then on, whenever he came to a river, he never failed to lie down with his load — until his master, discovering the trick, ordered him to be loaded with wool, on which, finding himself mistaken, he gave up the device. There are several beasts that very vividly represent the true image of our avarice; for we see them infinitely solicitous to gather all they can, and to hide it with the greatest care, even though they never make any use of it at all. As for thrift, they surpass us not only in foresight, in laying up and saving for the time to come, but they have moreover much of the science necessary for it. The ants bring out into the sun their grain and seed to air, freshen, and dry them, when they perceive them growing mouldy and musty, lest they should decay and rot. But the caution and prevention they use in gnawing their grains of wheat surpass all imagination of human prudence; for since the wheat does not always remain sound and dry, but grows soft, thaws, and dissolves as if it were steeped in milk, when hastening to germinate — for fear that it should shoot and lose the nature and property of a magazine for their subsistence, they nibble off the end at which it should shoot and sprout.

As to war, which is the greatest and most magnificent of human actions, I would gladly know whether we should make it an argument for some prerogative, or, on the contrary, a witness to our weakness and imperfection — for in truth the science of undoing and killing one another, of ruining and destroying our own kind, has in it nothing so tempting as to make it be coveted by beasts who do not have it.
Quando leoni / Fortior eripuit vitam leo? quo nemore unquam / Expiravit aper majoris dentibus apri?
["No lion drinks a weaker lion's gore, / No boar expires beneath a stronger boar."]
Yet they are not universally exempt from it; witness the furious encounters of bees, and the enterprises of the princes of the opposing armies:
Sæpe duobus / Regibus incessit magno discordia motu; / Continuoque animos vulgi et trepidantia bello / Corda licet longe præsciscere.
["But if contending factions arm the hive, / When rival kings in doubtful battle strive, / Tumultuous crowds the dread event prepare, / And palpitating hearts that beat to war."]

I never read this divine description but I seem to see human folly and vanity represented in their true and lively colours. For these warlike movements that so ravish us with their astounding noise and horror, this clatter of guns, drums, and cries —
Fulgur ibi ad cælum se tollit, totaque circum / Ære renidescit tellus, subterque virûm vi / Excitur pedibus sonitus, clamoreque montes / Icti rejectant voces ad sidera mundi;

["When burnished arms to heaven dart their rays, / And many a steely beam in the sunlight plays, / When trampled is the earth by horse and man, / Until the very centre groans again, / And the rocks, struck by the various cries, / Reverberate the sound unto the skies"]

in the dreadful drawing up of so many thousands of armed men in battle order, and with such fury, ardour, and courage, it is amusing to consider by what trifling occasions they are stirred up, and by how light ones appeased:
Paridis propter narratur amorem / Græciæ Barbariæ diro collisa duello:
["Of wanton Paris the illicit love / Did Greece and Troy to ten years' warfare move."]

All Asia was ruined and destroyed for the lust of Paris; the envy of one single man, a spite, a pleasure, a domestic jealousy — causes that ought not to set two fishwives by the ears — is the mover of all this mighty bustle. Shall we believe the very men who are themselves the principal authors of these mischiefs? Then let us hear the greatest, the most powerful, the most victorious emperor that ever was, turning into a joke, very pleasantly and ingeniously, several battles fought both by sea and land, the blood and lives of five hundred thousand men who followed his fortune, and the strength and riches of two parts of the world drained for the expense of his campaigns:

Quod futuit Glaphyran Antonius, hanc mihi pœnam / Fulvia constituit, se quoque uti futuam. / Fulviam ego ut futuam! quid, si me Manius oret / Pœdicem, faciam? Non puto, si sapiam. / Aut futue, aut pugnemus, ait. Quid, si mihi vita / Charior est ipsa mentula? Signa canant.

Qui? moi, que je serve Fulvie! / Suffit-il qu'elle en ait envie? / À ce compte, on verrait se retirer vers moi / Mille épouses mal satisfaites. / Aime-moi, me dit-elle, ou combattons. Mais quoi? / Elle est bien laide! Allons, sonnez trompettes.

['Cause Anthony is fired with Glaphire's charms / Fain would his Fulvia tempt me to her arms. / If Anthony be false, what then? must I / Be slave to Fulvia's lustful tyranny? / Then would a thousand wanton, waspish wives,]
(I use my Latin with the liberty of conscience you are pleased to allow me.) Now this great body, with so many fronts and so many motions, which seems to threaten heaven and earth:

Quam multi Lybico volvuntur marmore fluctus, / Sævus ubi Orion hibernis conditur undis, / Vel quam sole novo densæ torrentur aristæ, / Aut Hermi campo, aut Lyciæ flaventibus arvis; / Scuta sonant, pulsuque pedum tremit excita tellus:

["Not thicker billows beat the Lybian main, / When pale Orion sits in wintry rain; / Nor thicker harvests on rich Hermus rise, / Or Lycian fields, when Phoebus burns the skies, / Than stand these troops: their bucklers ring around; / Their trampling turns the turf and shakes the solid ground."]
This furious monster, with so many heads and arms, is still man — feeble, calamitous, miserable man! It is only an anthill disturbed and provoked:
It nigrum campis agmen:
["The black troop marches to the field."]

A contrary blast, the croaking of a flight of ravens, the stumble of a horse, the chance passage of an eagle, a dream, a voice, a sign, a morning mist — any one of these is enough to beat him down and overturn him. Dart but a sunbeam in his face, and he is melted and vanished. Blow but a little dust in his eyes, as our poet says of the bees, and all our standards and legions, with great Pompey himself at the head of them, are routed and crushed to pieces — for it was he, as I take it, that Sertorius beat in Spain with those same fine weapons, which also served Eumenes against Antigonus, and Surena against Crassus:
["Swarm to my bed like bees into their hives. / Declare for love, or war, she said; and frowned: / No love I'll grant: to arms bid trumpets sound."]
Hi motus animorum, atque hæc certamina tanta, / Pulveris exigui jactu compressa quiescent.
["Yet at thy will these dreadful conflicts cease, / Throw but a little dust and all is peace."]

Just let our flies loose upon them, and they will have the force and courage to defeat them. In recent memory, when the Portuguese were besieging the city of Tamly in the territory of Xiatine, the inhabitants brought a great many hives (which are plentiful in that place) up onto the wall, and with fire drove the bees so furiously upon the enemy that they gave up the enterprise, unable to stand their attacks and endure their stings; and so the citizens, by this new sort of help, won liberty and victory with such wonderful fortune that, when their defenders returned from the battle, they found that they had not lost a single man. The souls of emperors and cobblers are cast in the same mould. Considering the weight and importance of princes' actions, we persuade ourselves that they must be produced by causes as weighty and important; but we deceive ourselves. They are pushed on and pulled back in their motions by the same springs as we are in our little undertakings. The same reason that makes us quarrel with a neighbour causes a war between princes; the same reason that makes us whip a lackey, falling into a king's hands, makes him ruin a whole province. They are as easily moved as we, but they are able to do more. In a gnat and an elephant the passion is the same.

As for fidelity, there is no animal in the world so treacherous as man. Our histories have recorded the violent pursuits dogs have made after the murderers of their masters. King Pyrrhus, observing a dog that kept watch over a dead man's body, and understanding that for three days together he had performed this office, commanded the body to be buried and took the dog along with him. One day, as he was at a general muster of his army, this dog, spotting his master's murderers, leapt upon them with great barking and extreme signs of anger, and by this first accusation woke the revenge for that murder, which was soon after carried out by form of justice. As much was done by the dog of the wise Hesiod, which convicted the sons of Ganictor of Naupactus of the murder committed on the person of his master. Another dog, set to guard a temple at Athens, having spotted a sacrilegious thief carrying off the finest jewels, fell to barking at him with all his force; but the warders not waking at the noise, he followed him, and when day broke, kept off a little distance without losing sight of him; if the thief offered him anything to eat he would not take it, but would wag his tail at all the passers-by he met, and accepted whatever they gave him; and if the thief lay down to sleep, he likewise stayed in the same place. The news of this dog reaching the warders of the temple, they set off in pursuit, asking after the colour of the dog, and at last found him in the city of Cromyon, and the thief also, whom they brought back to Athens, where he received his reward; and the judges, in consideration of this good office, ordered a certain measure of corn for the dog's daily sustenance, at the public charge, and the priests to look after him. Plutarch reports this story as certain truth, and as having happened in the age in which he lived.
As for gratitude (for I think we need to bring this word back into a little repute), this one example, which Apion reports himself to have been an eyewitness of, shall suffice.

"One day," he says, "in Rome, they entertained the people with a show of fighting between several strange beasts, and principally of lions of an unusual size. There was one among the rest who, by his furious bearing, by the strength and largeness of his limbs, and by his loud and dreadful roaring, attracted the eyes of all the spectators. Among the slaves presented to the people in this combat of beasts there was one Androdus, of Dacia, belonging to a Roman lord of consular dignity. This lion, having seen him at a distance, first made a sudden stop, as if in a wondering posture, and then softly approached nearer in a gentle and peaceable manner, as though to renew acquaintance with him. This being done, and now sure of what he sought for, he began to wag his tail, as dogs do when they fawn on their masters, and to kiss and lick the hands and thighs of the poor wretch, who was beside himself and almost dead with fear. Androdus, brought a little to himself by this kindness of the lion, having taken heart enough to look at him and recognize him, it was a singular pleasure to see the joy and caresses that passed between them. At which, the people breaking into loud acclamations of joy, the emperor had the slave called to him, to learn the cause of so strange an event; and Androdus told him a new and a very strange story: 'My master,' he said, 'being proconsul in Africa, I was forced, by his severity and cruel usage, being daily beaten, to steal from him and run away; and, to hide myself safely from a person of such great authority in the province, I thought it best to flee to the solitudes, sands, and uninhabitable parts of that country, resolving that if I could no longer find means to support life, I would somehow kill myself. The sun being excessively hot at noon, and the heat intolerable, I came upon a private and almost inaccessible cave, and went into it. Soon after, this lion came in to me, with one foot wounded and bloody, complaining and groaning with the pain he endured. At his coming I was extremely afraid; but he, having spotted me hiding in the corner of his den, came gently up to me, holding out and showing me his wounded foot, as if he were asking my assistance in his distress. I then drew out a great splinter he had got there, and growing a little more familiar with him, squeezing the wound, I thrust out the matter, dirt, and gravel that had got into it, and wiped and cleansed it as best I could. He, finding himself somewhat better, and much eased of his pain, lay down to rest, and presently fell asleep with his foot in my hand. From that time forward, he and I lived together in this cave three whole years on the same diet; for of the beasts he killed hunting he always brought me the best pieces, which I roasted in the sun for want of fire, and so ate. At last, weary of this wild and brutish life, while the lion was one day gone out to hunt for our ordinary provision, I left the cave, and on the third day after was taken by the soldiers, who brought me from Africa to this city, to my master, who at once condemned me to die and to be exposed thus to the wild beasts. Now, from what I see, this lion was also taken soon after, and is now seeking to repay me for the kindness and cure he received at my hands.' This is the story Androdus told the emperor, who also passed it from hand to hand to the people; whereupon, at the general request, he was absolved from his sentence and set at liberty, and the lion was, by order of the people, presented to him. We afterwards saw," says Apion, "Androdus leading this lion, in nothing but a small leash, from tavern to tavern at Rome, and receiving whatever money everyone gave him, the lion being so gentle as to allow himself to be covered with the flowers the people threw upon him; everyone he met saying, 'There goes the lion who entertained the man; there goes the man who cured the lion.'"
We often grieve the loss of beasts we love, and so do they the loss of us:
Post, bellator equus, positis insignibus, Æthon / It lacrymans, guttisque humectat grandibus ora.
["To close the pomp, Æthon, the steed of state, / Is led, the funeral of his lord to wait. / Stripped of his trappings, with a sullen pace / He walks, and the big tears run rolling down his face."]

As some nations have their wives in common and others have each his own, is not the same seen among beasts, and marriages better kept than ours? As for the society and confederation they make among themselves — to league together and give one another mutual assistance — is it not well known that oxen, hogs, and other animals, at the cry of any of their kind that we offend, the whole herd runs to his aid and rallies for his defence? When the fish scarus has swallowed the angler's hook, his fellows all crowd round him and gnaw the line in pieces; and if, by chance, one of them has got into the bow-net, the others present him their tails on the outside, which he holds fast with his teeth, and so they disengage him and pull him out.

Mullets, when one of their companions is caught, cross the line over their back and, with a fin they have there indented like a saw, cut and saw it through. As for the particular offices we render one another for the service of life, there are several like examples among them. The whale, it is said, never moves but she has always before her a little fish like the sea-gudgeon, called for that reason the guide-fish; the whale follows him, suffering herself to be led and turned with as great ease as a rudder guides a ship. In recompense for this service — whereas all other things, beast or vessel, that enter the dreadful gulf of this monster's mouth are immediately lost and swallowed up — this little fish retires into it in great security, and there sleeps, during which time the whale never stirs; but as soon as it goes out, he follows immediately; and if by accident he loses sight of his little guide, he wanders here and there, striking his sides against the rocks like a ship that has lost her helm — which Plutarch affirms to have seen on the island of Anticyra. There is a like society between the little bird called the wren and the crocodile. The wren serves as a sentinel over this great animal; and if the ichneumon, his mortal enemy, approaches to fight him, this little bird, for fear lest he should surprise him asleep, both with his voice and beak rouses him and gives him notice of his danger. He feeds off this monster's leavings, which receives him familiarly into his mouth, suffering him to peck in his jaws and between his teeth, and pick out the bits of flesh that remain; and when he wants to shut his mouth, he first gives the bird warning to come out, closing it little by little, without bruising or doing it any harm at all. The shellfish called the naker lives in the same understanding with the shrimp, a little animal of the lobster kind, which serves him as a porter, sitting at the opening of the shell, which the naker keeps always gaping and open till the shrimp sees some little fish, proper prey for them, within the hollow of the shell, where she too enters, and pinches the naker so to the quick that she is forced to close her shell, where the two of them together devour the prey they have trapped in their fort. In the manner of living of the tunnies we observe a singular knowledge of the three parts of mathematics. As to astrology, they teach it to men, for they stay in the place where they are surprised by the winter solstice and never stir from it till the next equinox; for which reason Aristotle himself attributes this science to them. As to geometry and arithmetic, they always form their numbers in the figure of a cube, every way square, and make up the body of a battalion solid, close, and surrounded on six equal sides; they swim in this square order, as broad behind as before, so that whoever in seeing them can count one rank may easily number the whole troop, since the depth is equal to the breadth, and the breadth to the length.

As for magnanimity, it will be hard to give a better example than that of the great dog sent to Alexander the Great from the Indies. They first brought him a stag to engage with, then a boar, and after that a bear, all of which he disregarded, disdaining to stir from his place; but when he saw a lion he at once roused himself, evidently showing that he judged that animal alone worthy to enter the lists with him. As for repentance and acknowledgment of fault, it is reported of an elephant that, having in the impetuosity of his rage killed his keeper, he fell into such extreme sorrow that he would never afterwards eat, and starved himself to death. And as for clemency, it is said of a tiger — the cruellest of all beasts — that a kid having been put in to him, he endured two days' hunger rather than hurt it, and on the third broke the grate he was shut up in to seek elsewhere for prey, so unwilling was he to fall upon the kid, his familiar and his guest. And as for the laws of familiarity and agreement formed by life together, it commonly happens that we bring up cats, dogs, and hares tame together.

But what seamen know by experience, and particularly in the Sicilian Sea, of the quality of the halcyons, surpasses all human thought. With what kind of animal has nature so much honoured the birth? The poets indeed say that one island only, Delos, which was formerly a floating island, was fixed for the service of Latona's lying-in; but God has ordered that the whole ocean should be stilled, made stable and smooth, without waves, without winds or rain, while the halcyon produces her young, which is just about the solstice, the shortest day of the year — so that by her privilege we have seven days and seven nights in the very heart of winter when we may sail without danger. Their females never have to do with any male but their own, whom they serve and assist all their lives, without ever forsaking him. If he becomes weak and broken with age, they take him on their shoulders and carry him from place to place, and serve him till death. But the most inquisitive into the secrets of nature have never yet been able to arrive at the knowledge of the wonderful structure with which the halcyon builds her nest for her little ones, nor even to guess at the materials. Plutarch, who has seen and handled many of them, thinks it is the bones of some fish, which she joins and binds together, interlacing them — some lengthwise and others across — and adding ribs and hoops in such a way that she forms at last a round vessel fit to launch; when this is done, and the building finished, she carries it to the beach, where the sea beating gently against it shows her where to mend what is not well joined, and where best to fortify the seams that are leaky and open at the beating of the waves; on the contrary, what is well built and has had the proper finishing, the beating of the waves so closes and binds together that it is not to be broken or cracked by blows of stone or iron without great ado. And what is more to be admired is the proportion and figure of the cavity within, which is so composed and proportioned as to receive or admit no other thing than the bird that built it; for to anything else it is so impenetrable, close, and shut that nothing can enter, not even the seawater. This is a very clear description of this construction, borrowed from a very good hand; and yet I think it does not give us light enough into the difficulty of this architecture. From what vanity, then, can it proceed to despise and look down upon, and disdainfully to interpret, effects we can neither imitate nor comprehend?

To pursue a little further this equality and correspondence between us and beasts: the privilege our soul so much glories in — of bringing whatever she conceives to her own measure, of stripping all the things that come to her of their mortal and bodily qualities, of ordering and placing the things she thinks worthy of her notice, divesting them of their corruptible qualities, and making them lay aside length, breadth, depth, weight, colour, smell, roughness, smoothness, hardness, softness, and all sensible accidents, as mean and superfluous clothing, so as to accommodate them to her own immortal and spiritual condition (Rome and Paris, for example, that I hold in my fancy; Paris that I imagine — I imagine and grasp it without size and without place, without stone, without plaster, without wood) — this same privilege, I say, plainly appears to be in the beasts too. For a war-horse, accustomed to trumpets, musket-shots, and battle, that we see start and tremble in his sleep, stretched on his litter as if he were in a fight, it is almost certain that he conceives in his soul the beat of a drum without noise, and an army without arms and without bodies:
Quippe videbis equos fortes, cum membra jacebunt / In somnis, sudare tamen, spirareque sæpe, / Et quasi de palma summas contendere vires:
["You shall see managed horses in their sleep / Sweat, snort, start, tremble, and a clutter keep, / As if with all their force they striving were / The victor's palm proudly away to bear."]

The hare that a greyhound imagines in his sleep, after which we see him pant so while he sleeps, stretch out his tail, shake his legs, and perfectly represent all the motions of a course, is a hare without fur and without bones:

Venantumque canes in molli sæpe quiete / Jactant crura tamen subito, vocesque repente / Mittunt, et crebras reducunt naribus auras, / Ut vestigia si teneant inventa ferarum: / Expergefactique sequuntur inania sæpe / Cervorum simulacra, fugæ quasi dedita cernant; / Donec discussis redeant erroribus ad se:

["And hounds stir often in their quiet rest, / Spending their mouths, as if upon a quest, / Snuff, and breathe quick and short, as if they went / In a full chase upon a burning scent: / Nay, being waked, imagined stags pursue, / As if they had them in their real view, / Till, having shook themselves more broad awake, / They do at last discover the mistake."]

The watch-dogs we often observe snarling in their dreams, and afterwards barking out and starting up as if they perceived some stranger at hand — the stranger their soul discerns is a man spiritual and imperceptible, without dimension, without colour, and without being:
Consueta domi catulorum blanda propago / Degere, sæpe levem ex oculis volucremque soporem / Discutere, et corpus de terra corripere instant, / Proinde quasi ignotas facies atque ora tuantur.
["The fawning whelps of household curs will rise, / And, shaking the soft slumber from their eyes, / Oft bark and stare at every one within, / As upon faces they had never seen."]

As to the beauty of the body — before I go any further, I should know whether or not we are agreed on the description. It is likely we do not really know what beauty is in nature and in general, since to our own human beauty we give so many different forms; for if there were any natural rule and prescription, we should know it in common, like the heat of fire. But we make up the forms according to our own appetite and liking:
Turpis Romano Belgicus ore color:
["A German hue ill suits a Roman face."]

The Indians paint it black and tawny, with great swollen lips, wide flat noses, and load the cartilage between the nostrils with great gold rings to make it hang down to the mouth; and likewise the lower lip with great hoops, set with precious stones, that weigh it down to fall upon the chin, it being among them a singular grace to show their teeth, even below the roots. In Peru the largest ears are the most beautiful, and they stretch them out by art as far as they can. A man now living says he has seen, in an eastern nation, this care of enlarging them in such repute, and the ear loaded with such ponderous jewels, that he could with great ease put his arm, sleeve and all, through the hole of an ear. There are elsewhere nations that take great care to blacken their teeth, and hate to see them white; while others paint them red. Women are reputed more beautiful, not only in Biscay but elsewhere, for having their heads shaved; and, what is more, in certain frozen countries, as Pliny reports. The Mexicans esteem a low forehead a great beauty, and though they shave all the other parts, they nourish hair on the forehead and increase it by art; and they hold great breasts in such reputation that they take care to give their children suck over their shoulders. We would paint deformity that way. The Italians fashion it gross and massy; the Spaniards gaunt and slender; and among us one prefers it white, another brown; one soft and delicate, another strong and vigorous; one will have his mistress soft and gentle, another haughty and majestic. Just as the preference in beauty Plato attributes to the spherical figure, the Epicureans gave rather to the pyramidal or square — and could not swallow a god in the form of a ball. But, be it however it may, nature has no more privileged us in this respect from her common laws than in the rest. And if we will judge ourselves rightly, we shall find that, if there are some animals less favoured in this than we are, there are others, and in greater number, that are more favoured: _a multis animalibus decore vincimur_ ["many animals surpass us in beauty"] — even among the land animals, our compatriots; for as to those of the sea, setting aside their shape (which cannot fall into any sort of proportion, being so different in colour, clearness, smoothness, and arrangement), we sufficiently give place to them; and no less, in all qualities, to those of the air. And this prerogative the poets make so much of, our upright stature, looking towards heaven, our origin —
Pronaque cum spectent animalia cætera terram, / Os homini sublime dedit, cælumque tueri / Jussit, et erectos ad sidera tollere vultus,
["Whilst all the brutal creatures downward bend / Their sight, and to their earthly mother tend, / He set man's face aloft, that, with his eyes / Uplifted, he might view the starry skies."]

— is truly poetic; for there are several little beasts whose sight is absolutely turned towards heaven; and I find the bearing of camels and ostriches much more raised and upright than ours. What animals do not have their faces above and not in front, and do not look opposite as we do — and do not in their natural posture take in as much of heaven and earth as man does? And what qualities of our bodily constitution, in Plato and in Cicero, may not equally serve a thousand sorts of beasts? Those that most resemble us are the most despicable and deformed of the whole herd — for as to outward appearance and the form of the face, they are baboons:
Simia quam similis, turpissima bestia, nobis?
["How like to man, in visage and in shape, / Is, of all beasts the most uncouth, the ape?"]

And as to the internal and vital parts, the hog. In truth, when I consider man stark naked — even in that sex which seems to have the greatest share of beauty — his defects, his natural subjection, and his imperfections, I find we have more reason than any other animal to cover ourselves, and to be excused for borrowing from those to whom nature has been kinder in this than to us, to trick ourselves out in their beauties and hide ourselves under their spoils: their wool, feathers, hair, and silk. Let us observe, for the rest, that man is the only animal whose nudity offends his own companions, and the only one who in his natural actions withdraws and hides himself from his own kind. And really it is also an effect worth considering, that those who are masters in the trade prescribe, as a remedy for amorous passions, the full and free view of the body a man desires — that to cool the ardour there is no more needed than freely and fully to see what one loves:
Ille quod obscenas in aperto corpore partes / Viderat, in cursu qui fuit, hæsit amor.
["The love that's tilting when those parts appear / Open to view, flags in the hot career."]

And although this prescription may perhaps proceed from a fastidious and cold temperament, it is nevertheless a very great sign of our deficiency that use and familiarity should make us disgusted with one another. It is not so much modesty as cunning and prudence that makes our ladies so careful to deny us entrance into their dressing-rooms before they are painted and tricked up for public view:
Nec Veneres nostras hoc fallit; quo magis ipsæ / Omnia summopere hos vitæ postscenia celant, / Quos retinere volunt, adstrictoque esse in amore:
["Of this our ladies are full well aware, / Which makes them, with such privacy and care, / Behind the scene all those defects remove / Likely to check the flame of those they love."]

Whereas in several animals there is nothing we do not love and that does not please our senses; so that we extract from their very excrements not only something to enhance our sauces, but also our richest ornaments and perfumes. This discourse reflects on none but the ordinary sort of women, and is not so sacrilegious as to take in those divine, supernatural, and extraordinary beauties that we see shine occasionally among us like stars under a bodily and earthly veil.

For the rest, the very share we allow the beasts of nature's bounty, even by our own admission, is very much to their advantage. We attribute to ourselves imaginary and fantastic goods, future and absent goods, for which human capacity cannot answer by herself; or goods we falsely attribute to ourselves by the licence of opinion, like reason, knowledge, and honour — and leave to them as their portion essential, durable, and palpable goods: peace, repose, security, innocence, and health; health, I say, the fairest and richest present that nature can make us. Insomuch that philosophy, even the Stoic, is bold enough to say that Heraclitus and Pherecides, had they been able to trade their wisdom for health, and to have rid themselves — the one of his dropsy, the other of the lousy disease that tormented him — would have done well. By which they set a higher value on wisdom, comparing and putting it in the balance with health, than they do in this other proposition, which is also theirs: that if Circe had presented Ulysses with two potions, the one to make a fool become a wise man, the other to make a wise man become a fool, Ulysses ought rather to have chosen the latter than consent to the one by which Circe changed his human form into that of a beast; and they say that wisdom itself would have spoken to him in these terms: "Forsake me, let me alone, rather than lodge me under the body and figure of an ass." What! shall the philosophers, then, abandon this great and divine wisdom for this bodily and earthly covering? Then it is no longer by reason, by discourse, and by the soul that we excel the beasts; it is by our beauty, our fair complexion, and the fine symmetry of our parts, for which we must give up our intelligence, our prudence, and all the rest. Well, I accept this open and frank confession; certainly they knew that those things on which we set so much value are no other than vain fancy. If beasts had all the virtue, knowledge, wisdom, and Stoic perfection, they would still be beasts, and would not be comparable to man — miserable, wicked, mad man. For in short, whatever is not as we are is nothing worth; and God, in order to procure himself some esteem among us, must put himself into that shape, as we shall show shortly. By which it appears that it is not on any true ground of reason, but by a foolish pride and vain opinion, that we prefer ourselves to other animals and separate ourselves from their society and condition.

But to return to what I was upon before: we have for our part inconstancy, irresolution, uncertainty, sorrow, superstition, anxiety about things to come, even after we shall be no more, ambition, avarice, jealousy, envy, irregular, frantic, and untamed appetites, war, lying, disloyalty, slander, and curiosity. We have, no doubt, paid a strange price for this fine reason on which we so much pride ourselves, and this capacity of judging and knowing, if we have bought it at the price of this infinite number of passions to which we are eternally subject. Unless we shall also think fit to add, as even Socrates does, the notable prerogative above the beasts that, whereas nature has prescribed them certain seasons and limits for the delights of Venus, she has given us the reins at all hours and all seasons. _Ut vinum ægrotis, quia prodest raro, nocet sæpissime, melius est non adhibere omnino, quam, spe dubio salutis, in apertam perniciem incurrere; sic, haud scio an melius fuerit humano generi motum istum celerem cogitationis, acumen, solertiam, quam rationem vocamus, quoniam pestifera sint multis, admodum paucis salutaria, non dari omnino, quam tam munifice et tam large dari?_ ["As wine often hurts the sick, and very rarely does them good, it is better not to give them any at all than to run them into an apparent danger out of hope of an uncertain benefit; so I know not whether it would not have been better for mankind that this quick motion, this penetration, this subtlety we call reason, had not been given to man at all, considering how pestiferous it is to many and useful only to a few, than to have been conferred so abundantly and with so liberal a hand."] Of what advantage can we conceive the knowledge of so many things was to Varro and Aristotle? Did it exempt them from human inconveniences? Were they by it freed from the accidents that lay heavy on a porter's shoulders? Did they extract from their logic any consolation for the gout? Or, for knowing how this humour lodges in the joints, did they feel it the less? Did they enter into terms with death by knowing that some nations rejoice at his approach? or with cuckoldry, by knowing that in some parts of the world wives are held in common? On the contrary, having been reputed the greatest men for knowledge, the one among the Romans and the other among the Greeks, and in a time when learning most flourished, we have not heard that they had any particular excellence in their lives; in fact the Greek had enough to do to clear himself of some notable blemishes in his. Have we observed that pleasure and health have a better savour with the man who understands astrology and grammar than with others?
Illiterati num minus nervi rigent?
["The illiterate ploughman is as fit / For Venus' service as the wit."]
— or shame and poverty less troublesome to the first than to the second?
Scilicet et morbis et debilitate carebis, / Et luctum et curam effugies, et tempora vitæ / Longa tibi post hæc fato meliore dabuntur.
["Disease thy couch shall flee, / And sorrow and care; yes, thou, be sure, wilt see / Long years of happiness, till now unknown."]

I have known in my time a hundred artisans, a hundred labourers, wiser and happier than the rectors of the university, and whom I would much rather have resembled. Learning, it seems to me, has its place among the necessary things of life, like glory, nobility, dignity — or at most, like beauty, riches, and other such qualities, which are indeed useful to it, but remotely, and more by opinion than by nature. We need offices, rules, and laws to live by in our society no more than the cranes and ants do in theirs; and yet we see these carry themselves very regularly without erudition. If man were wise, he would judge everything at the true value, according as it was useful and proper to his life. Whoever will number us by our actions and deportment will find many more excellent men among the ignorant than among the learned — yes, in all sorts of virtue. Old Rome seems to me to have been of much greater worth, both in peace and war, than that learned Rome that ruined itself. And, all the rest being equal, integrity and innocence remain to the ancients, for they cohabit singularly well with simplicity. But I will leave this discourse, which would lead me further than I am willing to follow; and shall only add this: it is only humility and submission that can make a complete good man. We are not to leave the knowledge of his duty to every man's own judgment; we are to prescribe it to him, and not let him choose it at his own discretion; otherwise, given the imbecility and infinite variety of our reasons and opinions, we should at large forge ourselves duties that would, as Epicurus says, enjoin us to eat one another.

The first law God ever gave to man was a law of pure obedience; it was a commandment naked and simple, in which man had nothing to inquire after, nor to dispute, since to obey is the proper office of a rational soul, acknowledging a heavenly superior and benefactor. From obedience and submission spring all other virtues, as all sin springs from self-opinion. And, on the contrary, the first temptation the devil offered to human nature, its first poison insinuated itself into us by the promise made us of knowledge and wisdom: _Eritis sicut Dii, scientes bonum et malum._ ["You shall be as gods, knowing good and evil."] And the sirens in Homer, to allure Ulysses and draw him within the danger of their snares, offered to give him knowledge. The plague of man is the opinion of wisdom; and that is why ignorance is so recommended to us by our religion, as proper to faith and obedience: _Cavete ne quis vos decipiat per philosophiam et inanes seductiones, secundum elementa mundi._ ["Take heed lest any man deceive you by philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, and the rudiments of the world."] There is in this a general consent among all sorts of philosophers, that the sovereign good consists in the tranquillity of the soul and body; but where shall we find it?
Ad summum, sapiens uno minor est Jove, dives, / Liber, honoratus, pulcher, rex denique regum; / Præcipue sanus, nisi cum pituita molesta est:
["In short, the wise is only less than Jove, / Rich, free, and handsome; nay, a king above / All earthly kings; with health supremely blest, / Excepting when a cold disturbs his rest!"]

It seems, in truth, that nature, for the consolation of our miserable and wretched state, has given us only presumption for our inheritance. As Epictetus says, man has nothing properly his own but the use of his opinions; we have nothing but wind and smoke for our portion. The gods have health in essence, says philosophy, and sickness in intelligence; man, on the contrary, possesses his goods by fancy, his ills in essence. We have reason to magnify the power of our imagination, since all our goods exist only in dream. Hear this poor calamitous animal bluster! "There is nothing," says Cicero, "so charming as the employment of letters; letters, I say, by means of which the infinity of things, the immense grandeur of nature, the heavens even in this world, the earth, and the seas are discovered to us; it is they that have taught us religion, moderation, and the grandeur of courage, and that have rescued our souls from darkness, to make her see all things — high, low, first, last, and middling; it is they that furnish us with the means of living happily and well, and lead us through our lives without displeasure and without offence." Doesn't this man seem to speak of the condition of the ever-living and almighty God? But in fact a thousand little countrywomen have lived lives more even, more sweet, and more constant than his.

Deus ille fuit, deus, inclyte Memmi, / Qui princeps vitæ rationem invenit eam, quæ / Nunc appellatur sapientia; quique per artem / Fluctibus è tantis vitam, tantisque tenebris, / In tam tranquilla et tam clara luce locavit:

["That god, great Memmius, was a god no doubt / Who, prince of life, first found that reason out / Now wisdom called; and by his art, who did / That life in tempests tossed, and darkness hid, / Place in so great a calm, and clear a light."]

Here are brave ranting words; but a very slight accident put this man's understanding in a worse condition than that of the meanest shepherd, notwithstanding this instructing god, this divine wisdom. Of the same stamp and impudence is the promise of Democritus's book: "I am going to speak of all things"; and that foolish title that Aristotle prefixes to one of his — order alone afforded him a few lucid intervals which he employed in composing his book, and at last drove him to kill himself. — Eusebius's Chronicon.

Of the Mortal Gods; and the judgment of Chrysippus, that "Dion was as virtuous as God"; and my Seneca himself says that "God had given him life, but to live well was his own," conformably to this other: _In virtute vere gloriamur; quod non contingeret, si id donum a Deo, non a nobis haberemus:_ ["We truly glory in our virtue; which would not be, if it were a gift from God, and not from ourselves."] This is also Seneca's saying: that the wise man has fortitude equal to God's, but his is in spite of human frailty, in which respect therefore he more than equals God. There is nothing more ordinary than to meet with sallies of the like rashness; there is none of us who takes so much offence to see himself equalled with God as he does to see himself undervalued by being ranked with other creatures — so much more jealous are we of our own interest than of our Creator's.

But we must trample under foot this foolish vanity, and briskly and boldly shake the ridiculous foundation on which these false opinions are founded. As long as man shall believe he has any means and power of himself, he will never acknowledge what he owes to his Maker; his eggs shall always be chickens, as the saying is; we must therefore strip him to his shirt. Let us see some notable examples of the effects of his philosophy. Posidonius, tormented by a disease so painful that it made him writhe his arms and gnash his teeth, thought he had sufficiently scorned the pain by crying out against it: "Do thy worst — I will not confess that thou art an evil." He felt the pain as much as my footman, but he made a bravado of bridling his tongue, at least, and keeping it within the laws of his sect: _Re succumbere non oportebat, verbis gloriantem._ ["It did not become him, who spoke so big, to confess his frailty when he came to the test."] Arcesilaus, ill of the gout, when Carneades who had come to see him went away troubled at his condition, was called back, and showing him his feet and breast, said, "There is nothing comes from there to here." This has a slightly better grace, for he feels himself in pain and would be free of it, but his heart, nevertheless, is not conquered nor subdued by it. The other stands more obstinately to his point, but, I fear, more verbally than really. And Dionysius Heracleotes, afflicted with a vehement smarting in his eyes, was reduced to give up these Stoic resolutions. But even if knowledge should, in effect, do what they say, and could blunt the point and dull the edge of the misfortunes that attend us, what does she do, more than what ignorance does more purely and evidently? The philosopher Pyrrho, being at sea in great danger because of a mighty storm, offered nothing for imitation to those with him in that extremity but a hog they had on board that was fearless and unconcerned at the tempest. Philosophy, when she has said all she can, refers us at last to the example of a gladiator, wrestler, or muleteer, in which sort of people we commonly observe much less apprehension of death, much less sense of pain and other inconveniences, and more endurance, than knowledge ever furnished to anyone who was not born and bred to hardship. What makes us cut into the tender limbs of an infant, or of a horse, more easily than into our own — but ignorance only? How many has the mere force of imagination made sick? We often see men cause themselves to be let blood, purged, and physicked to cure them of diseases they only feel in opinion. When real infirmities fail us, knowledge lends us hers: that colour, that complexion portends some catarrhous defluxion; this hot season threatens us with a fever; this break in the life-line of your left hand gives you notice of some near and dangerous indisposition; and at last she roundly attacks health itself, saying, "This sprightliness and vigour of youth cannot continue in this state; some blood must be taken and the heat abated, lest it turn against yourself." Compare the life of a man subjected to such imaginings with that of a labourer who lets himself be led by his natural appetite, measuring things only by the present sense, without knowledge and without forecast, who feels no pain or sickness but when he is really ill — whereas the other has the stone in his soul before he has it in his bladder, as if it were not time enough to suffer the evil when it shall come, but he must anticipate it by fancy, and run to meet it.

What I say of medicine may generally serve as an example for all other sciences. From that comes the ancient opinion of the philosophers that placed the sovereign good in the discovery of the weakness of our judgment. My ignorance gives me as much occasion for hope as for fear; and having no other rule for my health but the examples of others, and of events I see elsewhere on like occasions, I find of all sorts, and rely on those that by comparison are most favourable to me. I receive health with open arms, free, full, and whole, and so much the more whet my appetite to enjoy it as it is at present less ordinary and more rare; so far am I from troubling its repose and sweetness with the bitterness of a new and constrained manner of living. Beasts show us sufficiently how much the agitation of our minds brings infirmities and diseases upon us. What is told of the Brazilians, that they never die but of old age, is attributed to the serenity and tranquillity of the air they live in; but I would rather attribute it to the serenity and tranquillity of their souls, free from all passion, thought, or business, strenuous or unpleasing — a people who pass through their lives in a wonderful simplicity and ignorance, without letters, without law, without king, without any kind of religion. And whence comes that which we find by experience, that the heaviest and dullest men are the most able and the most desired in amorous performances; and that the love of a muleteer is often more acceptable than that of a gentleman — if it is not that the agitation of the soul in the latter disturbs his bodily ability, dissolves and tires it, just as it ordinarily troubles and tires itself? What puts the soul beside itself, and more usually throws it into madness, but her own promptness, vigour, and agility — her own proper force? Of what is the most subtle folly made, but of the most subtle wisdom? As great friendships spring from great enmities, and vigorous health from mortal diseases, so from the rare and vivid agitations of our souls proceed the most wonderful and most distracted frenzies; it is but half a turn of the toe from the one to the other. In the actions of madmen we see how closely madness resembles the most vigorous operations of the soul. Who does not know how undiscernible is the difference between folly and the lively elevations of a free soul, and the effects of a supreme and extraordinary virtue? Plato says that melancholy persons are the most apt for instruction and the most excellent; and accordingly in none is there so great a tendency to madness. Great wits are ruined by their own force and pliability. Into what condition has one of the most judicious, ingenious, and most nearly formed to the air of the ancient and true poesy of any of the Italian poets lately fallen, through his own agitation and promptness of fancy! Doesn't he owe a vast debt to this vivacity that has destroyed him? to this light that has blinded him? to this exact and subtle apprehension of reason that has put him beside his own? to this curious and laborious search after the sciences that has reduced him to imbecility? to this rare aptitude for the exercises of the soul, that has left him without exercise and without soul? I was more angry, if possible, than compassionate, to see him at Ferrara in so pitiful a condition, surviving himself, forgetting both himself and his works, which, without his knowledge, although before his face, have been published unformed and uncorrected.

Would you have a man healthy? would you have him orderly, and in a steady and secure posture? Muffle him up in the shades of stupidity and sloth. We must be made beasts in order to be made wise, and hoodwinked before we are fit to be led. And if anyone tells me that the advantage of having a cold and dull sense of pain and other evils brings this disadvantage with it — that we become consequently less sensible also in the enjoyment of good and pleasure — this is true; but the misery of our condition is such that we have not so much to enjoy as to avoid, and the most extreme pleasure does not affect us to the degree that a slight grief does: _Segnius homines bona quam mala sentiunt._ ["Men feel goods less than they do ills."] We are not as sensible of the most perfect health as we are of the least sickness.

Pungit / In cute vix summa violatum plagula corpus; / Quando valere nihil quemquam movet. Hoc juvat unum, / Quod me non torquet latus, aut pes; cætera quisquam / Vix queat aut sanum sese, aut sentire valentem.

["The body with a little sting is grieved, / When the most perfect health is not perceived; / This only pleases me, that spleen nor gout / Neither offend my side nor wring my foot; / Excepting these, scarce any one can tell, / Or e'er observes, when he's in health and well."]

Our well-being is nothing but the not being ill. Which is why that sect of philosophers that sets the greatest value on pleasure has yet fixed it chiefly in unconsciousness of pain. To be freed from ill is the greatest good a man can hope for or desire, as Ennius says,
Nimium boni est, cui nihil est mali;

for that tickling and stinging which is in certain pleasures, and that seem to lift us above simple health and passiveness — that active, moving, and (I don't know how) itching and biting pleasure — even that very pleasure itself aims at nothing but insensibility as its mark. The appetite that drives us headlong to women's embraces has no other end but to cure the torment of our ardent and furious desires, and only asks to be glutted and laid at rest, and delivered from the fever. And so of the rest. I say, then, that if simplicity leads us to a state free from evil, it leads us to a very happy one, given our condition. And yet we are not to imagine it so stupid an insensibility as to be totally without sense; for Crantor had very good reason to dispute Epicurus's insensibility, if founded so deeply that the very first attack and birth of evils were not to be felt. "I do not approve such an insensibility as is neither possible nor to be desired. I am very content not to be sick; but if I am, I would know it; and if a caustic is applied, or incisions made anywhere, I would feel them." In truth, whoever would take away the knowledge and sense of evil would at the same time wipe out the sense of pleasure, and would in the end annihilate man himself: _Istud nihil dolere, non sine magna mercede contingit, immanitatis in animo, stuporis in corpore._ ["That feeling nothing is not to be purchased but at the price of inhumanity in the soul and stupidity of the body."] Evil belongs to man as a matter of course. Neither is pain always to be avoided, nor pleasure always pursued.

It is a great advantage to the honour of ignorance that knowledge itself throws us into her arms when she finds herself baffled in fortifying us against the weight of evil. She is constrained to come to this compromise, to give us the reins and permit us to fly into the lap of the other, and to shelter under her protection from the strokes and injuries of fortune. For what else does she mean when she instructs us to divert our thoughts from the ills that press upon us, and entertain them with the meditation of pleasures past and gone; to comfort ourselves in present afflictions with the remembrance of fled delights, and to call to our aid a vanished satisfaction, to oppose to the discomfort that lies heavy on us? _Levationes ægritudinum in avocatione a cogitanda molestia, et revocatione ad contemplandas voluptates, ponit_ ["He places the alleviations of grief in turning our thoughts away from things that vex us, and calling them back to contemplate pleasures."] — unless it is that where her power fails, she would supply it with cunning, and make use of sleight of hand where strength of limbs will not serve? For not only to a philosopher, but to any man in his right wits, when he has the thirst of a burning fever upon him, what satisfaction can it be to him to remember the pleasure he took in drinking Greek wine a month ago? It would rather only make matters worse for him:
Che ricordarsi il ben doppia la noia.
["The thinking of pleasure doubles trouble."]

Of the same stamp is this other counsel that philosophy gives, only to remember the happiness that is past, and to forget the misadventures we have undergone — as if we had the science of oblivion in our own power. And as for the counsel, in this too we are still in want.
Suavis laborum est præteritorum memoria.
["Sweet is the memory of past pain."]

How does philosophy, which should arm me to contend with fortune and steel my courage to trample all human adversities underfoot, sink to this degree of cowardice — to make me hide my head in this way, and save myself by these pitiful and ridiculous shifts? For the memory presents to us not what we choose but what she pleases — indeed, there is nothing that so much imprints anything in our memory as a desire to forget it. And it is a good way to retain and keep anything safely in the soul to urge her to lose it. And this is false: _Est situm in nobis, ut et adversa quasi perpetua oblivione obruamus, et secunda jucunde et suaviter meminerimus_ ["It is in our power to bury, as in a perpetual oblivion, all adverse accidents, and to retain a pleasant and delightful memory of our successes"]; and this is true: _Memini etiam quæ nolo; oblivisci non possum quæ volo._ ["I remember even what I do not want; I cannot forget what I want."] And whose counsel is this? His, _qui se unus sapientem profiteri sit ausus_ ["who alone dared profess himself a wise man."]
Qui genus humanum ingenio superavit, et omnes Præstinxit stellas, exortus uti æthereus Sol.
"Who from mankind the prize of knowledge won, And put the stars out like the rising sun."
To empty and clear out the memory — isn't this the very road to ignorance?
Iners malorum remedium ignorantia est.
"Ignorance is a dull remedy for evils."

We find several other precepts of this kind, by which we are allowed to borrow frivolous appearances from common opinion when the strongest reason will not serve our purpose, provided they offer some satisfaction and comfort. Where they cannot cure the wound, they are content to numb and dull it. I think they will not deny that if they could find order and constancy in a way of life that maintained itself in ease and pleasure thanks to some weakness of judgment, they would take it:
Potare, et spargere flores Incipiam, patiarque vel inconsultus haberi.
"Give me to drink, and, crown'd with flowers, despise The grave disgrace of being thought unwise."

There would be plenty of philosophers of Lycas's mind. The man was otherwise of perfectly regular habits, living quietly and contentedly with his family, fulfilling every duty toward his own and toward strangers, and carefully guarding himself against anything harmful. But some disorder in his brain gave him the fixed conceit that he was perpetually in the theatre, a spectator at the finest sights and the best comedies in the world. When the physicians cured him of his frenzy, he very nearly went to law to compel them to restore him to his pleasing delusion:
Pol I me occidistis, amici, Non servastis, ait; cui sic extorta voluptas, Et demptus per vim mentis gratissimus error;
"By heaven! you've killed me, friends, outright, And not preserved me; since my dear delight And pleasing error, by my better sense Unhappily return'd, is banished hence;"

Much the same madness as Thrasylaus, son of Pythodorus, who convinced himself that every ship weighing anchor from the port of Piraeus, and every one entering the harbour, was sailing for his own profit. He congratulated them on their safe voyages and welcomed them with the greatest joy. When his brother Crito had him restored to his right mind, he bitterly regretted that condition in which he had lived with so much delight and free from all anxiety. As the old Greek verse has it, "there is great convenience in not being over-wise."
And Ecclesiastes: "In much wisdom there is much sorrow," and "Who gets wisdom gets labour and trouble."

Even that to which philosophy generally consents — the last remedy she applies to every necessity, ending the life we cannot endure. _Placet?--Pare. Non placet?--Quâcumque vis, exi. Pungit dolor?--Vel fodiat sane. Si nudus es, da jugulum; sin tectus armis Vulcaniis, id est fortitudine, résisté;_ "Does it please? Obey it. Not please? Go where you will. Does grief sting you, or stab? If you are naked, present your throat; if covered with Vulcan's armour, that is, with fortitude, resist." And that phrase used in the Greek festivals, _aut bibat, aut abeat_, "either drink or be off" — which sounds better on the tongue of a Gascon, who naturally changes h into v, than on Cicero's:
Vivere si recte nescis, decede peritis. Lusisti satis, edisti satis, atque bibisti; Tempus abire tibi est, ne potum largius æquo Rideat et pulset lasciva decentius ætas.

"If to live well and right thou dost not know, Give way, and leave thy place to those that do. Thou'st eaten, drunk, and play'd to thy content, 'Tis time to make thy parting compliment, Lest youth, more decent in their follies, scoff The nauseous scene, and hiss thee reeling off;"
What is this but a confession of impotence — a sending us back not just to ignorance, where one might at least be safe, but to stupidity, insensibility, and nothingness?
Democritum postquam matura vetustas Admonuit memorem motus languescere mentis; Sponte sua letho caput obvius obtulit ipse.
"Soon as, through age, Democritus did find A manifest decadence in his mind, He thought he now surviv'd to his own wrong, And went to meet his death, that stay'd too long."
It is what Antisthenes said: "A man should either lay in sense enough to understand, or a halter enough to hang himself." And what Chrysippus quoted from the poet Tyrtaeus:
"Or to arrive at virtue or at death;"

And Crates said, "Love is cured by hunger, if not by time; and whoever dislikes either remedy, by a rope." That Sextius — whom both Seneca and Plutarch praise so highly — having given himself wholly to the study of philosophy, resolved to throw himself into the sea, judging the progress of his studies too tedious and slow. He ran toward death, since he could not catch up with knowledge. Here is the law's own phrasing on the subject: "If by chance some great misfortune happens for which there is no remedy, the harbour is near, and a man may save himself by swimming out of his body as out of a leaky boat. For it is the fear of dying, not the love of life, that ties the fool to his body."

As life becomes more pleasant through simplicity, it also becomes more innocent and better, as I was saying just now. "The simple and ignorant," says St. Paul, "raise themselves up to heaven and take possession of it; and we, with all our knowledge, plunge ourselves into the infernal abyss." I am not swayed by Valentinian, a declared enemy of all learning and letters, nor by Licinius — both Roman emperors who called learning the poison and pest of all political government — nor by Mahomet, who is said to have forbidden his followers any kind of learning. But the example of the great Lycurgus, with his authority and the reverence due to the divine Lacedaemonian polity — so great, so admirable, and so long flourishing in virtue and happiness, without any institution or practice of letters — must surely carry weight. Those who return from the new world discovered by the Spaniards in our fathers' day testify how much more honestly and regularly those nations live without magistrate or law than we do, where there are more officers and lawyers than men of any other sort or business:

Di cittatorie piene, e di libelli, D'esamine, e di carte di procure, Hanno le mani e il seno, e gran fastelli Di chioge, di consigli, et di letture: Per cui le faculta de* poverelli Non sono mai nelle città sicure; Hanno dietro e dinanzi, e d'ambi i lati, Notai, procuratori, ed avvocati.

"Their bags were full of writs, and of citations, Of process, and of actions and arrests, Of bills, of answers, and of replications, In courts of delegates, and of requests, To grieve the simple sort with great vexations; They had resorting to them as their guests, Attending on their circuit, and their journeys, Scriv'ners, and clerks, and lawyers, and attorneys."

It was what a Roman senator of the later age said: that their forefathers' breath stank of garlic, but their stomachs were perfumed with a good conscience; whereas the men of his own time were all sweet-smelling outside and stinking within of every kind of vice. Which is to say, as I read it, that they were full of learning and eloquence and very short on moral honesty. Incivility, ignorance, simplicity, and roughness are the natural companions of innocence; curiosity, subtlety, and knowledge bring malice along with them. Humility, fear, obedience, and affability — the things that mainly support and maintain human society — require an empty and pliant soul, one that presumes little upon itself.

Christians have a particular awareness of how natural and original an evil curiosity is in man. The thirst for knowledge, the desire to grow wiser, was the first ruin of mankind, the way by which he hurled himself into eternal damnation. Pride was his undoing. It is pride that diverts him from the common path and makes him embrace novelties, that makes him sooner choose to be head of a lost band wandering in error, to be a master and teacher of lies, than a disciple in the school of truth, content to be led and guided by another along the right and beaten road. That perhaps is the meaning of the old Greek saying that superstition follows pride and obeys it as if it were her father: [--Greek--] Ah, presumption — how much you hinder us!

When Socrates was told that the god of wisdom had assigned him the title of sage, he was astonished, and looking himself over thoroughly could find no foundation for so divine a judgment. He knew others as just, temperate, brave, and learned as himself — and more eloquent, handsomer, and more useful to their country than he was. At last he concluded that he was no different from the rest, and that he was wise only because he did not think he was; that his god regarded the opinion of knowledge and wisdom as a singular absurdity in man, and that his best doctrine was the doctrine of ignorance, and his best wisdom simplicity. The sacred word declares miserable those among us who have a good opinion of themselves: "Dust and ashes," it says to them, "what have you to glorify yourself in?" And elsewhere, "God has made man like a shadow" — and who can judge of a shadow when, the light being withdrawn, it has vanished? Man is a thing of nothing.

Our power is so far from being able to grasp the divine height that, of the works of our Creator, those bear his mark most clearly, and are most truly his, which we understand the least. Meeting with an incredible thing is for a Christian a reason to believe; the more it is against human reason, the more it is according to faith. If it were according to reason it would no longer be a miracle; if it were according to example, it would no longer be a singular thing. _Melius scitur Deus nesciendo_: "God is better known by not knowing him," says St. Augustine. And Tacitus: _Sanctius est ac reverentius de actis Deorum credere, quam scire_; "it is more holy and reverent to believe the works of the gods than to know them." And Plato holds that there is something impious in inquiring too curiously into God, the world, and the first causes of things: _Atque illum quidem parentem hujus universitatis invenire, difficile; et, quum jam inveneris, indicare in vulgus, nefas_: "to find out the parent of the universe is difficult, and when found, to reveal him to the common people is a sin," says Cicero. We talk of power, truth, justice — words signifying some great thing — but that thing itself we neither see nor conceive. We say that God fears, that God is angry, that God loves —
Immortalia mortali sermone notantes:
"Giving to things immortal mortal names."

These are all agitations and emotions that cannot exist in God in our form, nor can we imagine them in his. Only God can know himself and interpret his own works; and he does it in our language, stepping out of himself to stoop to us who crawl on the earth. How can prudence — which is the choice between good and evil — properly be attributed to one whom no evil can touch? How can reason and understanding, which we use to reach apparent things by way of obscure ones, since nothing is obscure to him? How justice, which gives every one his due, a thing born of the society and community of men — how is that in God? How temperance, which is the moderation of bodily pleasures that have no place in the Divinity? Fortitude to support pain, labour, and danger belongs to him as little as the others. These three things have no access to him. Which is why Aristotle holds him equally exempt from virtue and vice: _Neque gratia, neque ira teneri potest; quod quæ talia essent, imbecilla essent omnia_: "He can be touched neither by favour nor by anger, since whatever was such would be weak."

The share we have in the knowledge of truth, such as it is, is not won by our own strength. God has plainly let us understand as much, by the witnesses he has chosen out of the common people — simple, ignorant men he was pleased to employ to instruct us in his wonderful secrets. Our faith is not of our own getting; it is purely the gift of another's bounty. It is not by meditation, not by the force of our understanding, that we have acquired our religion, but by foreign authority and command — wherein the weakness of our own judgment helps us more than any strength of it, and our blindness more than our clear sight. We know whatever we know of the divine wisdom more through our ignorance than through our knowledge. No wonder, then, that our natural and earthly faculties cannot grasp that supernatural and heavenly knowledge. Let us bring nothing of our own but obedience and submission. For as it is written: "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and bring to nothing the understanding of the prudent. Where is the wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the disputer of this world? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world? For after that, in the wisdom of God, the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe."

Finally, if I were to examine whether it is in man's power to find what he seeks, and whether the long search in which he has busied himself for so many ages has enriched him with any new strength or any solid truth — I believe he will confess, if he speaks his conscience, that all he has gained by so long an inquiry is to have learned to recognize his own weakness. We have only, through long study, confirmed and verified the natural ignorance we were in before. The same thing has happened to truly wise men that happens to the ears of corn: they shoot up and hold their heads high while empty, but once full and swollen with grain in maturity they begin to droop and bow. So men, having tried and sounded all things, and having found in that mass of knowledge and that store of so many various things nothing solid, nothing firm — nothing but vanity — have given up their presumption and acknowledged their natural condition. It is what Velleius reproaches Cotta and Cicero with, "that they had learned of Philo that they had learned nothing." Pherecydes, one of the seven sages, writing to Thales on his deathbed, said: "I have given orders to my people, after my burial, to bring my writings to you. If they please you and the other sages, publish them; if not, suppress them. They contain no certainty that I myself am satisfied with. Nor do I pretend to know the truth or to attain to it. I open things rather than discover them." The wisest man that ever lived, asked what he knew, answered, "He knew this — that he knew nothing." Thereby he verified what has been said: that the greatest part of what we know is the least of what we do not know; that even what we think we know is only a piece, and a very small piece, of our ignorance. We know things in dreams, says Plato, and are ignorant of them in truth. _Omnes pene veteres nihil cognosci, nihil percipi, nihil sciri posse dixerunt; angustos sensus, imbecilles animos, brevia curricula vitae._ "Almost all the ancients declared that nothing could be known, perceived, or understood; that the senses are too limited, men's minds too weak, the course of life too short." And of Cicero himself, who owed his learning everything he was worth, Valerius says: "He began to lose his taste for letters in his old age; and even at his studies he was very independent of any one party, following what he thought probable now in one sect, now in another, forever wavering under the doubts of the Academy." _Dicendum est, sed ita ut nihil affirment, quaeram omnia, dubitans plerumque, et mihi diffidens._ "I must speak, but in such a way as to affirm nothing; I inquire into everything, but mostly in doubt, and distrusting myself."

I would have too easy a game if I considered man in his common way of living, in the gross. And yet I might do so by his own rule — for he judges truth not by weight but by number of votes. Let us set the common people aside,
Qui vigilans stertit,.... Mortua cui vita est prope jam vivo atque videnti;
"Half of his life by lazy sleep's possess'd, And when awake his soul but nods at best;"

who neither feel nor judge, and let most of their natural faculties lie idle. I will take man at his highest. Let us consider him in that small number of excellent men, picked out from the rest, who, gifted with a remarkable natural force, have moreover sharpened and tempered it by care, study, and art, and raised it to the highest pitch of wisdom it can reach. They have shaped their souls to every bent and bias, propped and supported them with every foreign help, enriched and adorned them with everything they could borrow inside or outside this world. In these men is set the supreme height that human nature can attain. They have ordered the world with politics and laws. They have instructed it with arts and sciences, and by the example of their admirable manners. None but such men will count with me — their testimony and their experience. Let us see how far they have gone and where they stopped. The errors and failures we shall find among these men, the world may boldly take to itself as its own.

Whoever goes searching for anything must come to one of these conclusions: that he has found it, that it cannot be found, or that he is still searching. All philosophy divides into these three branches; its design is to seek out truth, knowledge, and certainty. The Peripatetics, Epicureans, Stoics, and others have thought they had found it. They established the sciences we have, and treated them as certain knowledge. Clitomachus, Carneades, and the Academics have despaired in their search, and concluded that truth could not be grasped by our understanding. The result with them is weakness and human ignorance. This sect has had the most numerous and noblest followers. Pyrrho and the other skeptics or epechists — whose dogmas many of the ancients trace back to Homer, the seven sages, Archilochus, and Euripides, with Zeno, Democritus, and Xenophanes added to the list — say they are still inquiring after truth. They conclude that the others, who think they have found it, are infinitely deceived; and that the second group, who decide that human reason cannot attain to it, are guilty of too daring a vanity, for to set up a measure of our power to know and judge the difficulty of things is itself a great and extreme knowledge, of which they doubt man is capable:
Nil sciri quisquis putat, id quoque nescit, An sciri possit; quam se nil scire fatetur.
"He that says nothing can be known, o'erthrows His own opinion, for he nothing knows, So knows not that."

The ignorance that knows itself, judges and condemns itself, is not absolute ignorance. To be that, it would have to be ignorant of itself. So the Pyrrhonians' profession is to waver, doubt, and inquire — never to be sure of anything, never to vouch to themselves for anything. Of the three actions of the soul — imaginative, appetitive, and consentive — they accept the first two; the third they keep in suspense, neither inclining nor approving, however lightly. Zeno represented the movement of his imagination upon these divisions of the soul's faculties thus: an open hand stood for appearance; a half-closed hand with the fingers a little bent, consent; a clenched fist, comprehension; and when with the left hand he closed his right fist tighter, knowledge. Now this stance of their judgment — upright and inflexible, taking in every object without applying or consenting — leads them to their ataraxia, a peaceful condition of life, temperate, free of the agitations we feel from the impressions of opinion and supposed knowledge: out of which spring fear, greed, envy, immoderate desire, ambition, pride, superstition, love of novelty, rebellion, disobedience, obstinacy, and most of our bodily ills. Moreover, by the same means they are exempt from any jealousy about their own discipline. They argue very gently, fearing no retaliation in their disputes. When they say heavy things fall downward, they would be sorry to be believed and love to be contradicted, in order to breed doubt and suspension of judgment, which is their end. They put forward their propositions only to contest those they take to be in our belief. Take their arguments, they will as readily maintain the opposite — it is all one to them, they have no preference. Maintain that snow is black, they will argue it white; say it is neither one nor the other, they will maintain it is both. Hold by certain judgment that you know nothing, they will maintain you do. Yes, and if by an affirmative axiom you assure them you doubt, they will argue against you that you do not doubt, or that you cannot judge and determine that you doubt. And by this extremity of doubt, which jostles itself, they separate themselves off from many opinions, even from those they have variously maintained about doubt and ignorance. "Why should we not be allowed to doubt," they say, "as well as the dogmatists, of whom one says green and another yellow? Can anything be proposed to us to grant or deny that we may not consider as ambiguous?"
