And where others are carried — by the custom of their country, by parental instruction, or by accident as if by a tempest, without judgment or choice, often before the age of discretion — into this or that opinion, this or that Stoic or Epicurean sect, with which they are prepossessed, enslaved, and bound fast as to a thing they cannot leave: _Ad quamcumque disciplinam, velut tempestate, delati, ad eam, tanquam ad saxum, adhaerescunt_; "each clings to the doctrine he happens upon as to a rock onto which he has been thrown by a storm" — why should these not also be allowed to keep their liberty, and consider things without obligation or bondage? _Hoc liberiores et solutiores, quod integra illis est judicandi potestas_: "the freer and more unfettered for having full power of judgment." Is it not some advantage to be unhooked from the necessity that curbs others? Is it not better to stay suspended than to tangle yourself in the countless errors that human fancy has produced? Is it not far better to suspend your assent than to meddle in these wrangling and seditious divisions? "What shall I choose?" "Whatever you please, provided you do choose." A foolish answer; yet it is the answer all dogmatism seems to point to, by which we are not permitted to be ignorant even of what we are ignorant of.

Take the most eminent side, the one with the greatest reputation: it will never be so sure that you won't have to attack and contend with hundreds upon hundreds of adversaries to defend it. Isn't it better to stay out of this uproar? You are allowed to embrace Aristotle's opinions on the immortality of the soul with as much zeal as you would defend your honour and life, and to call Plato a liar on that point — and is it forbidden to doubt him? If Panaetius may maintain his opinion about augury, dreams, oracles, and prophecies, of which the Stoics had no doubt at all, why may a wise man not do the same in everything he dared to do in those matters he had learned from his masters, established by the common consent of the school he professes and belongs to? If it is a child that judges, he doesn't know what it is; if a wise man, he is prepossessed. They have reserved themselves a marvellous advantage in battle, having relieved themselves of the trouble of defence. If you strike them, they don't mind, as long as they strike too; they turn everything to their own use. If they win, your argument is lame; if you win, theirs is; if they fall short, they verify ignorance; if you fall short, you do. If they prove that nothing is known, well and good; if they cannot prove it, well and good too: _Ut quum in eadem re paria contrariis in partibus momenta inveniuntur, facilius ab utraque parte assertio sustineatur_: "That when equal weights are found on opposite sides of the same matter, judgment may be more easily suspended on both." And they reckon they can show why a thing is false more easily than why it is true; what is not, more easily than what is; what they do not believe, more easily than what they do. Their way of speaking is: "I assert nothing; it is no more so than otherwise, or than neither one nor the other; I don't understand it. Appearances are everywhere equal; the law of speaking for or against is the same. Nothing seems true that cannot seem false." Their sacramental word is — that is to say, "I stand, I stir not." That is the refrain of their song, and other refrains of the same stuff. The effect is a pure, entire, perfect, and absolute suspension of judgment. They use their reason to inquire and debate, but not to fix and determine. Whoever can imagine a perpetual confession of ignorance — a judgment with no bias, no leaning, no inclination, on any occasion whatever — conceives a true idea of Pyrrhonism. I express this fancy as well as I can, because many find it hard to conceive, and the authors themselves represent it somewhat variously and obscurely.

As to what concerns the conduct of life, they here go with the common fashion. They yield to their natural inclinations, to the power and impulse of the passions, to the constitution of laws and customs, and to the tradition of the arts. _Non enim nos Deus ista scire, sed tantummodo uti, voluit._ "For God would not have us know these things, but only use them." They let their ordinary actions be guided by all this, without dispute or judgment. For this reason I cannot agree with what is said of Pyrrho by those who represent him as heavy and immovable, leading a kind of savage and unsociable life, standing in the way of carts, walking on the edge of cliffs, refusing to fit himself to the laws. This is to overload his discipline. He never made himself a stock or a stone; he showed himself a living man, talking, reasoning, enjoying every reasonable convenience and pleasure, using all his bodily and mental faculties in proper measure and reason. The fantastic, imagined, false privileges that man had usurped — lording it, ordaining, establishing — these he simply renounced. Yet there is no sect that is not forced to let its wise man follow several things he does not understand, perceive, or consent to, if he means to live. And if he goes to sea, he follows that plan, not knowing whether the voyage will succeed, and only insists on the soundness of the ship, the pilot's experience, the right season, and other such likely circumstances. After that he must go, and let himself be guided by appearances, provided there is no clear and manifest contradiction in them. He has a body, he has a soul; the senses push them, the mind spurs them on. And though he does not find in himself that proper and singular sign for judging, and perceives that he should not engage his consent — there may, after all, be false appearances equal to these true ones — yet he carries on the business of life with great liberty and ease. How many arts are there that profess to consist more in conjecture than in knowledge, that do not decide between true and false, but only follow what seems so! There are true and false, they say, and we have wherewith to seek them; but not to make them stay when we touch them. We are far more prudent letting ourselves be regulated by the order of the world, without inquiry. A soul cleared of prejudice has a marvellous advance toward tranquillity and rest. Men who judge and control their judges never quite submit to them.

How much more docile and easy to govern, both by the laws of religion and of civil polity, are simple and incurious minds than those over-vigilant wits that keep prattling on about divine and human causes! Nothing of human invention carries so great a show of likelihood and usefulness as this. It presents man naked and empty, confessing his natural weakness, fit to receive some foreign force from above, unfurnished of human resources and therefore the more apt to receive divine knowledge — setting his own judgment aside to make room for faith, neither disbelieving nor establishing any dogma against common observance, humble, obedient, teachable, studious, a sworn enemy of heresy, and consequently free of the vain and irreligious opinions introduced by false sects. It is a blank sheet ready to receive whatever forms the finger of God shall please to write on it. The more we resign and commit ourselves to God, and the more we renounce ourselves, the more we are worth. "Take in good part," says Ecclesiastes, "the things that present themselves to you, as they seem and taste from hand to mouth; the rest is beyond your knowledge." _Dominus novit cogitationes hominum, quoniam vanæ sunt_: "The Lord knows the thoughts of men, that they are but vanity."

So we see that of the three general sects of philosophy, two openly profess doubt and ignorance; and in the third, the Dogmatists', it is easy to see that most of them only put on this face of confidence and certainty

for the better effect: they were not so much concerned to establish certainty for us as to show how far they had gone in their search for truth. _Quam docti fingunt magis quam nôrunt_: "Which the learned rather invent than know." Timaeus, about to instruct Socrates in what he knew of the gods, the world, and men, proposes to speak to him as one man to another; and that it is enough if his reasons are probable, as another's would be, for exact reasons are not in his hands or in any mortal's. One of his followers has imitated this thus: _Ut potero, explicabo: nec tamen, ut Pythius Apollo, certa ut sint et fixa quæ dixero; sed, ut homunculus, probabilia conjecturâ sequens_: "I will explain as well as I am able, asserting yet — not as the Pythian oracle — that what I say is fixed and certain, but as a mere man, following probabilities by conjecture." And this on the natural and common subject of the contempt of death. He has elsewhere translated it from the very words of Plato: _Si forte, de Deorum naturâ ortuque mundi disserentes, minus id quod habemus in animo consequimur, haud erit mirum; aequum est enim meminisse, et me, qui disseram, hominem esse, et vos, qui judicetis, ut, si probabilia dicentur, nihil ultra requiratis?_ "If perhaps, in discoursing of the nature of God and the origin of the world, we don't quite reach what we have in mind, it will be no great wonder. For it is just you should remember that both I who speak and you who are to judge are men; so that if probabilities are offered, you should require no more." Aristotle ordinarily heaps up many other men's opinions and beliefs, comparing them with his own and showing us how much further he has gone, how much nearer he has come to the likeness of truth — for truth is not to be judged by the authority and testimony of others, which is why Epicurus religiously avoided quoting any of them in his writings. This is the prince of all the dogmatists, and yet he himself tells us that the more we know, the more room we have for doubt. In earnest, we sometimes see him muffle and wrap himself in such thick and inextricable obscurity that we do not know what to make of his counsel; it is in effect Pyrrhonism under a resolute form. Listen to Cicero's protest, who unfolds another's fancy by his own: _Qui requirunt quid de quâque re ipsi sentiamus, curiosius id faciunt quam necesse est... Hoc in philosophiâ ratio, contra omnia disserendi, nullamque rem aperte judicandi, profecta a Socrate, repetita ab Arcesilâ, confirmata a Carneade, usque ad nostram viget aetatem... Hi sumus, qui omnibus veris falsa quaedam adjuncta esse dicamus, tantâ similitudine, ut in iis nulla insit certe judicandi et assentiendi nota._ "Those who want to know what we think on every subject are more inquisitive than they need to be. This practice in philosophy of arguing against everything and absolutely concluding nothing, begun by Socrates, taken up by Arcesilaus, confirmed by Carneades, is still in vigour in our own time. We are those who declare that among all true things there is so great a mixture of false ones, so closely resembling them, that there can be in them no certain mark to direct us either to judge or assent." Why has not only Aristotle but most of the philosophers affected difficulty, if not to set a greater value on the vanity of the subject, and to amuse the curiosity of our minds by giving them this hollow and fleshless bone to pick? Clitomachus declared "that he could never make out from Carneades's writings what opinion he held." This is what made Epicurus affect to be obscure, and earned Heraclitus the epithet [--Greek--]. Difficulty is a coin the learned use, like conjurers, to conceal the vanity of their art — and human dullness easily takes it for current pay.
Claras, ob obscuram linguam, magis inter manes... Omnia enim stolidi magis admirantur amantque Inversis quæ sub verbis latitantia cernunt.
"Bombast and riddle best do puppies please, For fools admire and love such things as these; And a dull quibble, wrapt in dubious phrase, Up to the height doth their wise wonder raise."

Cicero rebukes some of his friends for giving more time to astrology, logic, and geometry than these were really worth, saying they were thereby diverted from the duties of life and from more profitable and proper studies. The Cyrenaic philosophers likewise despised physics and logic. Zeno, at the very opening of his books on the commonwealth, declared all the liberal arts useless. Chrysippus said that what Plato and Aristotle had written about logic, they had only done in sport, by way of exercise; he could not believe they had spoken in earnest about so empty a thing. Plutarch says the same of metaphysics. Epicurus would have said as much of rhetoric, grammar, poetry, and mathematics, and — natural philosophy aside — of all the sciences. And Socrates of them all, except the one that treats of manners and life. Whoever asked Socrates for instruction, he would first demand an account of his present and past way of life, which he then examined and judged, holding all other learning subordinate and superfluous to that. _Parum mihi placeant eae litterae quae ad virtutem doctoribus nihil profuerunt._ "That learning is of small worth to me which has not profited its teachers themselves with virtue." Most of the arts have been likewise dismissed by this same kind of knowing; but they did not consider that it was beside their purpose to exercise their wits on those very matters that offered no solid benefit.

As for the rest, some have taken Plato as a dogmatist, others as a doubter, and others as both, in different places. Socrates, the conductor of his dialogues, is forever asking questions and stirring up debate, never deciding, never satisfying, and professes to have no science but that of opposing himself. Homer, their author, has equally laid the foundations of every sect of philosophy, to show how indifferent it was which way we chose. They say ten different sects sprang from Plato; and indeed, in my opinion, no teaching ever stumbled or halted if his does not.

Socrates said that midwives, in taking up the trade of helping others bring forth, gave up bringing forth themselves; and that by the title of wise man, which the gods had given him, he had been disqualified in his virile and mental love from the faculty of bringing forth — and contented himself with helping and assisting those who could: opening their nature, easing the passage, facilitating the birth, judging the infant, baptizing, nourishing, fortifying, swathing, and circumcising it, exercising his understanding in the perils and fortunes of others.

So it is with most of this third sort of authors, as the ancients have noted in the writings of Anaxagoras, Democritus, Parmenides, Xenophanes, and others. Their way of writing is doubtful both in substance and design, inquiring rather than teaching, even when they mix some dogmatic stretches into the style. Don't we see the same thing in Seneca and Plutarch? How many contradictions are to be found in them if a man pries narrowly! So many that the reconciling lawyers ought first to reconcile each of them with himself. Plato seems to have affected this method of philosophizing in dialogues, so that he might with greater decency, through several mouths, deliver the diversity and variety of his own fancies. It is just as well to treat things variously as conformably — and better, that is to say more fully and to greater profit. Take an example from ourselves: judgments are the highest point of all dogmatic and definitive speech; and yet those _arrêts_ our parliaments deliver to the people, even the most exemplary, the ones most fit to nourish in them the reverence due that dignity — owing chiefly to the competence of the persons involved — draw their beauty not so much from the conclusion (with judges, an everyday matter) as from the heat and dispute of the various and contrary arguments that the matter of law and equity allows. And the broadest field for reproach that some philosophers have against others is drawn from the diversities and contradictions in which every one of them is caught up — either on purpose, to show the wavering of the human mind on every subject, or unwittingly compelled by the slipperiness and incomprehensibility of all matter. Which is the sense of the maxim: "In a slippery and sliding place let us suspend our belief." For, as Euripides says,
"God's various works perplex the thoughts of men."

Just like the line Empedocles, as if seized by a divine fury and compelled by truth, scattered here and there in his writings: "No, no, we feel nothing, we see nothing; everything is hidden from us; there is not one thing of which we can say positively what it is." In the words of Scripture: _Cogitationes mortalium timidae, et incertae adinventiones nostrae et providentiae._ "For the thoughts of mortal men are fearful, and our devices and forethoughts uncertain." It is not strange that men, despairing of overtaking what they hunt, have not lost the pleasure of the chase; the study is so pleasant in itself — so pleasant that among the pleasures the Stoics forbid even the one that comes from the exercise of the mind, will have it curbed, and find a kind of intemperance in too much knowledge.

Democritus, having eaten figs at his table that tasted of honey, fell at once to wondering with himself where this unusual sweetness came from; and to be satisfied, he was about to rise and go see the place the figs had been gathered from. His maid, noticing this and knowing the cause, told him with a smile that he need not bother himself, for she had put the figs in a jar in which there had been honey. He was vexed at the discovery, that she had robbed him of the occasion for inquiry and his curiosity of matter to work on. "Go your way," he said. "You have done me an injury; but I will look for the cause as though it were natural" — and would gladly have found a true reason for a false and imagined effect. This story of a famous and great philosopher shows us very clearly that studious passion that drives us after things we despair of acquiring. Plutarch gives a similar example of someone who would not have his doubt resolved, lest he lose the pleasure of inquiring into it — like the other man who would not let his physician relieve the thirst of his fever, lest he lose the pleasure of quenching it by drinking. _Satius est supervacua discere, quam nihil._ "It is better to learn more than necessary than nothing at all." Just as, in every kind of feeding, the pleasure of eating is very often by itself, and what we take, agreeable to the palate, is not always nourishing or wholesome — so what our minds draw from learning does not cease to be pleasant though there is nothing in it nutritious or healthful. So they say: "The contemplation of nature is a proper diet for our minds. It raises and elevates us, makes us disdain low and earthly things by comparing them with what is heavenly and high. The mere inquiry into great and hidden things is very pleasant, even to those who get from it no other benefit than the reverence and awe of judging it." That is what they profess. The vain image of this sickly curiosity is still more plain in this other example they so often cite: "Eudoxus wished and prayed to the gods that he might once see the sun close up, to grasp its form, size, and beauty — even though he should be burned up in the same instant." He would have paid with his life for a knowledge of which the use and possession would be taken from him at the same moment; and for this sudden and vanishing knowledge he would have lost all the other knowledge he then had, or might afterward acquire.

I cannot easily persuade myself that Epicurus, Plato, and Pythagoras gave us their atom, idea, and numbers for hard currency. They were too wise to ground their articles of faith on things so debatable and uncertain. But in the obscurity and ignorance the world then was in, each of these great men tried to present some kind of image or reflection of light, and worked their brains to invent things that might have a pleasant and subtle appearance — provided that, though false, they could hold their ground against opponents. _Unicuique ista pro ingenio finguntur, non ex scientiae vi._ "Such things every one fancies according to his wit, not by any force of knowledge."
One of the ancients, reproached "that he professed philosophy and yet in his own judgment made no great account of it," answered, "That is truly to philosophize."

They wished to consider everything, weigh everything, and found that an employment well suited to our natural curiosity. Some things they wrote for the benefit of public society — their religions, for instance — and on that score it was reasonable they should not push public opinions to the quick, lest they disturb the common obedience to the laws and customs of their country.

Plato treats this mystery with rather manifest irony. Where he writes by his own method, he gives no fixed rule. When he plays the legislator, he borrows a magisterial and positive style and boldly foists in his most fantastic inventions, fit to persuade the common people, impossible for himself to believe — knowing very well how fit we are to receive every kind of impression, especially the most immoderate and preposterous. And yet in his _Laws_ he takes singular care that nothing be sung in public except poetry whose fictions and fabulous tales tend to some useful end; it being so easy to imprint every kind of phantasm on human minds that it would be unjust not to feed them with profitable untruths rather than untruths that are useless and harmful. He says very roundly, in his _Republic_, "That it is often necessary, for the benefit of men, to deceive them." It is easy to see that some of the sects have followed truth more, and others utility — by which the latter have won their reputation. It is the misery of our condition that what presents itself to our imagination as truest is often not the most useful for life. The boldest sects — the Epicurean, the Pyrrhonian, the New Academic — are nevertheless forced to submit to the civil law at the end of the day.

There are other subjects which they have tossed about, some to the right, others to the left, every one trying — rightly or not — to give them some colour. Having found nothing so abstruse that they would not venture to speak of it, they are often forced to forge weak and ridiculous conjectures; not that they themselves took these as any foundation, or as establishing any certain truth, but merely for exercise. _Non tam id sensisse quod dicerent, quam exercere ingenia materiae difficultate videntur voluisse._ "They seem not so much to have believed what they said as to have wanted to exercise their wits on the difficulty of the matter." And if we did not take it this way, how could we account for so much inconstancy, variety, and vanity of opinion as we see produced by those excellent and admirable men? What, for example, can be more vain than to try to imagine, to guess at God, by our analogies and conjectures? To direct and govern him and the world by our capacities and our laws? To serve ourselves, at the divinity's expense, with the small share of capacity he has been pleased to allow our natural condition; and because we cannot stretch our sight to his glorious throne, to bring him down to our corruption and misery?

Of all human and ancient opinions about religion, the most likely and most excusable to me is the one that recognized God as an incomprehensible power, the source and preserver of all things, all goodness, all perfection, receiving and accepting in good part the honour and reverence man paid him under whatever method, name, or ceremony —
Jupiter omnipotens, rerum, regumque, deûmque, Progenitor, genitrixque.
"Jove, the almighty, author of all things, The father, mother, of both gods and kings."

This zeal has universally been looked on from heaven with a gracious eye. All governments have reaped fruit from their devotion. Impious men and acts have everywhere had fitting outcomes. Pagan histories acknowledge dignity, order, justice, prodigies, and oracles employed for their profit and instruction in their fabulous religions — God in his mercy graciously consenting, through these temporal benefits, to nourish the tender principles of the brutish knowledge of him that natural reason gave them, through the deceiving images of their dreams. Not only deceiving and false, but impious and injurious, are those that man has forged of his own invention. And of all the religions St. Paul found in repute at Athens, the one they had dedicated "to the unknown God" seemed to him most excusable.

Pythagoras shadowed the truth a little more closely, judging that the knowledge of this first cause and being of beings ought to be indefinite, without limit, without declaration; that it was nothing else than the utmost effort of our imagination toward perfection, each enlarging the idea according to the talent of his capacity. But if Numa attempted to model his people's devotion on this plan — to tie them to a purely mental religion, with no fixed object and no material mixture — he undertook a useless thing. The human mind could never bear up, floating in such an infinity of formless thoughts. Some definite image must be presented to it after its own model. The divine majesty has, in a sense, allowed himself to be circumscribed in bodily limits for our benefit. His supernatural and heavenly sacraments wear the signs of our earthly condition; his worship goes by perceptible offices and words — for it is man who believes and prays. I omit the other arguments on this subject; but a man would have a hard time making me believe that the sight of our crucifixes, the picture of our Saviour's passion, the ornaments and ceremonial movements of our churches, the voices tuned to the devotion of our thoughts, and the stirring of the senses, do not warm the souls of the people with a religious passion of very advantageous effect.
Among those to whom they have given a body, as necessity required in that universal blindness, I think I would lean most to those who worshipped the sun:

La Lumière commune, L'oil du monde; et si Dieu au chef porte des yeux, Les rayons du soleil sont ses yeulx radieux, Qui donnent vie à touts, nous maintiennent et gardent, Et les faictsdes humains en ce monde regardent: Ce beau, ce grand soleil qui nous faict les saisons, Selon qu'il entre ou sort de ses douze maisons; Qui remplit l'univers de ses vertus cognues; Qui d'un traict de ses yeulx nous dissipe les nues; L'esprit, l'ame du monde, ardent et flamboyant, En la course d'un jour tout le Ciel tournoyant; Plein d'immense grandeur, rond, vagabond, et ferme; Lequel tient dessoubs luy tout le monde pour terme: En repos, sans repos; oysif, et sans séjour; Fils aisné de nature, et le père du jour:

"The common light that equal shines on all, Diffused around the whole terrestrial ball; And, if the almighty Ruler of the skies Has eyes, the sunbeams are his radiant eyes, That life and safety give to young and old, And all men's actions upon earth behold. This great, this beautiful, the glorious sun, Who makes their course the varied seasons run; That with his virtues fills the universe, And with one glance can sullen clouds disperse; Earth's life and soul, that, flaming in his sphere, Surrounds the heavens in one day's career; Immensely great, moving yet firm and round, Who the whole world below has made his bound; At rest, without rest, idle without stay, Nature's first son, and father of the day:"

for, beyond this grandeur and beauty, it is the only piece of this machine we make out at the remotest distance from us — and so little known on that account that they may be pardoned for entering into such admiration and reverence of it.

Thales, who first inquired into this kind of matter, believed God to be a Spirit that made all things of water. Anaximander, that the gods were always dying and coming back into life, and that there were an infinite number of worlds. Anaximenes, that the air was God, procreate and immense, always in motion. Anaxagoras was the first of the opinion that the description and arrangement of all things was directed by the power and reason of an infinite spirit. Alcmaeon assigned divinity to the sun, moon, stars, and the soul. Pythagoras made God a spirit spread through the nature of all things, from which our souls are drawn. Parmenides, a circle surrounding the heavens, holding the world up by the heat of light. Empedocles pronounced the four elements, of which all things are composed, to be gods. Protagoras had nothing to say whether they were or were not, or what they were. Democritus thought at one time that the images and their circulations were gods; at another, the nature that throws off those images; and then, our science and intelligence. Plato divides his belief into several opinions: in his _Timaeus_, he says that the Father of the World cannot be named; in his _Laws_, that men should not inquire into his being; and elsewhere, in the very same books, he makes the world, the heavens, the stars, the earth, and our souls into gods, accepting moreover those received by ancient institution in every republic.

Xenophon reports a similar perplexity in Socrates's teaching: at one point men are not to inquire into the form of God, then a moment later he makes him hold that the sun is God, and the soul God; that there is only one God, and then that there are many. Speusippus, Plato's nephew, makes God a certain power that governs all things, and says he has a soul. Aristotle says at one time it is the spirit, at another the world; at one time he gives the world another master, at another he makes God the heat of heaven. Xenocrates makes eight: five named among the planets; a sixth composed of all the fixed stars as so many members; the seventh and eighth, the sun and moon. Heraclides Ponticus does nothing but float between opinions, finally stripping God of sense and making him shift from one form to another, until in the end he calls him heaven and earth. Theophrastus wanders in the same indecision among his fancies, attributing the superintendence of the world now to understanding, now to heaven, now to the stars. Strato says it is nature, having the power of generation, increase, and diminution, without form or sentience. Zeno says it is the law of nature, commanding good and forbidding evil — which law is an animal; and he sets aside the customary gods, Jupiter, Juno, Vesta. Diogenes of Apollonia, that it is air. Xenophanes makes God round, seeing and hearing, not breathing, and having nothing in common with human nature. Aristo thinks the form of God incomprehensible, strips him of sense, and does not know whether he is an animal or something else. Cleanthes at one time supposes it to be reason, at another the world, at another the soul of nature, at another the supreme heat rolling and surrounding all. Perseus, Zeno's disciple, was of the opinion that men have given the title of god to those who have been useful and added some notable advantage to human life — even to useful things themselves. Chrysippus made a confused heap of all the preceding theories, and counted, among a thousand forms of gods he invents, men who have been deified. Diagoras and Theodorus flatly denied that there were any gods at all. Epicurus makes the gods shining, transparent, and air-permeable, lodged as between two forts, between two worlds, safe from blows, clothed in human shape and with members like ours — members that serve them no purpose:
Ego Deum genus esse semper duxi, et dicam colitum; Sed eos non curare opinor quid agat humanum genus.
"I ever thought that gods above there were, But do not think they care what men do here."

Trust your philosophy, gentlemen, and boast that you have found the prize in the cake — when you see what a rattle is here with so many philosophical heads! The perplexity of so many worldly forms has won this much from me: that customs and opinions contrary to mine no longer so much displease me as instruct me; that they make me less proud and more humble when I compare them. And any other choice but what comes from the express and immediate hand of God seems to me a choice of very little privilege. The policies of the world are no less opposed to one another on this subject than the schools — by which we can see that fortune itself is not more variable and inconstant, nor more blind and inconsiderate, than our reason. The things most unknown are most apt to be deified; and to make gods of ourselves, as the ancients did, exceeds the extreme weakness of understanding. I would much rather go along with those who worshipped the serpent, the dog, or the ox — since their nature and being is less known to us, and we have more room to imagine what we please about those beasts and to ascribe to them extraordinary faculties. But to have made gods of our own condition, whose imperfections we ought to know, and to have given them desire, anger, revenge, marriages, generation, alliances, love, jealousy, our limbs and bones, our fevers and pleasures, our death and funerals — this can only have proceeded from a marvellous drunkenness of the human understanding.
Quæ procul usque adeo divino ab numine distant, Inque Deûm numéro quæ sint indigna videri;
"From divine natures these so distant are, They are unworthy of that character."

_Formae, aetates, vestitus, ornatus noti sunt; genera, conjugia, cognationes, omniaque traducta ad similitudinem imbecillitatis humanae: nam et perturbatis animis inducuntur; accipimus enim deorum cupiditates, aegritudines, iracundias_; "Their forms, ages, clothes, and ornaments are known; their lineages, marriages, and kinships, and everything brought down to the likeness of human weakness; for they are represented to us with troubled minds, and we read of the lusts, sicknesses, and angers of the gods." Having ascribed divinity not only to faith, virtue, honour, concord, liberty, victory, and piety, but to voluptuousness, fraud, death, envy, old age, misery, fear, fever, ill fortune, and the other injuries of our fragile and passing life:
Quid juvat hoc, templis nostros inducere mores? O curvæ in terris animæ et colestium inanes!
"O earth-born souls! by earth-born passions led, To every spark of heav'nly influence dead! Think ye that what man values will inspire In minds celestial the same base desire?"

The Egyptians, with an impudent prudence, forbade on pain of hanging that anyone should say their gods, Serapis and Isis, had formerly been men; yet no one was ignorant they had been. Their effigies, represented with a finger to the mouth, signified (says Varro) the mysterious order to their priests to conceal their mortal origin, since revealing it would by necessary consequence cancel all the veneration paid to them. Since man so much desired to equal himself to God, he would have done better, says Cicero, to draw those divine conditions to himself, and bring them down here below, than to send his corruption and misery up on high. But, to take it as it stands, he has done both, with equal vanity of opinion.

When philosophers search closely into the hierarchy of their gods, and make a great fuss about distinguishing their alliances, offices, and powers, I cannot believe they speak as they think. When Plato describes Pluto's orchard for us, and the bodily conveniences or pains that attend us after the ruin and dissolution of our bodies, and fits them to the feelings we have in this life —
Secreti celant calles, et myrtea circum Sylva tegit; curæ non ipsâ in morte relinquunt;
"In secret vales and myrtle groves they lie, Nor do cares leave them even when they die."

When Mahomet promises his followers a Paradise hung with tapestry, gilded and enamelled with gold and precious stones, furnished with women of striking beauty, rare wines, and delicate dishes — it is easy to see these are deceivers who fit their promises to our sensuality, to attract and lure us by hopes and opinions matched to our mortal appetites. And yet some among us have fallen into the same error, promising themselves after the resurrection a terrestrial and temporal life accompanied by every kind of worldly convenience and pleasure. Can we believe that Plato — he who had such heavenly conceptions, and was so well acquainted with the Divinity as to be called the Divine Plato — ever thought that the poor creature man had anything in him that could be applied to that incomprehensible power? That he believed the weak holds we are able to take were capable, or the force of our understanding sufficient, to share in beatitude or eternal pain? We should then say to him, on behalf of human reason: "If the pleasures you promise us in the next life are of the same kind I have enjoyed here below, that has nothing in common with infinity. Though all five of my natural senses were loaded with pleasure and my soul filled with all the contentment it could hope for or desire, we know what it all comes to: it would be nothing. If anything of mine is there, there is nothing divine in it. If this is no more than may belong to our present condition, it can have no value. All mortal contentment is mortal. Even the knowledge of our parents, children, and friends — if that can affect and delight us in the other world, if it still gives us satisfaction there — we are still in earthly and finite conveniences. We cannot conceive, as we ought, the greatness of those high and divine promises if we could in any sort conceive them. To have a worthy imagination of them, we must imagine them unimaginable, inexplicable, and incomprehensible, and entirely other than those of our wretched experience." "Eye has not seen," says St. Paul, "nor ear heard, neither has entered into the heart of man, the things that God has prepared for them that love him." And if, to make us capable, our being were to be reformed and changed (as you, Plato, say, by your purifications), it would have to be a change so extreme and total that, by physical doctrine, it would no longer be us:
Hector erat tunc cum bello certabat; at ille Tractus ab Æmonio non erat Hector eqao;
He Hector was whilst he could fight, but when Dragg'd by Achilles' steeds, no Hector then;
It would have to be something else that received those rewards:
Quod mutatur... dissolvitur; interit ergo; Trajiciuntur enim partes, atque ordine migrant.
"Things changed dissolved are, and therefore die; Their parts are mix'd, and from their order fly."

For in Pythagoras's metempsychosis, and the changes of habitation he imagined for souls, can we believe that the lion in whom Caesar's soul is now lodged espouses Caesar's passions, or that the lion is Caesar? If it were still Caesar, the people who, arguing this with Plato, reproach him would be right — that the son might be seen riding his mother transformed into a mule, and other such absurdities. And can we believe that in the changes of bodies of animals into others of the same kind, the newcomers are not other than their predecessors? From a phoenix's ashes, they say, a worm is born, and from that another phoenix; who can imagine that this second phoenix is the same as the first? We see our silkworms, as it were, die and wither; from the withered body a butterfly is produced, and from that another worm — how absurd it would be to imagine that this was still the first! What once ceased to be is no more:

Nec, si materiam nostram collegerit ætas Post obitum, rursumque redegerit, ut sita nunc est, Atque iterum nobis fuerint data lumina vitæ, Pertineat quidquam tamen ad nos id quoque factum, Interrupta semel cum sit repetentia nostra.

"Neither tho' time should gather and restore Our matter to the form it was before, And give again new light to see withal, Would that new figure us concern at all; Or we again ever the same be seen, Our being having interrupted been."

And, Plato, when you say in another place that it is the spiritual part of man that will be concerned in enjoying the reward of another life, you are telling us something with as little appearance of truth:
Scilicet, avolsis radicibus, ut nequit ullam Dispicere ipsa oculus rem, seorsum corpore toto;
"No more than eyes once from their optics torn, Can ever after any thing discern;"
For on that account it would no longer be man, nor consequently us, who were to enjoy this. We are made up of two principal essential parts, whose separation is the death and ruin of our being:
Inter enim jecta est vital pausa, vageque Deerrarunt passim motus ab sensibus omnes;
"When once that pause of life is come between, 'Tis just the same as we had never been;"
We cannot say that the man suffers when the worms feed upon his members, and the earth consumes them:
Et nihil hoc ad nos, qui coitu conjugioque Corporis atque animæ consistimus uniter apti.
"What's that to us? for we are only we, While soul and body in one frame agree."

Moreover, on what foundation of their justice can the gods take notice of or reward man's virtuous actions after his death, since it was they themselves who set him on the path and in the mind to do them? And why should they be offended at, or punish him for, his wicked ones, since they themselves created him in so frail a condition, and could, with one glance of their will, have prevented him from falling? Might not Epicurus, with great show of human reason, have objected this to Plato, did he not often shield himself with the saying: "That it is impossible to establish anything certain about the immortal nature by the mortal"? Reason does nothing but err throughout, but especially when she meddles with divine things. Who perceives this more evidently than we? For although we have given her certain and infallible principles, and have lit her steps with the sacred lamp of truth it has pleased God to communicate to us, we still see daily that if she swerves the least bit from the ordinary path, if she strays from the way set out and beaten by the church, how soon she loses, confounds, and entangles herself, tumbling and floating in this vast, turbulent, surging sea of human opinions, without restraint, without any determinate end. As soon as she loses that great common road, she enters a labyrinth of a thousand cross-paths.

Man cannot be anything but what he is, nor imagine anything beyond the reach of his capacity. "It is greater presumption," says Plutarch, "in mere men to attempt to speak and discourse of the gods and demi-gods, than in a man utterly ignorant of music to deliver an opinion on singing, or in a man who has never seen a camp to dispute about arms and warfare, presuming by some slight conjecture to understand the effects of an art he is wholly a stranger to." Antiquity, I believe, thought to pay a compliment to the divine grandeur, and to add something to it, by likening it to man — investing it with man's faculties, decking it out with his ugly humours and most shameful necessities; offering it our food to eat, presenting it with our dances, mummeries, and farces to amuse it, our clothes to cover it, our houses to live in; coaxing it with the scent of incense and the sound of music, with festoons and nosegays; and to suit it to our vicious passions, flattering its justice with inhuman vengeance, and with the ruin and dissipation of the things it created and preserves. So Tiberius Sempronius burnt the rich spoils and arms he had taken from the enemy in Sardinia, as a sacrifice to Vulcan; Paulus Aemilius did the same with the spoils of Macedonia, to Mars and Minerva; Alexander, on reaching the Indian Ocean, threw several great vessels of gold into the sea in honour of Thetis; and loaded her altars too with the slaughter not only of innocent beasts, but of men, as several nations, ours included, were commonly used to do. I believe there is no nation under the sun that has not done the same:
Sulmone creatos Quatuor hîc juvenes, totidem quos educat Ufens, Viventes rapit, inferias quos immolet umbris.
"Four sons of Sulmo, four whom Ufens bred, He took in flight, and living victims led, To please the ghost of Pallas, and expire In sacrifice before his fun'ral pyre."

The Getae held themselves immortal, and considered their death nothing but a journey to their god Zamolxis. Every five years they dispatched one of their number to him, to beg whatever necessities they needed. This envoy was chosen by lot. The manner of dispatching him, after he had been instructed by word of mouth what he was to deliver, was this: three of those present held up javelins, on which the rest threw his body with all their force. If he were wounded in some mortal part and died on the spot, it was taken as a sure sign of divine favour; if he escaped, he was viewed as a wicked, accursed wretch, and another was sent in his place after the same manner. Amestris, mother of Xerxes, when she had grown old, had fourteen young men of the best families of Persia buried alive at once, according to the religion of the country, to gratify some underworld deity. Even today the idols of Temixtitan are cemented with the blood of small children, and the gods take delight in no sacrifice but these pure and infant souls — a justice thirsty for innocent blood:
Tantum religio potuit suadere maloram.
"Such impious use was of religion made, So many demon acts it could persuade."

The Carthaginians sacrificed their own children to Saturn; those who had none of their own bought them from others, while the father and mother were obliged to attend the ceremony with a glad and contented face.

It was a strange fancy to think to gratify the divine bounty with our afflictions — like the Lacedemonians, who feasted their Diana with the tormenting of young boys, whom they had whipped for her sake, very often to death. It was a savage humour to imagine you could please the architect by tearing down his building, and to think to lift the punishment due the guilty by punishing the innocent. As if poor Iphigenia, at the port of Aulis, by her death and immolation should acquit, before God, the whole army of the Greeks from all the crimes they had committed —
Et casta inceste, nubendi tempore in ipso, Hostia concideret mactatu mosta parentis;
"That the chaste virgin in her nuptial band Should die by an unnat'ral father's hand;"

And that the two noble and generous souls of the two Decii, father and son, to win the favour of the gods for Rome's affairs, should hurl themselves into the thick of the enemy: _Quo fuit tanta deorum iniquitas, ut placari populo Romano non possent, nisi tales viri occidissent?_ "How great an injustice in the gods was it that they could not be reconciled to the people of Rome unless such men perished!" To which one may add that it is not for the criminal to have himself scourged according to his own measure, nor at his own time. That belongs entirely to the judge, who counts nothing as punishment but the penalty he appoints, and cannot call that punishment which proceeds from the consent of the one who suffers. Divine vengeance presupposes our absolute dissent, both for its justice and for our own penalty. So it was a ridiculous humour of Polycrates, tyrant of Samos, who, to interrupt the unbroken run of his good fortune and balance it, threw the dearest and most precious jewel he had into the sea — thinking by this voluntary, anticipated mishap to bribe and satisfy the turn of fortune. And she, to mock his folly, contrived that the same jewel returned to his hands, found in the belly of a fish. And to what end were those tearings and dismemberments of the Corybantes, the Maenads, and, in our own time, the Mahometans, who slash their faces, breasts, and limbs to gratify their prophet? Since the offence lies in the will, not in the breast, eyes, genitals, shoulders, or throat. _Tantus est perturbatae mentis, et sedibus suis pulsae, furor, ut sic dii placentur, quemadmodum ne homines quidem saeviunt._ "So great is the fury of a mind disturbed and driven from its seat, that men think to appease the gods in ways that men themselves are not so cruel as to approve." The use of this natural fabric of ours concerns not only us, but also the service of God and other men. It is as unjust to wound or hurt it voluntarily as to kill ourselves on any pretext whatever. It seems great cowardice and treason to use cruelty upon the body's functions, stupid and servile as they are, and to destroy them — to spare the soul the care of governing them according to reason: _Ubi iratos deos timent, qui sic propitios habere merentur? In regiae libidinis voluptatem castrati sunt quidam; sed nemo sibi, ne vir esset, jubente domino, manus intulit._ "Where are they so afraid of the gods' anger as to deserve their favour at that rate? Some, indeed, have been made eunuchs for the lust of princes; but no man at his master's command has ever laid his own hand on himself to unman himself." So they filled their religion with several ill effects:
Sæpius olim Religio peperit scelerosa atque impia facta.
"In elder times Religion did commit most fearful crimes."
Now nothing of ours can in any way be compared or likened to the divine nature without staining it with much imperfection.

How can that infinite beauty, power, and goodness admit any correspondence or resemblance to such abject things as we are, without extreme wrong and manifest dishonour to his divine greatness? _Infirmum dei fortius est hominibus; et stultum dei sapientius est hominibus._ "For the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men." Stilpo the philosopher, asked "Whether the gods are delighted with our adorations and sacrifices?" — "You are indiscreet," he answered; "let us withdraw apart if you want to talk of such things." Nevertheless we prescribe bounds for him, we keep his power besieged with our reasons (and I call our ravings and dreams reason, by the dispensation of philosophy, which says "That the wicked man, and even the fool, go mad by reason, but a particular form of reason"). We would subject him to the weak and feeble appearances of our understandings — him who made both us and our knowledge. Because nothing is made of nothing, God therefore (we conclude) could not make the world without matter. What! Has God put into our hands the keys and most secret springs of his power? Is he bound not to exceed the bounds of our knowledge? Suppose, O man, you have been able to mark some footprint of his effects: do you therefore think he has employed all he can, and crowded all his forms and ideas into this work? You see nothing but the order and revolution of this little cave in which you are lodged — if, indeed, you see even that much; whereas his divinity has an infinite jurisdiction beyond. This part is nothing compared with the whole:
Omnia cum colo, terràque, manque, Nil sunt ad summam summal totius omnem.
"The earth, the sea, and skies, from pole to pole, Are small, nay, nothing to the mighty whole."

It is a municipal law you cite — you do not know what is universal. Tie yourself to what you are subject to; but not him. He is not of your brotherhood, your fellow-citizen, or your companion. If he has in some sort communicated himself to you, it is not to lower himself to your littleness, nor to make you comptroller of his power. The human body cannot fly to the clouds; the rules are for you. The sun runs his ordinary course every day; the bounds of sea and land cannot be confused; water is unstable and without firmness; a wall, unless broken, is impenetrable to a solid body; a man cannot keep his life in the flames; he cannot be both in heaven and on earth, and corporally in a thousand places at once. These rules are for you; they concern you. He has shown Christians that he has freed himself from them all when he pleased. And really — almighty as he is — why should he have limited his power within any certain bounds? In whose favour should he have renounced his privilege? Your reason has no greater likelihood and foundation in anything than in what persuades you there is a plurality of worlds:
Terramque et solem, lunam, mare, estera quo rant, Non esse unica, sed numéro magis innumerali.
"That earth, sun, moon, sea, and the rest that are, Not single, but innumerable were."
The most eminent minds of older times believed it; and some in our own age, compelled by the appearances of human reason, do the same — since in this fabric we see, there is nothing single and one,
Cum in summà res nulla sit una, Unica quo gignatur, et unica solaque crescat;
"Since nothing's single in this mighty place, That can alone beget, alone increase;"

And since all the kinds are multiplied in some number, it does not seem likely that God should have made this one work alone without a companion, and that the matter of this form should have been totally drained into this single instance.
Quare etiam atque etiam tales fateare necesse est Esse alios alibi congressus materiali; Qualis hic est, avido complexu quem tenet æther.
"Wherefore 'tis necessary to confess That there must elsewhere be the like congress Of the like matter, which the airy space Holds fast within its infinite embrace."

Especially if it be a living creature, which its motions make so plausible that Plato affirms it, and many of our people either confirm or do not dare to deny it — no more than the ancient opinion that the heavens, the stars, and the other members of the world are creatures composed of body and soul: mortal as to their composition, but immortal by the determination of the Creator. Now if there are many worlds, as Democritus, Epicurus, and almost all philosophy believed, what do we know but that the principles and rules of this one of ours apply to the rest? They may very well have another form and another polity. Epicurus supposes them either like or unlike. We see in this world an infinite difference and variety, only by distance of place. Neither corn, nor wine, nor any of our animals are to be seen in that new corner of the world our fathers discovered; there everything is different. And in times past, only consider in how many parts of the world they had no knowledge of either Bacchus or Ceres. If Pliny and Herodotus are to be believed, there are in certain places kinds of men very little resembling us, mongrel and ambiguous forms between human and brute. There are countries where men are born without heads, with mouth and eyes in their chest; where they are all hermaphrodites; where they go on all fours; where they have but one eye in the forehead and a head more like a dog's than ours; where the lower half is fish and they live in the water; where the women bear young at five years old, and live only eight; where the head and skin of the forehead is so hard that a sword will not touch it but rebounds; where the men have no beards; nations that do not know the use of fire; others that produce seed of a black colour. What shall we say of those who naturally change themselves into wolves, colts, and then back into men? And if it is true, as Plutarch says, that in some place in the Indies there are men without mouths, who feed themselves on the scent of certain odours — how many of our descriptions are then false? He is no longer laughable, nor perhaps capable of reason or society. The arrangement and cause of our internal composition would then for the most part be without point or use.

Furthermore, how many things are there in our own experience that contradict the fine rules we have cut out for and laid down to nature? And yet we undertake to draw God himself within them! How many things do we call miraculous and contrary to nature? Every nation and every man does this in proportion to his own ignorance. How many occult properties and quintessences do we daily discover? For us to go "according to nature" is no more than to go "according to our understanding," so far as it can follow and so far as we can see into it; everything beyond that is, forsooth, monstrous and irregular. By that account, all things will be monstrous to the wisest and most understanding men — for human reason has persuaded them that there is no kind of ground or foundation, not so much as to be assured that snow is white, and Anaxagoras held it to be black; whether there is anything, or nothing; whether there is knowledge or ignorance, which Metrodorus of Chios denied man could determine; or whether we live, as Euripides doubts whether the life we live is life, or whether what we call death is not life: [--Greek--] and not without some appearance. For why do we derive the title of being from this instant, which is but a flash in the infinite course of an eternal night, and so short an interruption of our perpetual and natural condition — death possessing all the before and after this moment, and also a good part of the moment itself? Others swear there is no motion at all, like the followers of Melissus, and that nothing stirs. For if there is but one, neither can the spherical motion be of any use to him, nor motion from one place to another, as Plato proves; "that there is neither generation nor corruption in nature." Protagoras says there is nothing in nature but doubt; that a man may equally dispute of all things, even of this — whether a man can equally dispute of all things. Nausiphanes, that of things that seem to be, none is more than it is not; that there is nothing certain but uncertainty. Parmenides, that of what seems, there is not one thing in general; that there is but one thing. Zeno, that one same is not, and that there is nothing; if there were one thing, it would either be in another or in itself; if in another, they are two; if in itself, they are also two — the comprehending and the comprehended. By these doctrines the nature of things is no other than a shadow, either false or empty.

This way of speaking in a Christian has always seemed to me very indiscreet and irreverent. "God cannot die; God cannot contradict himself; God cannot do this or that." I do not like to have the divine power so limited by the laws of men's mouths; and the idea that presents itself to us in those propositions ought to be more religiously and reverently expressed.

Our speaking has its failings and defects, like everything else. Most of the world's disturbances are grammatical ones. Our lawsuits arise only from disputes over the interpretation of laws; and most wars come from ministers' inability clearly to express the conventions and treaties of friendship between princes. How many quarrels — and how serious — has the doubt over the meaning of this syllable, _hoc_,* created in the world? Take the clearest conclusion that logic itself
* Montaigne is referring to the controversies between Catholics and Protestants over transubstantiation.

presents us with. If you say, "It is fine weather," and you say true, then it is fine weather. Isn't this a very certain form of speech? And yet it will deceive us. To see that it will, follow the example: If you say, "I lie," if you say true, you do lie. The art, the reasoning, and the force of this conclusion are the same as the other — and yet we are stuck. The Pyrrhonian philosophers, I see, cannot express their general conception in any kind of speech; they would need a new language for the purpose. Ours is wholly built of affirmative propositions, which are entirely against them; so that when they say "I doubt," they are at once seized by the throat to make them confess that at least they know and are sure they do doubt. By which means they have been forced to take shelter under this medical comparison, without which their humour would be inexplicable. When they pronounce, "I know not" or "I doubt," they say this proposition carries itself off with the rest, no more nor less than rhubarb, which drives out the bad humours and carries itself off with them. The fancy will be more surely caught by interrogation: "What do I know?" — which I bear as my motto, with the emblem of a balance.

See what use they make of this irreverent way of speaking. In the present disputes about our religion, if you press its adversaries too hard, they will roundly tell you "that it is not in God's power to make his body be in paradise and on earth, and in several places at once." And see what advantage the old scoffer made of this. "At least," he says, "it is no small consolation to man to see that God cannot do all things, for he cannot kill himself though he would — which is the greatest privilege we have in our condition; he cannot make mortal immortal, nor revive the dead; nor make it that one who has lived has not; nor that one who has had honours has not had them, having no other right to the past than that of oblivion." And, that the comparison of man to God may yet be made out with jocose examples: "He cannot bring it about," he says, "that twice ten shall not be twenty." This is what he says, and what a Christian ought to be careful not to let escape his lips. Whereas, on the contrary, it seems men study this foolish daring of speech, to reduce God to their own measure:
Cras vel atrâ Nube polum, Pater, occupato, Vel sole puro; non tamen irritum Quodcumque retro est efficiet, neque Diffinget infectumque reddet Quod fugiens semel hora vexit.
"To-morrow, let it shine or rain, Yet cannot this the past make vain: Nor uncreate and render void That which was yesterday enjoyed."

When we say that the infinity of ages, past and to come, is but one instant with God; that his goodness, wisdom, and power are one with his essence — our mouths say it, but our understanding does not grasp it. And yet such is our vain opinion of ourselves that we must make Divinity pass through our sieve; and from that come all the dreams and errors with which the world abounds, while we reduce and weigh in our balance a thing so far above our scales. _Mirum quo procedat improbitas cordis humani, parvulo aliquo intritata successu._ "It is wonderful how far the wickedness of man's heart will proceed, if elevated by the least success." How imperiously and insolently Epicurus reproves the Stoics for maintaining that the truly good and happy being belongs to God alone, and that the wise man has only a shadow and resemblance of it! How rashly they have bound God to destiny — a thing which, with my consent, no man who bears the name of Christian shall ever do again! And Thales, Plato, and Pythagoras have enslaved him to necessity. This arrogance of trying to discover God with our eyes has been the cause that one eminent man among us has attributed to the Divinity a bodily form; and is the reason for what happens every day, of attributing important events to God by particular assignment. Because they weigh with us, they conclude they also weigh with him — that he has a more attentive and watchful regard for them than for others of less moment to us, or of ordinary course: _Magna Dii curant, parva negligunt_: "The gods are concerned with great matters, but slight the small." Listen to him; he will clear this up for you by his reason: _Nec in regnis quidem reges omnia minima curant_: "For kings, too, in their administration, do not take notice of all the least concerns." As if to that King of kings it were more or less to subvert a kingdom or to move the leaf of a tree; or as if his providence acted differently in tipping the outcome of a battle than in the leap of a flea. The hand of his government is laid upon everything in the same manner, with the same power and order; our interest contributes nothing; our inclinations and measures sway nothing with him. _Deus ita artifex magnus in magnis, ut minor non sit in parvis_: "God is so great an artificer in great things that he is no less in the least." Our arrogance sets this blasphemous comparison before us forever. Because our employments are a burden to us, Strato has courteously been pleased to exempt the gods from all duties, as their priests are exempt; he makes nature produce and support all things, and with her weights and motions construct the several parts of the world, freeing human nature from the awe of divine judgments: _Quod beatum aeternumque sit, id nec habere negotii quicquam, nec exhibere alteri_: "What is blessed and eternal has no business itself and gives none to another." Nature will have it that in like things there should be a like relation. So the infinite number of mortals implies a like number of immortals; the infinite things that kill and destroy presuppose as many that preserve and benefit. As the souls of the gods, without tongue, eye, or ear, all feel among themselves what each other feels, and judge our thoughts; so the souls of men, when at liberty and loosed from the body, by sleep or some ecstasy, divine, foretell, and see things that, joined to the body, they could not see. "Men," says St. Paul, "professing themselves to be wise, became fools, and changed the glory of the incorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man." Notice the juggling in the ancient deifications. After the great and stately pomp of the funeral, as soon as the fire began to mount the top of the pyramid and to catch the couch where the body lay, they at the same time released an eagle, which flew upward — signifying that the soul had gone to Paradise. We have a thousand medals, especially of the worthy Faustina, where this eagle is shown carrying these deified souls to heaven heels-up. It is a pity we should fool ourselves with our own follies and inventions,
Quod finxere, timent,
"They fear their own inventions,"
Like children frightened by the same face of their playfellow which they themselves have smeared and smudged. _Quasi quicquam infelicius sit homine, cui sua figmenta dominantur:_

"As though anything could be more wretched than a man insulted by his own inventions." It is far from honouring the One who made us, to honour one we have made. Augustus had more temples than Jupiter, served with as much religion and belief in miracles. The Thracians, in return for the benefits they had received from Agesilaus, came to inform him that they had canonized him. "Has your nation," he said to them, "the power to make gods of whom they please? Please deify some one of yourselves first; and when I have seen what advantage he has by it, I will thank you for your offer." Man is truly stark mad: he cannot make a worm, and yet he will make gods by the dozen. Hear Trismegistus in praise of our capacity: "Of all wonderful things, it surmounts all wonder that man could find out the divine nature and make it." And take here the school of philosophy's own arguments:
Nosse cui divos et coli munina soli, Aut soli nescire, datum.
"To whom to know the deities of heaven, Or know he knows them not, alone 'tis given."

"If there is a God, he is a living creature; if he is a living creature, he has sense; and if he has sense, he is subject to corruption. If he be without a body, he is without a soul, and so without action; and if he has a body, it is perishable." Isn't this a triumph? We are incapable of having made the world; there must then be some more excellent nature that has set hand to the work. It would be foolish, ridiculous arrogance to think ourselves the most perfect thing in the universe. There must therefore be something better, and that must be God. When you see a stately and stupendous building, though you do not know who owns it, you would still conclude it was not built for rats. And this divine structure we see of the celestial palace — have we not reason to believe it is the residence of some possessor much greater than we? Isn't the most supreme always the most worthy? But we are in the lowest form. Nothing without a soul and without reason can produce a living creature capable of reason. The world produces us; the world then has soul and reason. Every part of us is less than the whole of us. We are part of the world; the world therefore is endowed with wisdom and reason, and more abundantly than we are. It is a fine thing to have a great government; the government of the world, then, belongs to some happy nature. The stars do us no harm; they are therefore full of goodness. We need nourishment; so the gods need it too, and feed on the vapours of the earth. Worldly goods are not goods to God; therefore they are not goods to us. Offending and being offended are equally signs of weakness; it is therefore folly to fear God. God is good by nature; man by his industry, which is more. The divine and human wisdom have no difference but that the first is eternal; but duration is no addition to wisdom — therefore we are companions. We have life, reason, and liberty; we esteem goodness, charity, and justice; therefore these qualities are in him. In short, building and destroying — the conditions of the Divinity — are forged by man, according as they suit himself. What a pattern, and what a model! Let us stretch, let us raise and swell human qualities as much as we please; puff yourself up, poor man, more and more, and more:
Non, si tu ruperis, inquit.
"Not if thou burst," said he.

_Profecto non Deum, quem cogitare non possunt, sed semetipsos pro illo cogitantes, non illum, sed seipsos, non illi, sed sibi comparant._ "Certainly they do not imagine God, whom they cannot imagine; they imagine themselves in his place; they do not compare him, but themselves — not to him, but to themselves." In natural things, effects only partly relate to their causes. What is this to the purpose? His condition is above the order of nature, too elevated, too remote, and too mighty, to allow itself to be bound and fettered by our conclusions. It is not through ourselves that we arrive there; our ways are too low. We are no nearer heaven on top of Mount Cenis than at the bottom of the sea; measure the distance with your astrolabe. They drag God down even to the carnal knowledge of women, so many times, and so many generations. Paulina, the wife of Saturninus, a matron of great reputation at Rome, thinking she lay with the god Serapis, found herself in the arms of a lover of hers, through the pandering of the priests of his temple. Varro, the most subtle and learned of all the Latin authors, in his book on theology, writes that the sexton of Hercules's temple, throwing dice with one hand for himself and with the other for Hercules, played him for a supper and a wench; if he won, at the expense of the offerings; if he lost, at his own. The sexton lost and paid for the supper and the wench. Her name was Laurentina; she saw by night this god in her arms, who furthermore told her that the first man she met the next day should give her a heavenly reward; which turned out to be Taruncius, a rich young man, who took her home to his house, and in time left her his heiress. She, in her turn, thinking to do something pleasing to the god, left the people of Rome as her heirs; and so divine honours were paid to her. As if it were not enough that Plato was originally descended from the gods by a double line, and that he had Neptune as the common father of his race — it was confidently believed at Athens that Aristo, wanting to enjoy the fair Perictione, could not, and was warned by the god Apollo in a dream to leave her unpolluted and untouched until she should first have given birth. These were the father and mother of Plato. How many ridiculous stories there are of like cuckoldings, committed by the gods against poor mortal men! And how many husbands wrongly slandered in favour of the children! In the Mahometan religion, the people's belief furnishes plenty of Merlins — that is, fatherless children, spiritual, divinely conceived in the wombs of virgins, who carry names that signify as much in their language.

We must observe that to every thing nothing is dearer or more estimable than its own being (the lion, the eagle, the dolphin prize nothing above their own kind); and that every thing assimilates the qualities of all other things to its own. We may indeed stretch this or contract it, but that's all. Beyond that relation and principle, our imagination cannot go, can guess at nothing else, cannot possibly go out of itself or reach beyond. From this come these ancient conclusions: of all forms, the most beautiful is man's; therefore God must be of that form. No one can be happy without virtue, nor virtue without reason, and reason cannot inhabit anywhere but in human shape; God is therefore clothed in a human figure. _Ita est informatum et anticipatum mentibus nostris, ut homini, quum de Deo cogitet, forma occurrat humana._ "It is so imprinted in our minds, and our fancy is so prepossessed with it, that when a man thinks of God, a human figure always presents itself to the imagination." That was why Xenophanes pleasantly said that if beasts make gods for themselves, as they likely do, they certainly make them like themselves, and glorify themselves in it, as we do. For why may not a goose say: "All the parts of the universe regard me; the earth serves me to walk on, the sun to light me; the stars have their influence over me; I have such an advantage from the winds, such from the waters; there is nothing yonder heavenly roof looks upon so favourably as me; I am nature's darling. Doesn't man keep me, lodge me, serve me? It is for me that he both sows and grinds; if he eats me, he does the same with his fellow-men, and so do I with the worms that kill and devour him." As much might be said by a crane, and with greater confidence, on account of the liberty of his flight and his command of that high and beautiful region. _Tam blanda conciliatrix, et tam sui est lena ipsa natura._ "So flattering and wheedling a bawd is nature to herself."

Now by the same logic, the destinies are then for us; for us the world; it shines, it thunders for us; creator and creatures, all are for us. We are the mark and point at which the universal whole is aimed. Look into the records that philosophy has kept for two thousand years and more of the affairs of heaven — the gods all that while have neither acted nor spoken but for man. She allows them no other consultation, no other employment. See them here at war against us:
Domitosque Herculeâ manu Telluris juvenes, unde periculum Fulgens contre mu it domus Saturai veteris.
"The brawny sons of earth, subdu'd by hand Of Hercules on the Phlegræan strand, Where the rude shock did such an uproar make, As made old Saturn's sparkling palace shake."
And here you shall see them sharing in our troubles, in return for our having so often shared in theirs:
Neptunus muros, magnoque emota tridenti Fundamenta quatit, totamque à sedibus urbem Emit: hie Juno Scæas sævissima portas Prima tenet.
"Amidst that smother Neptune holds his place, Below the walls' foundation drives his mace, And heaves the city from its solid base. See where in arms the cruel Juno stands, Full in the Scæan gate."

The Caunians, jealous of the authority of their own gods, armed themselves on their days of devotion and ran through all their precincts cutting and slashing the air with their swords, to drive away and banish all foreign gods from their territory. Their powers are graded to fit our needs: one cures plague, one scurf, one consumption; one cures one kind of itch, another another. _Adeo minimis etiam rebus prava religio inserit Deos?_ "At such a rate does false religion stick gods into the meanest concerns." This god makes grapes grow, that one onions; this presides over lechery, that over commerce; for every kind of artisan, a god. This one has his province and reputation in the east, that in the west:
"Here lay her armour, here her chariot stood."
O sancte Apollo, qui umbilicum certum terrarum obtines!
"O sacred Phoebus, who with glorious ray, From the earth's centre, dost thy light display."
Pallada Cecropidæ, Minola Creta Dianam, Vulcanum tellus Hypsipylea colit, Junonem Sparte, Pelopeladesque Mycenæ; Pinigerum Fauni Mænalis ora caput; Mars Latio venerandus.

"Th' Athenians Pallas, Cynthia Crete adore, Vulcan is worshipped on the Lemnian shore. Proud Juno's altars are by Spartans fed, Th' Arcadians worship Faunus, and 'tis said To Mars, by Italy, is homage paid."
as our needs demand; this one cures horses, that one men,
Hic illius arma, Hic currus fuit.
This one has only one town or one family in his keeping; that one lives alone; that one in company, whether by choice or necessity:
Junctaque sunt magno templa nepotis avo.
"And temples to the nephew joined are, To those were reared to the great-grandfather."

Some are so wretched and lowly (for the number runs to thirty-six thousand) that they must be packed five or six together to produce a single ear of corn, and take their several names from that. Three to a door — that of the plank, that of the hinge, that of the threshold. Four to a child — protectors of his swaddling-clothes, his drink, his food, and his sucking. Some certain, some uncertain and doubtful, and some not yet admitted into Paradise:
Quos, quoniam coli nondum dignamur honore, Quas dedimus certè terras habitare sinanras:
"Whom, since we yet not worthy think of heaven, We suffer to possess the earth we've given."

Among them are physicians, poets, and lawyers. Some of a middle nature between divine and human — mediators between God and us, adorned with a kind of second-rank, diminished adoration; infinite in titles and offices; some good, others bad; some old and decrepit, and some that are mortal. For Chrysippus held that in the last conflagration of the world all the gods would die except Jupiter. Man makes a thousand pretty societies between God and himself. Is he not God's countryman?
Jovis incunabula Creten.
"Crete, the cradle of Jupiter."

And this is the excuse, on considering this subject, that Scaevola, a high priest, and Varro, a great theologian of their time, give us: "That it is necessary the people should be ignorant of many things that are true, and believe many things that are false." _Quum veritatem qua liberetur inquirat, credatur ei expedire quod fallitur._ "Since he inquires after the truth that would set him free, it is held expedient for him to be deceived." Human eyes cannot perceive things except by the forms they know; and we have forgotten what a tumble poor Phaethon took for trying to guide his father's horses with a mortal hand. Man's mind falls into as deep a chasm, and is bruised and shattered in the same way by its own rashness. If you ask philosophy what matter the heavens and the sun are made of, what answer will she give, if not that it is iron, or, with Anaxagoras, stone, or some other matter of her devising? If a man asks Zeno what nature is — "A fire," he says, "an artificer, fit for generation, regularly proceeding." Archimedes, master of that science which claims for itself precedence over all others for truth and certainty, says "the sun is a god of red-hot iron." A fine imagination, this, drawn from the inevitable necessity of geometrical demonstrations! Yet not so inevitable or useful but that Socrates thought it enough to know so much geometry as to measure the land one buys and sells; and Polyaenus, who had been a great and famous doctor in it, despised it as full of falsity and manifest vanity once he had tasted the delicate fruits of Epicurus's idle gardens. Socrates, in Xenophon, says of Anaxagoras — reckoned by antiquity learned above all others in celestial and divine matters — "that he had cracked his brain, as all other men do who too immoderately search into kinds of knowledge that do not concern them." When he made the sun out to be a burning stone, he did not consider that a stone does not shine in fire; and worse, that it consumes there; and that, in making the sun and fire one, fire does not blacken complexions while shining on them, that we can look fixedly at fire, and that fire kills herbs and plants. It is Socrates's opinion, and mine too, that the best way of judging the heavens is not to judge them at all.
