Plato, having occasion in his _Timaeus_ to speak of the demons, says: "This undertaking is beyond my ability. We must therefore believe those ancients who said they were begotten by them; it is against all reason to refuse to take the children of the gods at their word, though what they say is not proved by any necessary or probable reasons — seeing that they engage to speak of domestic and familiar matters."

Let us see if we have a little more light in the knowledge of human and natural things. Is it not a ridiculous undertaking, for us to forge for those to whom by our own confession our knowledge cannot reach, another body, and to lend it a false form of our own invention — as is plain in this matter of the motion of the planets, where, since our wits cannot possibly arrive at or conceive their natural conduct, we lend them material, heavy, substantial springs of our own by which to move:
Temo aureus, aurea summæ Curvatura rotæ, radiorum argenteus ordo.
"Gold was the axle, and the beam was gold; The wheels with silver spokes on golden circles roll'd."

You would say we had had coachmakers, carpenters, and painters go up on high to make engines with various motions, and to arrange the wheelwork and interlacings of the heavenly bodies in differing colours around the axis of necessity, according to Plato:
Mundus domus est maxima rerum, Quam quinque altitonæ fragmine zonæ Cingunt, per quam limbus pictus bis sex signis Stellimicantibus, altus in obliquo æthere, lunæ Bigas acceptat.

"The world's a mansion that doth all things hold, Which thundering zones, in number five, enfold, Through which a girdle, painted with twelve signs, And that with sparkling constellations, shines, In heaven's arch marks the diurnal course For the sun's chariot and his fiery horse."

These are all dreams and fanatical fancies. Why won't nature, just once, please open her bosom to us, and plainly show us the means and conduct of her movements, and prepare our eyes to see them? Good God, what abuse, what mistakes would we then discover in our poor science! I am mistaken if that weak knowledge of ours has hold of even one thing as it really is — and I shall depart from here more ignorant of everything else than I am of my own ignorance.

Did I not read in Plato that divine saying, that "nature is nothing but enigmatic poetry"? As though one might see a veiled and shaded picture, breaking out here and there with an infinite variety of false lights to baffle our guesses: _Latent ista omnia crassis occultata et circumfusa tenebris; ut nulla acies humani ingenii tanta sit, quae penetrare in caelum, terram intrare, possit._ "All these things lie concealed and wrapped in such dense darkness that no edge of human wit is sharp enough to pierce the heavens or enter the earth." Certainly philosophy is nothing but sophisticated poetry. From whom do the ancient writers draw their authority but from the poets? And the first of them were poets themselves, and wrote as such. Plato is just a poet uncoiled. Timon calls him, in mockery, "a monstrous forger of miracles." All superhuman sciences make use of the poetic style. Just as women use ivory teeth where their natural ones are missing, and substitute some artificial substance for their true complexion; as they stuff themselves out with cotton to look plump, and in everyone's sight paint, patch, and trick themselves out with a false, borrowed beauty — so does science (and even our law itself has, they say, legitimate fictions on which it builds the truth of its justice). She gives us on presupposition, and as good currency, things that she herself tells us she has invented; for these _epicycles, eccentrics, and concentrics_ that astrology uses to track the motions of the stars, she gives us as the best she could invent on the subject. So too in everything else: philosophy presents us not with what really is, or with what she really believes, but with what she has contrived with the greatest and most plausible appearance of truth and the quaintest invention. Plato, discussing the state of human bodies and those of beasts, says: "I would know that what I have said is true, had I confirmation from an oracle; but I will affirm this much, that what I have said is the most likely to be true of anything I could say."
It is not to heaven alone that art sends her ropes, engines, and wheels. Let us consider a little what she says of us ourselves, and of our structure.

There is no more retrogradation, trepidation, accession, recession, and astonishment in the stars and heavenly bodies than they have found in this poor little human body. They have good reason, on that very score, to call it the little world, so many tools and parts have they used to build and erect it. To support the movements they see in man, and the various functions we find in ourselves, into how many parts have they divided the soul, in how many places lodged it? In how many orders have they divided it, and to how many storeys have they raised this poor creature, man, beyond what is natural and perceivable? And how many offices and vocations have they assigned him? They make of him an imaginary public thing. It is a subject they hold and handle; and they have full power granted them to rip, place, displace, patch, and stuff it, each according to his own fancy — and yet they do not possess it. Not in reality only, but even in dreams, they cannot govern it so that there will not be some cadence or sound escaping their architecture, enormous and botched with a thousand false, fantastic patches as it is. And it is not reasonable to excuse them; for though we are satisfied with painters when they paint heaven, earth, seas, mountains, and remote islands, and give us only some slight mark of them and, as of unknown things, content themselves with a faint, obscure description — yet when they come to draw us from life, or any other creature familiar to us, we require of them a perfect and exact representation of features and colours, and despise them if they fail in it.

I am very pleased by the Milesian girl who, observing the philosopher Thales always contemplating the celestial arch and forever gazing upward, laid something in his way to trip him up, to remind him that there would be time enough to take up things in the clouds when he had looked after what was at his feet. She advised him well: rather look to himself than to gaze at heaven. As Democritus says, by Cicero's mouth,
Quod est ante pedes, nemo spectat: coeli scrutantur plagas.
"No man regards what is under his feet; They are always prying towards heaven."

But our condition has it that the knowledge of what we hold in our hands is as remote from us, and as far above the clouds, as that of the stars. As Socrates says in Plato, "whoever meddles with philosophy may be reproached as Thales was by the woman: that he sees nothing of what is right before him. For every philosopher is ignorant of what his neighbour is doing — and indeed of what he is doing himself, and is ignorant of what they both are, whether beasts or men."
Those people who find Sebond's arguments too weak — who are ignorant of nothing, who govern the world, who know everything,
Quæ mare compescant causæ; quid temperet annum; Stellæ sponte suâ, jussæve, vagentur et errent; Quid premat obscurum lunæ, quid proférât orbem; Quid velit et posait rerum concordia discors;

"What governs ocean's tides, And through the various year the seasons guides; Whether the stars by their own proper force, Or foreign power, pursue their wand'ring course; Why shadows darken the pale queen of night; Whence she renews her orb and spreads her light;-- What nature's jarring sympathy can mean;"

have they not sometimes sounded, in their writings, the difficulties they meet with in knowing their own being? We see plainly that the finger moves, the foot moves, that some parts take on a voluntary motion without our consent, and that others move only at our direction; that one kind of apprehension occasions blushing, another paleness; such an imagination works only on the spleen, another on the brain; one occasions laughter, another tears; another stupefies and astonishes all the senses, and arrests the movement of all our members; at one object the stomach rises, at another a member that lies somewhat lower. But how a spiritual impression can make such a breach into a solid, massive subject — and the nature of the connection and structure of these admirable springs and movements — no one has ever known. _Omnia incerta ratione, et in naturae majestate abdita._ "All uncertain in reason, and concealed in the majesty of nature," says Pliny. And St. Augustine: _Modus quo corporibus adhaerent spiritus... omnino mirus est, nec comprehendi ab homine potest; et hoc ipse homo est._ "The way souls cleave to bodies is altogether wonderful, and cannot be conceived by man; and yet this is man." And yet it is hardly even doubted. For men's opinions are received by ancient belief, on authority and on trust, as if they were religion and law. It is received as gibberish that is commonly spoken; this truth, with all its bustle of arguments and proofs, is admitted as a firm and solid body, no more to be shaken, no more to be judged. On the contrary, every man, to the best of his talent, props up and fortifies this received belief with the utmost power of his reason — which is a supple instrument, pliable, fit to be shaped to any figure. And so the world comes to be filled with lies and follies. The reason men doubt of various things is that they never examine common impressions. They do not dig down to the root, where the faults and defects lie; they debate only at the branches. They do not ask whether such and such a thing is true, but whether it has been understood this way or that. It is not asked whether Galen has said anything to the point, but whether he has said so or so. In truth, it was very fitting that this curb on our liberty of judgment and this tyranny over our opinions should be extended to the schools and the arts. The god of scholastic knowledge is Aristotle; it is irreligion to question any of his decrees, as it was to question those of Lycurgus at Sparta. His doctrine is a magisterial law, which may perhaps be as false as any other. I do not know why I should not as willingly embrace the ideas of Plato, or the atoms of Epicurus, or the plenum and vacuum of Leucippus and Democritus, or the water of Thales, or the infinity of nature of Anaximander, or the air of Diogenes, or the numbers and symmetry of Pythagoras, or the infinity of Parmenides, or the One of Musaeus, or the water and fire of Apollodorus, or the similar parts of Anaxagoras, or the discord and friendship of Empedocles, or the fire of Heraclitus, or any other of that infinite confusion of opinions and conclusions which this fine human reason produces by its certainty and clarity in everything it meddles with, as I should the opinion of Aristotle on this subject of the principles of natural things — which principles he builds of three pieces: matter, form, and privation. And what can be more empty than to make nothingness itself the cause of the production of things? Privation is a negative; from what humour, then, could he make it the cause and origin of things that are? Yet this would not even be debated, but for the exercise of logic. There is nothing in it disputed in order to bring it into doubt, but to defend the school's author from outside objections. His authority is the _non ultra_, beyond which it is not permitted to inquire.

It is easy, on approved foundations, to build whatever we please; for, by the law and ordering of the starting principles, the other parts of the structure are easily carried on without failure. By this means we find our reason well-grounded, and we discourse confidently. For our masters take and gain beforehand as much room in our belief as they need afterwards to conclude whatever they please — as geometricians do by their granted demands; the consent and approval we give them allows them to draw us right and left and to whirl us about at their pleasure. Whatever springs from these presuppositions is our master and our God. He will take the level of his foundations so ample and so easy that by them he may carry us up to the clouds, if he so pleases. In this practice and business of science, we have taken Pythagoras's saying, "That every expert person ought to be believed in his own art," for ready coin. The logician refers the meaning of words to the grammarians; the rhetorician borrows the state of the question from the logician; the poet borrows his metre from the musician; the geometer takes his proportions from the arithmetician; the metaphysicians take physical conjectures for their foundations. For every science has its presupposed principles by which human judgment is everywhere kept in check. If you push against the bar where the principal error lies, they have this sentence at the ready: "There is no disputing with people who deny principles." Now men can have no principles unless they are revealed to them by divinity; of all the rest, the beginning, middle, and end is nothing but dream and vapour. To those who argue from presupposition, we must, on the contrary, presuppose against them the very axiom in dispute. For every human presupposition and declaration has as much authority as any other, if reason does not make the difference. So all are to be put in the balance — and first the general ones, those that tyrannize over us. The persuasion of certainty is sure testimony of folly and extreme uncertainty; and there are no more foolish men, nor less philosophical, than the Philodoxes of Plato. We must inquire whether fire is hot, whether snow is white; whether there is any such thing as hard or soft, within our knowledge.

And as for those answers of which they tell old stories — the man who doubted whether there was such a thing as heat, whom they bade throw himself into the fire, and the man who denied the coldness of ice, whom they bade put ice in his bosom — these are pitiful things, unworthy of the profession of philosophy. If they had let us alone in our natural being, to receive the appearance of things outside us as they present themselves to us through our senses, and had permitted us to follow our own natural appetites, governed by the condition of our birth, they might then have had reason to talk that way. But it is from them we have learned to make ourselves judges of the world; from them we have this conceit, "That human reason is controller-general of everything inside and outside the vault of heaven; that it comprehends everything, can do everything; by it everything is known and understood." That answer would be good among the cannibals, who enjoy the happiness of a long, quiet, peaceable life without Aristotle's precepts and without ever having heard the name of physics; that answer would perhaps have more value and force than all those the cannibals would borrow from their reason and invention. All animals, and all peoples in whom the law of nature is still pure and simple, would be as capable of it as we are — but they have renounced it. There is no point in their telling us, "It is true, for you see and feel it"; they must tell me whether I really feel what I think I feel, and if I do feel it, they must then tell me why I feel it, and how, and what; they must tell me the name, the origin, the parts and joinings of heat and cold, the qualities of the agent and the patient; or else give up their profession, which is to admit or approve of nothing except by way of reason. That is their touchstone in all kinds of trials — but it is a touchstone full of falsity, error, weakness, and defect.

How can we test it better than by itself? If we are not to believe her when speaking of herself, she can hardly be thought fit to judge of foreign things. If she knows anything, it must at the very least be her own being and home. She lives in the soul, and is either a part or an effect of it; for true and essential reason, from which we borrow the name by a false colour, is lodged in the bosom of the Almighty — that is her habitation and her dwelling; from there she sends out her rays when God is pleased to send any beam of it to mankind, as Pallas issued from her father's head to communicate herself to the world.

Now let us see what human reason tells us of herself and of the soul — not of the soul in general, of which almost all philosophy makes the celestial and first bodies participants; nor of that which Thales attributed to things reputed inanimate, led to it by his consideration of the loadstone; but of that which belongs to us, and which we ought best to know:

Ignoratur enim, quæ sit natura animai; Nata sit; an, contra, nascentibus insinuetur; Et simul intereat nobiscum morte dirempta; An tenebras Orci visat, vastasque lacunas, An pecudes alias divinitus insinuet se.

"For none the nature of the soul doth know, Whether that it be born with us, or no; Or be infused into us at our birth, And dies with us when we return to earth, Or then descends to the black shades below, Or into other animals does go."

Crates and Dicaearchus were of the opinion that there was no soul at all, but that the body moves by a natural motion. Plato, that it is a substance moving of itself. Thales, a nature without repose. Asclepiades, an exercise of the senses. Hesiod and Anaximander, a thing composed of earth and water. Parmenides, of earth and fire. Empedocles, of blood:
Sanguineam vomit ille animam;
"He vomits up his bloody soul."
Posidonius, Cleanthes, and Galen, that it is heat, or a hot complexion —
Igneus est ollis vigor, et colestis origo;
"Their vigour of fire and of heavenly race."

Hippocrates, a spirit diffused throughout the body. Varro, that it is an air taken in at the mouth, heated in the lungs, moistened in the heart, and diffused throughout the body. Zeno, the quintessence of the four elements. Heraclides Ponticus, that it is light. Xenocrates and the Egyptians, a mobile number. The Chaldeans, a power without any determinate form:
Habitum quemdam vitalem corporis esse, Harmoniam Græci quam dicunt.
"A certain vital habit in man's frame, Which harmony the Grecian sages name."

Let us not forget Aristotle, who held the soul to be that which naturally causes the body to move, which he calls entelechia — as cold an invention as any of the rest, for he speaks neither of the essence, nor of the origin, nor of the nature of the soul, but only takes note of the effect. Lactantius, Seneca, and most of the Dogmatists have confessed that it was a thing they did not understand. After all this enumeration of opinions, _Harum sententiarum quae vera sit, Deus aliquis viderit:_ "Of these opinions, which is the true one, let some god determine," says Cicero. "I know from myself," says St. Bernard, "how incomprehensible God is, seeing I cannot comprehend the parts of my own being."

Heraclitus, who held that every being was full of souls and demons, nevertheless maintained that no one could go far enough toward the knowledge of the soul ever to arrive at it, so deep was its essence.
Nor is there less controversy and debate over its location. Hippocrates and Herophilus place it in the ventricle of the brain. Democritus and Aristotle, throughout the whole body:
Ut bona sæpe valetudo cum dicitur esse Corporis, et non est tamen hæc pars ulla ralentis;
"As when the body's health they do it call, When of a sound man, that's no part at all."
Epicurus, in the stomach;
Hic exsultat enim pavor ac metus; Hæc loca circum Lætitiæ mulcent.
"For this the seat of horror is and fear, And joys in turn do likewise triumph here."

The Stoics, around and within the heart. Erasistratus, adjoining the membrane of the epicranium. Empedocles, in the blood — as also Moses, which was why he forbade the eating of the blood of beasts, because the soul is seated there. Galen thought every part of the body had its own soul. Strato has placed it between the eyebrows. _Qua facie quidem sit animus, aut ubi habitet, ne quaerendum quidem est:_ "What shape the soul is of, or where it lives, is not even to be asked," says Cicero. I very willingly deliver this author to you in his own words; for why should I alter eloquence itself? Besides, it would be a poor prize to steal the matter of his inventions; they are neither very frequent nor of any great weight, and are sufficiently known. But the reason Chrysippus argues that it is around the heart, as do all the rest of that sect, ought not to be omitted: "It is," he says, "because when we mean to affirm anything we lay our hand upon our breast; and when we pronounce ἐγώ, which means I, we let the lower jaw drop toward the stomach." This passage ought not to pass without a remark on the vanity of so great a man; for besides that these considerations are infinitely slight in themselves, the last is only a proof to the Greeks that they have their souls lodged in that part. No human judgment is so sprightly and watchful that it does not sometimes nod. Why are we afraid to say so? The Stoics, fathers of human prudence, hold that the soul of a man crushed under a ruin labours and struggles a long time to get out, like a mouse caught in a trap, before it can free itself from the burden. Some hold that the world was made to give bodies, by way of punishment, to spirits fallen by their own fault from the purity in which they had been created — the first creation having been incorporeal; and that, according as they are more or less deprived of their spirituality, they are more or less brightly or dully incarnated; and that from this comes all the variety of so much created matter. But the spirit that, for his punishment, was clothed in the body of the sun must certainly have a very rare and singular measure of change.

The outer reaches of our inquiry all end in astonishment and blindness. As Plutarch says of the testimony of histories, that, according to charts and maps, the utmost bounds of known countries are taken up with marshes, impenetrable forests, deserts, and uninhabited places: so the grossest and most childish ravings are most found in those authors who treat the most elevated subjects, and go furthest in them, losing themselves in their own curiosity and presumption. The beginning and end of knowledge are equally foolish. Notice how high Plato flies in his poetic clouds; observe there the gibberish of the gods. But what was he dreaming of when he defined man as "a two-legged animal without feathers," giving those who had a mind to mock him a fine pretext — for, having plucked a capon alive, they went around calling it the man of Plato?

And what were the Epicureans thinking of, out of what simplicity did they first imagine that their _atoms_ — which they said were bodies of some weight, and with a natural downward motion — had made the world? Until they were reminded by their adversaries that, by this description, the atoms could not unite and join, their fall being so direct and perpendicular, and forming so many parallel lines throughout. So they had to add afterwards a fortuitous, sideways motion, and equip their atoms with hooked tails by which they might unite and cling to one another. And even then, do not their attackers, on this second consideration, give them a hard time? "If the atoms by chance formed so many kinds of figures, why did it never happen that they formed a house or a shoe? At the same rate, why should we not believe that an infinite number of Greek letters, strewn over a certain place, might fall into the contexture of the _Iliad_?" — "Whatever is capable of reason," says Zeno, "is better than that which is not capable; nothing is better than the world; the world therefore is capable of reason." Cotta, by this kind of argument, makes the world a mathematician; and it is also made a musician and an organist by this other argument of Zeno: "The whole is more than a part; we are capable of wisdom, and are part of the world; therefore the world is wise." There are countless examples of arguments not only false in themselves but silly, that don't even hold together, and that accuse their authors not so much of ignorance as of imprudence — in the reproaches that philosophers fling at one another over their disagreements in sects and opinions.

Whoever could bundle up a hearty faggot of the follies of human wisdom would produce wonders. I willingly muster these few as a sample, by a certain meaning no less profitable to consider than the soundest and most moderate instructions. Let us judge by these what opinion we are to hold of man, of his sense and reason, when in those great persons who raised human knowledge so high, so many gross mistakes and manifest errors are to be found.

For my part, I am inclined to think that they have handled knowledge casually, like a plaything, with both hands; and have contended over reason as if it were a vain, frivolous instrument, setting on foot every sort of fancy and invention, sometimes more vigorous, sometimes weaker. This same Plato who defines man as if he were a chicken, says elsewhere, after Socrates, that he does not, in truth, know what man is, and that man is one of the hardest members of the world to understand. By this variety and instability of opinions, they tacitly lead us, as if by the hand, to this resolution of their irresolution. They do not always profess to deliver their opinions bare and apparent; they have at one time disguised them in the fabulous shadows of poetry, at another in some other vizor. For our imperfection brings this with it too — that raw meat is not always fit for our stomachs; we have to dry, alter, and mix it. They do the same: they sometimes hide their real opinions and judgments, and falsify them to accommodate themselves to public use. They will not openly profess ignorance and the weakness of human reason, so as not to frighten the children; but they sufficiently reveal it to us under the appearance of a troubled and inconstant science.

I once advised a man in Italy, who wanted very much to speak Italian, that provided he only wished to make himself understood and was not ambitious to excel any further, he had only to use the first word that came to his tongue's tip — whether Latin, French, Spanish, or Gascon — and that, adding the Italian termination, he could not fail to hit upon some idiom of the country, whether Tuscan, Roman, Venetian, Piedmontese, or Neapolitan, and so light upon some one of those many forms. I say the same of Philosophy: she has so many faces, such variety, and has said so many things, that all our dreams and ravings are to be found there. Human fancy can conceive nothing good or bad that is not in there: _Nihil tam absurde dici potest, quod non dicatur ab aliquo philosophorum._ "Nothing can be said so absurd that has not already been said by some of the philosophers." And I am the more willing to expose my whimsies in public, since, though they are spun out of myself and without any pattern, I know they will be found related to some ancient humour, and some will not stick to say, "See where he took it from!" My manners are natural; I have not called on any school's help to set them up; but, weak as they are, when it came into my head to lay them open to the world's view, and to put them out in a slightly more decent garb by adorning them with reasons and examples, I was astonished to find them, by accident, in conformity with so many philosophical discourses and examples. I never knew what regimen my life was on until it was nearly worn out and spent — a new figure: an unpremeditated and accidental philosopher.
But to return to the soul. Since Plato has placed reason in the brain, anger in the heart, and concupiscence in the liver, it is likely that this was rather an interpretation of the movements of

the soul than a division and separation of it, as of a body, into several members. And the most likely of their opinions is that it is always one soul, which by its faculty reasons, remembers, comprehends, judges, desires, and exercises all its other operations through various bodily instruments — as the pilot guides his ship by his experience, one moment tightening or slackening the cordage, one moment hoisting the mainyard or moving the rudder, producing various effects by one and the same power; and that it is lodged in the brain, which shows in the fact that wounds and accidents touching that part immediately injure the faculties of the soul; and it is not incongruous that it should from there spread itself through the other parts of the body
Medium non deserit unquam Coeli Phoebus iter; radiis tamen omnia lustrât.
["Phoebus never deviates from the zodiac's way; yet all things he illuminates with his ray."]
as the sun sheds its light and influence from heaven, and fills the world with them:
Cætera pars animas, per totum dissita corpus, Paret, et ad numen mentis momenque movetur.
"The other part o' th' soul diffus'd all o'er The body, does obey the reason's lore."
Some have said there is a general soul, as it were a great body from which all particular souls are drawn, and to which they return, restoring themselves to that universal matter:

Deum namque ire per omnes Terrasque, tractusque maris, columque profundum; Hinc pecudes, armenta, viros, genus omne ferarum, Quemque sibi tenues nascentem arcessere vitas: Scilicet hue reddi deinde, ac resoluta referri Omnia; nec morti esse locum:

"For God goes forth, and spreads throughout the whole Heaven, earth, and sea, the universal soul; Each at its birth, from him all beings share, Both man and brute, the breath of vital air; To him return, and, loos'd from earthly chain, Fly whence they sprung, and rest in God again, Spurn at the grave, and, fearless of decay, Dwell in high heaven, and star th' ethereal way."

Others, that they only rejoin and reunite themselves to it; others, that they were produced from the divine substance; others, by the angels of fire and air; others, that they were from all antiquity; and some, that they were created at the very moment the bodies needed them. Others make them descend from the orb of the moon, and return there. Most of the ancients believed they were begotten from father to son, after the same manner as, and along with, all other natural things — taking their argument from the resemblance of children to their fathers;
Instillata patris virtus tibi; Fortes creantur fortibus, et bonis;
"Thou hast thy father's virtues with his blood: For still the brave spring from the brave and good;"
and from the fact that we see passed down from fathers to children not only bodily marks, but a resemblance in humours, complexions, and inclinations of the soul:

Denique cur acris violentia triste leonum Seminium sequitur? dolus vulpibus, et fuga, cervis A patribus datur, et patrius pavor incitât artus? Si non certa suo quia semine seminioque Vis animi pariter crescit cum corpore toto.

"For why should rage from the fierce lion's seed, Or from the subtle fox's craft, proceed; Or why the tim'rous and flying hart His fear and trembling to his race impart; But that a certain force of mind does grow, And still increases as the bodies do?"

That it is on this basis that the divine justice is founded — punishing in the children the faults of the fathers, since the contagion of paternal vices is in some sort imprinted on the soul of children, and the misgovernment of their will extends to them. Moreover, that if souls had any origin other than as a natural sequence of the body, and had been something else outside the body, they would retain some memory of their first being, considering the natural faculties that are proper to them of reasoning, discoursing, and remembering:
Si in corpus nascentibus insinuatur, Cur super anteactam ætatem meminisse nequimus, Nec vestigia gestarum rerum ulla tenemus?
"For at our birth if it infused be, Why do we then retain no memory Of our foregoing life, and why no more Remember any thing we did before?"

For to make the condition of our souls such as we would wish it, we must suppose them all-knowing, even in their natural simplicity and purity; by these means they would have been so, being free from the prison of the body, both before they entered it and (as we hope) after they are gone out of it. And from this knowledge it would follow that they should remember, once in the body — as Plato said, that "what we learn is nothing but a recollection of what we knew before"; a thing which everyone may show, from experience, to be false. First, because we accurately remember only what we have been taught, and if memory truly did her office, she would at least suggest something more to us than what we have learned. Second, what she knew in her purity was a true knowledge — knowing things as they are, by her divine intelligence — whereas here we have her receive falsehood and vice when we instruct her, in which she cannot employ her recollection, since that image and concept have never been planted in her. To say the corporeal prison so suffocates her natural faculties that they are quite extinguished there is, in the first place, contrary to the other belief — that of recognizing her power to be so great, and the operations of it that we perceive in this life so admirable, as to have concluded from them a past divinity and eternity, and an immortality to come:
Nam si tantopere est anirai mutata potestas, Omnia ut actarum exciderit retinentia rerum, Non, ut opinor, ea ab letho jam longior errat.
"For if the mind be changed to that degree As of past things to lose all memory, So great a change as that, I must confess, Appears to me than death but little less."

Moreover, it is here with us, and not elsewhere, that the force and effects of the soul ought to be considered. All her other perfections are vain and useless to her. It is by her present condition that all her immortality is to be rewarded and paid; she has to render account only of the life of man. It would have been injustice to have stripped her of her means and powers, to have disarmed her in her time of captivity and imprisonment in the flesh, of her weakness and infirmity in the time when she was forced and constrained, in order to pass on her an infinite, perpetual sentence of condemnation — and to fix on the consideration of so short a time (perhaps an hour or two, or at the most a century, which has no more proportion with infinity than an instant), in this momentary interval to ordain and definitively determine her whole being. It would also be an unreasonable disproportion to assign an eternal recompense in consequence of so short a life. Plato, to defend himself from this difficulty, will have future payments limited to a hundred years, in proportion to human duration; and a fair number of our own people have given them temporal limits. By this, they judged that the generation of the soul followed the common condition of human things — as did her life, in the opinion of Epicurus and Democritus, the most widely received — owing to the fine appearances they saw: that she was born; that as the body became more capable, they saw her increase in vigour, as the body did; that her feebleness in infancy was very plain, and in time her better strength and maturity, and after that her decline and old age, and at last her decrepitude:
Gigni pariter cum corpore, et una Crescere sentimus, pariterque senescere mentem.
"Souls with the bodies to be born we may Discern, with them t' increase, with them decay."

They perceived her capable of various passions, and agitated by various painful movements, from which she fell into lassitude and unease — capable of alteration and change, of cheerfulness, stupidity and languor, and subject to diseases and injuries, like the stomach or the foot;
Mentem sanari, corpus ut ægrum, Ceraimus, et flecti medicinâ posse videmus;
"Sick minds, as well as bodies, we do see By Med'cine's virtue oft restored to be;"
dazzled and drunk with the fumes of wine, knocked off her seat by the vapours of a burning fever, put to sleep by certain medicines and woken by others —
Corpoream naturam animi esse necesse est, Corporeis quoniam telis ictuque laborat;
["It must of necessity be that the nature of the mind is corporeal, since it suffers from corporeal weapons and blows."]

they saw the soul shaken and overthrown in all its faculties by the mere bite of a mad dog, and in that condition retain no stability of reason, no sufficiency, no virtue, no philosophical resolve, no resistance that could exempt it from such accidents. The slaver of a worthless cur, splashed on the hand of Socrates, would have been enough to shake all his wisdom and all his great, well-regulated imaginations, and to annihilate them so completely that no trace of his former knowledge would remain —
Vis... animal Conturbatur, et... divisa seorsum Disjectatur, eodem illo distracta veneno;
["The power of the soul is disturbed; and when once it is divided and sundered from itself, it is dispersed and scattered by that same poison."]

And this poison meets no more resistance in that great soul than in a four-year-old child — a poison strong enough to drive all philosophy, were philosophy embodied, into raving madness. So much so that Cato, who always despised death and fortune, could not bear the sight of a mirror or of water, overwhelmed with horror and terror at the thought that the contagion of a mad dog might cast him into the disease the doctors call hydrophobia:
Vis morbi distracta per artus Turbat agens animam, spumantes æquore salso Ventorum ut validis fervescunt viribus undæ.
["The disease, spreading through the limbs, drives and disturbs the soul, as on the salt sea the foaming waves boil under the strong force of the winds."]

Now on this point philosophy has armed man well enough against every other kind of accident, either with patience or — if that search is too costly — by an infallible escape, by stripping him entirely of all sensation. But these are remedies only of use to a soul still itself, in its full power, capable of reason and deliberation. They do nothing for this trouble, where the philosopher's soul becomes the soul of a madman, troubled, overturned, lost. And many things can produce it: a too-violent agitation kindled in the soul by some passion of its own; a wound to some part of the body; vapours from the stomach — any of which can stupefy the understanding and turn the brain.
Morbis in corporis avius errat Sæpe animus; dementit enim, deliraque fatur; Interdumque gravi lethargo fertur in altum Æternumque soporem, oculis nutuque cadenti:
["In bodily diseases the mind often goes astray; it grows mad and speaks deliriously; sometimes it is carried by a heavy lethargy into deep and everlasting sleep, eyes and head dropping."]

It seems to me the philosophers have not pressed very hard on this string, any more than on another of equal importance. They have this dilemma always in their mouths, to console us for our mortal condition: "The soul is either mortal or immortal. If mortal, it will feel no pain. If immortal, it will change for the better." They never touch the other branch — what if it changes for the worse? — and leave the threat of future torments to the poets. By that omission they give themselves an easy game. These are two evasions I keep running into in their discourses. Back to the first.

This soul loses the use of the sovereign Stoic good, so constant and so firm. Here our fine human wisdom must yield and lay down its arms. As to the rest, they also recognised, by the vanity of human reason, that the mixture and association of two things as opposite as the mortal and the immortal was unimaginable:

Quippe etenim mortale æterno jungere, et una Consentire putare, et fungi mutua posse, Desipere est. Quid enim diversius esse putandum est, Aut magis inter se disjunctum discrepitansque, Quam, mortale quod est, immortali atque perenni Junctum, in concilio, sævas tolerare procellas?

["To join the mortal with the eternal and think they can agree and pursue a common purpose together is folly. For what should be thought more different, or more disjointed and discordant in itself, than the mortal joined with the immortal and everlasting, made to endure together the savage storms?"]
Moreover, they noticed that the soul tends toward death just as the body does:
Simul ævo fessa fatiscit:
["Worn out together with age, it gives way."]

Which, according to Zeno, the image of sleep sufficiently demonstrates; for he regards sleep "as a fainting and falling of the soul as well as of the body": _Contrahi animum et quasi labi putat atque decidere._ And when they observed in some people that the soul kept its force and vigour to the last gasp of life, they attributed that to the variety of diseases — as one sees in men at the point of death, that some retain one sense and some another, this one his hearing, that one his sense of smell, without any defect or alteration; and that there is no deprivation so universal that some parts do not remain vigorous and entire:
Non alio pacto, quam si, pes cum dolet ægri, In nullo caput interea sit forte dolore.
["Just as when a sick man's foot is in pain, while his head, perhaps, is not in pain at all."]

The eye of our judgment is to truth what the owl's eyes are to the splendour of the sun, says Aristotle. By what better can we convict him than such gross blindness in such an apparent light? For the contrary opinion, the immortality of the soul — which, Cicero says, was first introduced, according to the testimony of books at least, by Pherecydes
of Syros, in the time of King Tullus (though some attribute it to Thales, and others to others) — is the part of human science treated with the greatest doubt and

reservation. The most positive dogmatists are forced, precisely on this point, to take refuge in the Academy. No one is in doubt about what Aristotle has established on this subject — no more than about the ancients in general, who handle it with a wavering belief: _Rem gratissimam promittentium magis quam probantium._ "A matter more agreeable in the promising than in the proving." He hides himself in clouds of words of difficult and unintelligible sense, and has left his followers as much to argue about in his judgment as in the thing itself.
Two things made this opinion plausible to them. First, that without the immortality of souls there would be nothing on which to ground the vain hopes of glory — a consideration of wonderful

weight in the world. Second, that it is a very useful impression, as Plato says: that vices which escape the eye of human justice still fall within reach of the divine, which will pursue them even after the death of the guilty. Man is excessively anxious to prolong his being, and has provided for it as far as he can. There are monuments to preserve the body, and glory to preserve the name. He has put all his wit and all his opinion to work to rebuild himself, impatient of his fortune, propping himself up by his inventions. The soul, because of its anxiety and impotence, unable to stand on its own, wanders up and down in search of consolations, hopes, foundations, foreign circumstances to which it may cling and fasten. And however light or fantastic invention delivers them, the soul relies more willingly and with greater assurance on them than on itself. But it is striking to see how the most constant and obstinate champions of this just and clear belief in the immortality of the soul fall short, and how weak their arguments are when they try to prove it by human reason: _Somnia sunt non docentis, sed optantis._ "These are the dreams not of a teacher, but of a wisher," says one of the ancients. By this testimony man may know that he owes the truth he stumbles on to chance and accident, since even when it falls into his hand he has no way of holding and maintaining it, and his reason has not the force to make use of it. Everything produced by our own meditation and understanding, true or false, is subject to uncertainty and dispute. It was to chasten our pride and to instruct us in our wretched condition and incapacity that God wrought the perplexity and confusion of the tower of Babel. Whatever we undertake without his help, whatever we see without the lamp of his grace, is only vanity and folly. We corrupt the very essence of truth, which is uniform and constant, by our weakness, when fortune puts it into our hands. Whatever course man takes by himself, God allows it to come to the same confusion, the image of which he so vividly represents to us in the just punishment with which he crushed Nimrod's presumption and frustrated the vain attempt of his proud structure: _Perdam sapientiam sapientium, et prudentiam prudentium reprobabo._ "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and bring to nothing the understanding of the prudent." The diversity of tongues and idioms with which he disturbed that work — what is it but this infinite and perpetual alteration and disagreement of opinions and reasons, which accompany and confound the vain building of human wisdom? And to good effect: for what would hold us, if we had even the least grain of knowledge? This saint has put me deeply in his debt: _Ipsa veritatis occultatio aut humilitatis exercitatio est, aut elationis attritio._ "The very concealment of truth is either an exercise of humility or a quelling of pride." To what a pitch of presumption and insolence we raise our blindness and folly!

But to return to my subject. It was indeed right that we should be beholden only to God, and to the favour of his grace, for the truth of so noble a belief — since it is from his sole bounty that we receive the fruit of immortality, which consists in the enjoyment of eternal beatitude. Let us frankly confess that God alone has dictated it to us, and faith with it; for it is no lesson of nature or of our own reason. And whoever will inquire into his own being and powers, inside and out, without this divine privilege — whoever will consider man impartially and without flattery — will see in him no power or faculty that tastes of anything but death and earth. The more we give and confess we owe to God, the more Christianly we behave. What this Stoic philosopher says he holds from the fortuitous consent of popular opinion — would it not have been better to hold it from God? _Cum de animarum æternitate disserimus, non leve momentum apud nos habet consensus hominum aut timentium inferos, aut colentium. Utor hâc publicâ persuasione._ "When we discuss the eternity of souls, the agreement of men who either fear or worship the powers below carries no small weight with us. I make use of this public conviction." Now the weakness of human arguments on this subject is particularly manifest in the fabulous details they have added on as consequences of this opinion, to work out what sort of condition this immortality of ours might be. Set aside the Stoics — _usuram nobis largiuntur tanquam cornicibus; diu mansuros aiunt animos; semper, negant._ "They grant us a long life, as also to crows; they say our souls will last a long while, but that they will last forever, they deny" — who give souls a life after this one, but a finite one. The most universal and accepted fancy, which still survives in various places down to our own time, is the one they make Pythagoras the author of — not because he was the original inventor, but because his approval gave it great weight and reputation: "that souls, when they leave us, simply move from one body to another, from a lion to a horse, from a horse to a king, travelling on at this rate from lodging to lodging." Pythagoras himself said he remembered having been Aethalides, then Euphorbus, then Hermotimus, and finally had passed from Pyrrhus into Pythagoras, with a memory of himself going back two hundred and six years. And some have added that these same souls sometimes mount up to heaven and come down again:
O pater, anne aliquas ad cælum hinc ire putandum est Sublimes animas, iterumque ad tarda reverti Corpora? Quæ lucis miseris tam dira cupido?
["O father, are we to think that any of these noble souls go from here up to heaven, and then come back again to dull bodies? What dreadful longing for light can possess the poor wretches?"]

Origen makes them eternally come and go from a better to a worse state. The opinion Varro mentions is that, after a revolution of four hundred and forty years, they are reunited to their first bodies. Chrysippus held that this would happen after some unknown and undefined span of time. Plato, who claims to have taken this belief from Pindar and the ancient poets — that we undergo infinite vicissitudes of change, for which the soul is prepared, having neither punishment nor reward in the other world that is not temporal, just as its life here is temporal — concludes that the soul has a singular knowledge of the affairs of heaven, hell, and the world, through all of which it has passed and re-passed and made stays on its various voyages — all matters for its memory. Watch his account of its progress elsewhere: "The soul that has lived well is reunited to the star to which it is assigned; the one that has lived badly is moved into a woman; and if it does not reform there, is moved again into a beast of a kind suited to its vicious habits, and will see no end of its punishments until it has returned to its natural constitution and, by the force of reason, purged itself of those gross, stupid, elementary qualities it was polluted with." But I will not skip the Epicureans' objection against this transmigration from one body to another; it is a fine one. They ask what is to be done if the number of those dying happens to exceed the number of those being born. For the souls turned out of their old lodgings will jostle and shove to be first into the new ones. And further, what do they do with their time while waiting for new quarters to be made ready? Or conversely, if more animals are born than die, the body, they say, would be in poor shape while it waited for a soul to be infused into it — and you would end up with some bodies dying before they had ever been alive.

Denique connubia ad Veneris, partusque ferarum Esse animas præsto, deridiculum esse videtur; Et spectare immortales mortalia membra Innumero numero, certareque præproperanter Inter se, quæ prima potissimaque insinuetur.

["It seems ridiculous to think that, whenever wild beasts couple and give birth, souls are standing ready — that immortal souls in countless number watch mortal limbs and race each other in a rush to be the first to slip in."]

Others have detained the soul in the body of the dead, to animate the snakes, worms, and other creatures said to be bred out of the corruption of our limbs and even of our ashes. Others divide the soul into two parts, one mortal and one immortal. Others make it corporeal and yet immortal. Some make it immortal but without

sense or knowledge. There are some — even among us — who have believed that devils were made out of the souls of the damned, as Plutarch thinks gods were made out of those that were saved. For there are few things this author is as positive about as he is about this, while elsewhere he keeps to a doubtful and ambiguous way of expression. "We are told," he says, "and ought firmly to believe, that the souls of virtuous men, according to nature and divine justice, become saints, and from saints demigods, and from demigods, after they have been perfectly cleansed and purified as in purifying sacrifices and freed from all suffering and all mortality, they become — not by any civil decree, but in real truth and in all reasonable probability — entire and perfect gods, receiving a most happy and glorious end." But anyone who wants to see him — him, the soberest and most moderate of the whole gang of philosophers — let loose with greater boldness and recount his miracles on this subject, I refer to his treatise _On the Moon_ and _On the Demon of Socrates_, where he can see as plainly as anywhere else that the mysteries of philosophy have many strange things in common with those of poetry; human understanding loses itself in trying to plumb everything to the bottom — just as we, worn out by a long course of life, return to infancy and dotage. There you have the fine, certain instructions we extract from human knowledge about the soul.

There is no less rashness in what they teach us about our bodily parts. Let us pick out one or two examples, or we shall lose ourselves in this vast and stormy ocean of medical errors. First, do they even agree about the material from which men reproduce one another? As to our first creation, no wonder that human understanding finds itself puzzled and perplexed by something so lofty and so far in the past. Archelaus the physician, whose disciple and favourite Socrates was according to Aristoxenus, said that both men and beasts were made of a milky slime drawn out by the heat of the earth. Pythagoras says our seed is the foam or cream of our best blood. Plato, that it is the distillation of the marrow of the backbone, basing his argument on the fact that this part is the first to feel tired by the work. Alcmaeon, that it is part of the substance of the brain — and that this is so, he says, is proved by the weakness of the eyes in those who indulge in that exercise too freely. Democritus, that it is a substance extracted from the whole mass of the body. Epicurus, an extract from soul and body together. Aristotle, an excrement drawn from the nourishment of the blood, the last to be distributed throughout our limbs. Others, that it is blood, concocted and digested by the heat of the genitals — which they argue from the fact that in excessive exertion a man passes pure blood; here there seems to be more likelihood, if one could draw any appearance out of so infinite a confusion. Now to get this seed to do its work, how many contrary opinions do they put forward? Aristotle and Democritus are of the opinion that women have no sperm, and that what they shed is only a sweat distilled by heat and pleasure and movement, which contributes nothing to generation. Galen, on the contrary, and his followers, believe that without the meeting of seeds there can be no generation. Here are the physicians, the philosophers, the lawyers, and the divines, all by the ears with our wives over the dispute: "How long do women carry their fruit?" And I, for my part, on the example of myself, side with those who maintain that a woman goes eleven months with child. The world is built on this experience. There is no woman so commonplace that she cannot give her opinion on all these controversies; and still we cannot agree.

That is enough to verify that man is no better instructed in the knowledge of himself in his bodily part than in his spiritual one. We have set man before himself, and his reason before his reason, to see what she could say. I think I have shown well enough how little she understands of herself in herself; and whoever does not understand himself in himself — what can he understand? _Quasi vero mensuram ullius rei possit agere, qui sui nesciat._ "As if he could take the measure of anything, who does not know his own." In truth, Protagoras was telling us a pretty lie when he made man the measure of all things, when man has never known so much as his own measure. And if it is not man, his dignity would not permit any other creature to have this privilege. Now since he is so self-contradictory, with one judgment ceaselessly subverting another, this flattering proposition was only a mockery, leading us inevitably to conclude that both the compass and the one holding it are nothing. When Thales said that knowing man is very hard for man to grasp, he gave him to understand at the same time that all other knowledge is impossible.

You,* for whom I have taken the trouble — contrary to my custom — to write so long a discourse, will not refuse to defend your Sebond by the usual forms of argument you are instructed in every day, and to exercise your wit and learning in it. For this last fencing trick is only to be used as a last resort: it is a desperate thrust, in which you give up your own arms to make your adversary abandon his — a secret sleight to be put into practice only very rarely, and very carefully. It is great rashness to lose yourself in order to destroy another. You must not die to be revenged, as Gobrias did. He was locked in close combat with a Persian lord when Darius came running up sword in hand and hesitated to strike for fear of killing Gobrias; Gobrias called out to him boldly to strike,
* The author, as already mentioned, is addressing Marguerite de Valois.

even if he ran them both through at once. I have known desperate weapons, and terms in single combat, in which the man offering them put both himself and his adversary on the certainty of mutual death, censured as unjust. The Portuguese in the Indian Sea took some Turks prisoner; the Turks, unable to bear captivity, hit on the plan — and pulled it off — of striking the ship's nails against each other to make a spark fall into the kegs of powder stored in the place they were guarded in, and blow themselves, their masters, and the ship to ashes. Here we touch the outer edge and farthest limit of the sciences, where the extreme is vicious, as it is in virtue. Keep to the common road; it is not good to be too subtle and cunning. Remember the Tuscan proverb:
Chi troppo s'assottiglia, si scavezza.
["He who refines himself too much, breaks."]

My advice is that, in all your opinions and your discourse, as in your manners and everything else, you keep moderate and measured, and avoid novelty. I am an enemy of all extravagant ways. You, who by the authority of your high birth, and still more by the advantages those qualities give you that are more your own, can command at a glance whom you please, should have entrusted this charge to someone of letters who could have proved and illustrated these things to you better. But here is as much as you will need.

Epicurus said of laws that "the worst of them are so necessary to us that without them men would devour one another." Plato says that "without laws we should live like beasts." Our wit is a wandering, dangerous, and reckless tool; it is hard to fit any order or measure to it. In our own time, among those endowed with any rare excellence above others or any extraordinary vivacity of understanding, we see almost all of them break out into licentiousness of opinion and behaviour; it is almost a miracle to find one temperate and sociable. It is entirely reasonable to keep human wit within the strictest possible limits. In study, as in everything else, its steps and advances should be numbered and fixed, and the limits of its inquiries set by art. It is curbed and shackled by religions, laws, customs, sciences, precepts, mortal and immortal penalties. And yet we see it escape all those bonds by its volubility and dissoluteness. It is a vain body with nothing to grip or hold; a various and deformed body, incapable of being either bound or held. In truth there are few souls so regular, firm, and well-born that they can be trusted with their own guidance, and that can sail with moderation and without rashness in the freedom of their own judgments, beyond the common and received opinions. It is wiser to keep them under tutelage. Wit is a dangerous weapon, even to its possessor, if he does not know how to use it carefully; there is no beast to whom a head-board is more justly to be fitted, to keep its eyes down and forward, and stop it wandering here and there off the tracks custom and the laws have laid down. So it is better for you to stick to the beaten path, whatever it may be, than to fly out at random in this unbridled liberty. But if any of these new doctors should try to show off in your presence at the expense of his own soul and yours, to ward off this dangerous plague that is set in your way every day to infect you, this antidote, in the extremest necessity, will prevent the danger and stop the contagion of its poison from harming you or your company.

The freedom, then, and the bold forwardness of these ancient wits produced in philosophy and the human sciences several sects of differing opinions, each one undertaking to judge and choose what to stick to and defend. But now that everyone goes one way — _Qui certis quibusdam destinatisque sententiis addicti et consecrati sunt, ut etiam, quæ non probant, cogantur defendere_, "who are so tied and obliged to certain opinions that they are bound to defend even those they do not approve" — and that we receive the arts by civil authority and decree, so that the schools have only one pattern, one prescribed institution and discipline, we no longer notice what the coin weighs and is really worth; everyone takes it at the value common approval and use have set on it. The alloy is not questioned, only what it passes for. In the same way everything passes; we take physic as we do geometry; and conjuring tricks, enchantments, love-spells, traffic with the souls of the dead, prognostications, casting of houses, even this ridiculous pursuit of the philosophers' stone — all pass as current coin, with no scruple or contradiction. We need only know that Mars's house is in the middle of the triangle of the hand, Venus's in the thumb, and Mercury's in the little finger; that when the table-line cuts the tubercle of the forefinger it is a sign of cruelty; that when it falls short of the middle finger and the natural median line makes an angle with the vital on the same side, it is the sign of a miserable death; that if in a woman the natural line is open and does not close the angle with the vital, this means she will not be very chaste. I leave you to judge whether a man equipped with such knowledge can pass with respect and reputation in any company.

Theophrastus said that human knowledge, guided by the senses, can judge the causes of things up to a certain point; but once it reaches the first and ultimate causes, it must stop and pull back, either through its own weakness or the difficulty of the matter. A moderate and gentle opinion: that our understanding can carry us to the knowledge of some things, and has certain measures of its power, beyond which it is reckless to push it. The view is plausible, and put forward by men of well-composed minds. But it is hard to set limits to our wit, which is curious and greedy and will no more stop at a thousand paces than at fifty, having found by experience that where one has failed, another has succeeded, and that what was unknown to one age the next has cleared up; that arts and sciences are not cast in a mould but are slowly shaped and perfected, by repeated handling and polishing — as bears lick their cubs leisurely into form. What my own force cannot discover, I still do not stop probing and trying; and by handling and kneading this new matter over and over, by turning and warming it, I open up to whoever comes after me a certain ease in enjoying it more freely, and make it more pliable and supple for him,
Ut hymettia sole Cera remollescit, tractataque pollice multas Vertitur in facies, ipsoque fit utilis usu;
["As Hymettian wax softens in the sun, and worked between the fingers takes on many shapes, and so by use becomes useful."]
as the second will do for the third. This is why the difficulty need not make me despair — nor my own incapacity, since it is only my own.

Man is as capable of all things as of some; and if he confesses, as Theophrastus says, his ignorance of first causes, let him at the same time give up all the rest of his knowledge. If he is defective in his foundations, his reason is run aground; argument and inquiry have no other goal or stopping-point than principles. If this goal does not stop his career, he runs into endless irresolution. _Non potest aliud alio magis minusve comprehendi, quoniam omnium rerum una est definitio comprehendendi:_

"One thing can no more or less be comprehended than another, because the definition of comprehending all things is the same." Now it is very likely that if the soul knew anything, it would first know itself; and if it knew anything outside itself, it would be its own body and its own case before anything else. If we see the gods of medicine arguing to this very day about our anatomy,
Mulciber in Trojam, pro Trojâ stabat Apollo;
["Vulcan stood against Troy, Apollo for Troy."]

when are we to expect them to agree? We are nearer neighbours to ourselves than whiteness is to snow, or weight to stones. If man does not know himself, how can he know his powers and functions? It isn't that we have no real knowledge in us; but it gets there by chance — since errors come into our soul by the same route, in the same manner, and with the same conduct, the soul has no way to distinguish them, no way to pick truth from falsehood.

The Academics admitted a certain partiality of judgment, and thought it too crude to say that it was no more likely that snow was white than that it was black, or that we were any more sure of the motion of a stone thrown by the hand than of the motion of the eighth sphere. And to avoid this awkwardness and oddness — which can hardly lodge itself in our imagination — though they concluded that we are in no way capable of knowledge, and that truth is sunk in such a deep abyss as cannot be reached by human sight, they still acknowledged that some things were more likely than others, and admitted into their judgment this faculty of being able to lean toward one appearance more than another. They allowed it that inclination, but barred all firm conclusion. The Pyrrhonist opinion is bolder, and also somewhat more likely. For this Academic leaning, this inclination toward one proposition rather than another — what is it but a recognition of some more apparent truth in this than in that? If our understanding is capable of the form, lineaments, bearing, and face of truth, it could see it whole as well as in parts, in its first springing and still imperfect. This appearance of likelihood, which makes them rather take the left hand than the right, is what augments the weight; multiply this ounce of verisimilitude — which tips the scales — into a hundred, into a thousand ounces; it will end with the balance itself settling the controversy and determining one choice, one entire truth. But why do they let themselves be inclined and swayed by likelihood, if they do not know the truth? How can they know the likeness of a thing whose essence they do not know? Either we can judge absolutely, or we absolutely cannot. If our intellectual and sensory faculties are without footing or foundation, if they only push and pull, it is pointless to let our judgment be carried away by any part of their operation, whatever appearance it may present to us. The surest, happiest seat of our understanding would be one in which it kept itself temperate, upright, inflexible, neither tottering nor agitated: _Inter visa, vera aut falsa, ad animi assensum, nihil interest._ "Among the things that appear, whether true or false, it makes no difference to the mind's assent." That things do not lodge in us in their form and essence, and do not make their way in by their own force and authority, is clear enough. If they did, we would all receive them the same way; wine would taste the same to the sick as to the well; the man with a chapped or numb finger would find the same hardness in the wood or iron he handles as another would. Foreign subjects, then, give themselves up to our mercy and are seated in us as we please. Now if on our side we received anything without alteration — if the human grasp were strong and large enough to seize on truth by our own means — these means being common to all men, this truth would be handed from one to another; and there would be at least one thing in the world, among so many, that would be believed by all men with a universal consent. But the fact that there is no proposition that is not debated and contested among us, or that may not be, makes it very plain that our natural judgment does not very clearly grasp what it embraces. For my judgment cannot make my fellows approve of what it approves; which is a sign that I seized it by some means other than a natural power that is in me and in all other men.

Let us set aside this infinite confusion of opinions that we see even among the philosophers themselves, and this perpetual and universal dispute about the knowledge of things. For this is truly presupposed: that men — I mean the most knowing, the best born, the most able — are not agreed on any one thing, not even that the heavens are over our heads. Those who doubt everything doubt that too; and those who deny that we can comprehend anything say that we have not comprehended that the heavens are over our heads. These two opinions are, beyond comparison, the stronger in number.

Besides this infinite diversity and division — through the trouble our judgment gives ourselves and the uncertainty everyone feels in himself — it is easy to see that our seat is very unstable and insecure. How variously do we judge of things? How often do we change our opinions? What I hold and believe today I hold and believe with my whole belief; all my instruments and engines seize on this opinion and stand surety for it, as far as in them lies. I could not embrace nor preserve any truth with greater confidence and assurance than I do this one; I am wholly and entirely possessed by it. But has it not happened to me, not just once but a hundred — a thousand — times, every day, to have embraced some other thing with all the same instruments, in the same condition, which I have since judged to be false? A man must at least become wise at his own expense. If I have often found myself betrayed in this way; if my touch turns out commonly false, and my balance unequal and unjust — what assurance can I now have more than at other times? Is it not stupidity and madness to let myself be so often deceived by my guide? Yet let fortune shift us five hundred times from place to place; let her do nothing but ceaselessly empty and refill our belief, as into a vessel, with new and newer opinions — still the present and the latest is the certain and infallible one, for which we are to abandon goods, honour, life, health, and all.
Posterior... res illa reperta Perdit, et immutat sensus ad pristina quæque.
["The latest thing discovered spoils all the rest and changes our taste for what came before."]

Whatever is preached to us, whatever we learn, we should still remember that it is a man who gives and a man who receives; it is a mortal hand that holds it out, and a mortal hand that accepts it. The things that come to us from heaven alone have the right and authority to persuade, alone bear the mark of truth — which we also do not see with our own eyes nor receive by our own means. That great and sacred image could not abide in so wretched a dwelling if God did not prepare it for that purpose, if God did not fortify and reform it by his particular and supernatural grace and favour. At least our frail and defective condition ought to make us behave with more reserve and moderation in our innovations and changes. We ought to remember that whatever we take into our understanding, we often take in things that are false — and we take them in by the same instruments that so often give themselves the lie and are so often deceived.

Now it is no wonder they should so often contradict themselves, when they are so easily turned and swayed by the lightest occasions. It is certain that our perceptions, our judgment, and the faculties of the soul in general suffer along with the movements and alterations of the body — alterations that are continual. Aren't our minds livelier, our memories prompter and quicker, our thoughts more vivid in health than in sickness? Don't joy and gaiety make us receive the subjects that present themselves to our soul quite differently than care and melancholy do? Do you believe Catullus's verses, or Sappho's, please an old miserly fool the way they please a vigorous, amorous young man? Cleomenes, son of Anaxandridas, when he was ill, was reproached by his friends for having strange new humours and whims. "I believe it," he said; "and so I am not the same man as when I am in health. Being a different person now, my opinions and fancies are also different from before." In our courts of law a phrase is often used of criminals when they find the judges in a good humour, gentle and mild: _Gaudeat de bonâ fortunâ_, "let him enjoy his good luck." For it is most certain that men's judgments are sometimes more prone to condemnation, sharper and more severe, and at other times easier, milder, more inclined to excuse. A judge who carries with him from home the pain of gout, jealousy, or theft by his servant, with his whole soul possessed by anger — there is no doubt that his judgment will lean that way. That venerable senate of the Areopagites used to hear and decide cases by night, for fear that the sight of the parties might corrupt their justice. Even the air itself, and the serenity of the sky, will work some change in us, as the lines in Cicero say:
Tales sunt hominum mentes, quali pater ipse Jupiter auctiferâ lustravit lampade terras.
["Men's minds are such as the light with which Father Jupiter himself, with his fertilising lamp, has illumined the lands."]

It is not only fevers, debaucheries, and great accidents that overthrow our judgments — the least things in the world will do it. We need not doubt, though we may not feel it, that if a continuous fever can overwhelm the soul, a tertian will alter it in some proportionate measure; if an apoplexy can stupefy and totally put out the sight of our understanding, we need not doubt that a heavy cold will dazzle it. And so there is hardly a single hour in a man's whole life in which our judgment is in its due place and proper condition, our bodies being subject to so many continual alterations, and stocked with so many different sorts of springs, that I believe the doctors that some one of them must always be out of order.

As to the rest, this disorder does not easily declare itself, unless it is extreme and past remedy. Reason always limps and goes lame, and that as much with falsehood as with truth; so it is hard to detect her deviations and mistakes. I always call "reason" that appearance of meditation each of us forges in himself. This reason, of which a hundred contrary versions can be made about one and the same subject, is an instrument of lead and wax, ductile, pliable, accommodating to all sorts of biases and all sorts of measures, so that nothing remains but the art and skill of turning and moulding it. However uprightly a judge may mean to act, if he does not watch himself closely — which few care to do — his inclination to friendship, to kinship, to beauty or revenge, and not only such weighty things but the merely fortuitous impulse that makes us prefer one thing to another, and that without reason's leave thrusts our choice on us between two equal subjects, or some shadow of similar vanity, may insensibly insinuate into his judgment a favour or disfavour for a cause, and make the balance dip.
I, who watch myself as closely as I can, and have my eyes always trained on myself, like one who has no great business elsewhere,
Quis sub Arcto Rex gelidæ metuatur oræ, Quid Tyridatem terreat, unice Securus,
["Untroubled which king is feared in the frozen north, or what frightens Tiridates."]

barely dare to tell the vanity and weakness I find in myself. My footing is so unstable and so insecure, I find myself so apt to totter and reel, and my sight so disordered, that fasting I am quite another man than when I am full. If a fair day and good health smile on me, I am very affable and good-natured; if a corn troubles my toe, I am sullen, out of humour, and not to be seen. The same pace of a horse seems to me at one moment hard, at another easy; the same road one moment short, another long; the same shape one moment more, another less pleasing. One while I am for doing everything, another while for doing nothing at all; and what pleases me now would be a torment to me at another time. I have a thousand pointless, accidental movements within myself: either I am gripped by melancholy or swayed by anger; sometimes by its own private authority sadness predominates in me, and a moment later I am as cheerful as a cricket. When I take up a book, I have sometimes found admirable graces in such and such a passage, and such as struck my soul; let me come across them at another time, and I may turn and toss, tumble and rattle the pages to no purpose — it is then to me a shapeless undiscovered mass. Even in my own writings I do not always find the air of my first fancy; I have no idea what I meant to say, and am often hard put to it to correct and pump for some new sense, because I have lost the first one, which was better. I do nothing but go and come; my judgment does not always advance — it floats and roams:
Velut minuta magno Deprensa navis in mari vesaniente vento.
["Like a tiny boat caught on the great sea when the wind goes mad."]

Very often, as I am apt to do, having for exercise taken up an opinion contrary to my own, my mind, bending and applying itself that way, so engages me in it that I no longer discern the reason of my former belief, and I forsake it. I am, as it were, led away by the side I lean to, whatever it is, and carried off by my own weight. Almost everyone would say the same of himself, if he considered himself as I do. Preachers know very well that the emotions that steal up on them as they speak push them toward belief; that in passion we are warmer in defending our proposition, take a deeper impression of it, and embrace it with greater vehemence and approval than in our colder and more temperate state. You give your lawyer only a simple brief of your case; he returns you a dubious and uncertain answer, by which you see he is indifferent which side he takes. Have you paid him well so he may relish it the better? Does he begin to be really concerned, and do you find him interested and zealous in your cause? His reason and learning will gradually grow hot for your side; an apparent and undoubted truth presents itself to his understanding; he sees a new light in your business and in good earnest believes and persuades himself that it is so. In fact, I am not sure that the ardour that springs from spite and obstinacy, against the power and violence of the magistrate and the danger involved, or out of concern for reputation, may not have made some men maintain at the stake the very opinion for which, free and among friends, they would not have burned a finger. The shocks and jostles that the soul receives from the body's passions can do a great deal in it; but its own passions can do still more — and the soul is so subject to them that perhaps it can be said it has no other pace and motion than the breath of those winds, without whose agitation it would be becalmed and motionless, like a ship in mid-sea when the winds deny it their help. And whoever maintained this, siding with the Peripatetics, would not do us much wrong, since it is very well known that the soul's greatest and noblest actions proceed from this push of the passions and need their help. Valour, they say, cannot be perfect without the help of anger; _Semper Ajax fortis, fortissimus tamen in furore_, "Ajax was always brave, but bravest of all in his fury."
