Nor do we engage the wicked and the enemy vigorously enough unless we are angry; and the advocate, they say, must inspire indignation in the judges to obtain justice.

Disordered desires drove Themistocles and Demosthenes, and pushed philosophers to watching, fasting, and pilgrimages; and they lead us to honour, learning, and health — all very useful ends. This meanness of soul, in bearing anxiety and trouble, serves to breed remorse and repentance in the conscience, and to make us feel the scourge of God and the prudent correction sent for the chastening of our offences. Compassion is a spur to mercy; the prudence that preserves and governs us is roused by our fear; and how many brave actions by ambition! How many by presumption! In short, there is no brave or noble virtue without some irregular agitation. May this not be one of the reasons that moved the Epicureans to discharge God from all care and concern for our affairs — because even the effects of his goodness could not be exercised on our behalf without disturbing his repose by means of passions, which are so many spurs and instruments pricking the soul into virtuous action? Or did they think otherwise, and take the passions for tempests that shamefully drag the soul out of its tranquillity? _Ut maris tranquillitas intelligitur, nullâ, ne minima quidem, aura fluctus commovente: Sic animi quietus et placatus status cernitur, quum perturbatio nulla est, quâ moveri queat._ "As the sea is understood to be calm when not the least breath of air is stirring the waves, so the state of the soul is seen to be quiet and at peace when there is no perturbation to move it."

What variety of sense and reason, what contrariety of imaginings, the diversity of our passions inspires us with! What assurance, then, can we take of a thing so movable and unstable, subject by its condition to the dominion of disturbance, and never going at anything but a forced and borrowed pace? If our judgment is even at the mercy of sickness and upheaval, if it is from folly and rashness that it must take the impression of things, what security can we expect from it?

Is it not a piece of great audacity in philosophy to hold that men perform the greatest actions, and come nearest the Divinity, when they are furious, mad, and beside themselves? We better ourselves, it seems, by the loss of our reason, by training it down. The two natural ways to enter the cabinet of the gods and there foresee the course of destiny are fury and sleep.

This is amusing to consider: by the dislocation that passions cause in our reason, we become virtuous; by its extirpation, brought on by madness or by the image of death, we become diviners and prophets. I have never been so willing to believe philosophy in anything as in this. It is pure enthusiasm with which sacred truth has inspired the spirit of philosophy, when it makes philosophy confess — contrary to its own premise — that the calmest, most composed and healthful state in which it can seat the soul is not its best condition; that our waking is more a sleep than sleep itself; that our wisdom is less wise than folly; that our dreams are worth more than our meditations; that the worst place we can stand is in ourselves. But does philosophy not realise that we are wise enough to consider that the voice that issues from the spirit when it is freed from the man — so clear-sighted, so great, so perfect — and which, while it is in the man, is so earthbound, ignorant and dark, is a voice proceeding from the spirit of dark, earthbound, ignorant man, and for that reason a voice not to be trusted or believed?

I, being of a soft and heavy complexion, have no great experience of these violent agitations, most of which take the soul by surprise without giving it the leisure to recollect itself. But the passion said to be produced by idleness in the hearts of young men, though it advances at leisure and with a measured progress, plainly shows, to those who have tried to oppose its power, the violence our judgment suffers in this alteration and conversion. I once tried to withstand and repel it; for I am so far from being one of those who invite vices that I do not even follow them if they do not haul me along. I felt it spring, grow, and increase in spite of my resistance; and at last, living and seeing as I was, it took complete hold of me. So that, as if waking from drunkenness, the images of things began to appear to me quite otherwise than they used to. I clearly saw the advantages of the object I desired growing and expanding under the influence of my imagination, the difficulties of my attempt becoming smoother and easier; and my reason and conscience were both laid aside. But this fire having evaporated in an instant, as from a flash of lightning, I was aware that my soul resumed another kind of sight, another state, another judgment. The difficulties of retreat appeared great and invincible, and the same things had quite another taste and aspect than the heat of desire had presented them to me. Which of the two more truly? Pyrrho knows nothing about it. We are never without sickness. Agues have their hot and cold fits; from the effects of an ardent passion we fall back into shivering. As much as I had advanced, so much did I retire:

Qualis ubi alterno procurrens gurgite pontus, Nunc ruit ad terras, scopulosque superjacit undam Spumeus, extremamque sinu perfundit arenam; Nunc rapidus retro, atque æstu revoluta resorbens Saxa, fugit, littusque vado labente relinquit.

["As when the sea, running in alternate surge, now rushes to the shore and hurls its foaming wave over the rocks and floods the farthest beach with its bosom; now, swift in retreat and sucking back the stones rolled by the tide, flees, and leaves the shore as the shallow draws away."]

Now from knowing this volubility of mine I have accidentally bred in myself a certain constancy of opinions, and have not much altered those that were first and natural to me. For whatever appearance there may be in novelty, I do not easily change, for fear of losing by the bargain; and since I am not capable of choosing, I take other men's choice and keep myself in the station where God has placed me. Otherwise I could not keep from rolling perpetually. Thus by the grace of God I have preserved myself entire, without anxiety or trouble of conscience, in the ancient faith of our religion, amid all the sects and divisions our age has produced. The writings of the ancients — the best authors, I mean — being full and solid, tempt and carry me almost any way they please. Whoever I am reading seems always to have the most force; and I find that each, in his turn, is in the right — though they contradict one another. The facility good wits have of making everything they want to recommend seem likely, and the fact that nothing is so strange that they cannot give it enough colour to deceive a simplicity like mine, plainly shows the weakness of their testimony. The heavens and the stars had been three thousand years in motion, and the whole world held to that belief, when Cleanthes the Samian — or, according to Theophrastus, Nicetas of Syracuse — took it into his head to maintain that it was the earth that moved, turning on its axis along the oblique circle of the zodiac. And Copernicus in our own time has so well grounded this doctrine that it serves regularly for all astronomical calculations. What use can we make of this, except to conclude that we ought not to care much which of the two is the true opinion? And who knows whether a third opinion, a thousand years from now, may not overthrow them both?

Sic volvenda ætas commutat tempora rerum: Quod fuit in pretio, fit nullo denique honore; Porro aliud succedit, et e contemptibus exit, Inque dies magis appetitur, floretque repertum Laudibus, et miro est mortales inter honore.

["Thus rolling time changes the seasons of things: what was once prized is at last held in no honour; another thing comes to take its place, rises out of contempt, and is more sought after every day, and once found flourishes with praises, and is in marvellous esteem among mortals."]

So when any new doctrine presents itself to us, we have great reason to mistrust it, and to remember that, before it was set on foot, the contrary opinion was generally received; and as that one has been overthrown by this, so a third invention, in time to come, may start up and damn the second. Before the principles Aristotle introduced were in repute, other principles satisfied human reason, as these do us now. What patent do these people have, what particular privilege, that the career of our invention should stop at them, and that the possession of our whole future belief should belong to them? They are no more exempt from being thrust out of doors than their predecessors were. When anyone presses me with a new argument, I ought to think that what I cannot answer, another can. To believe every likely thing that one cannot refute is great simplicity; by that means the entire common run — and we are all common — would have their belief as turnable as a weathercock. Their souls, being so easy to impose on, and offering no resistance, must perforce go on receiving impression after impression, the last each time wiping out the footprints of the one before. He who feels himself weak ought to answer, as is the practice, that he must speak with his counsel, or refer himself to wiser men, from whom he received his instruction. How long has medicine been practised in the world? They say a newcomer called Paracelsus is now changing and overthrowing the whole order of the ancient rules, and maintaining that, up to now, medicine has been good for nothing but killing people. I dare say he will easily prove this, but I do not think it would be wisdom to risk my life testing his own experience. We are not to believe everyone, the precept says, because everyone can say all things. A man of this profession of novelties and physical reforms told me not long since that all the ancients were notoriously mistaken about the nature and motion of the winds, which he would clearly demonstrate to me if I would give him a hearing. After I had patiently listened to his arguments, which all had every appearance of truth: "Then," I asked, "did those who sailed by Theophrastus go westward when they had their prow toward the east? Did they go sideways or backward?" "That's chance," he answered, "but it remains that they were mistaken." I replied that I would rather follow effects than reason. Now these things often clash with each other; and I have been told that in geometry — which claims to have reached the highest point of certainty of any science — there are inescapable demonstrations that overturn the truth of all experience. Jacques Pelletier told me in my own house that he had found two lines stretching toward each other to meet, which he affirmed could nevertheless never meet, even extended to infinity. And the Pyrrhonians make no other use of their arguments and their reason than to ruin the appearance of experience; and it is a wonder how far the suppleness of our reason has followed them in this attempt to contest the evidence of effects. For they affirm that we do not move, that we do not speak, and that there is neither weight nor heat, with the same force of argument with which we affirm the most likely things. Ptolemy, who was a great man, had set the bounds of this world of ours; all the ancient philosophers thought they had its measure, except for some remote islands that might escape their knowledge. It would have been Pyrrhonism a thousand years ago to doubt the science of cosmography, and the opinions everyone had received from it; it was heresy to admit the antipodes. And see — in our own age there is an infinite extent of mainland discovered, not an island or a single country but a portion of the world nearly equal in size to the one we knew before. The geographers of our time do not hesitate to assure us that now all is found, all is seen:
Nam quod adest præsto, placet, et pollere videtur;
["For what is at hand pleases, and seems to prevail."]

But it remains to be seen whether, as Ptolemy was once mistaken on the foundation of his reason, it would not be very foolish to trust now what these people say? And whether it is not more likely that this great body we call the world is something quite other than what we imagine.

Plato says it changes its face in every respect; that the heavens, the stars, and the sun sometimes have motions retrograde to what we see, changing east into west. The Egyptian priests told Herodotus that from the time of their first king, eleven thousand and odd years before (and they showed him the effigies of all their kings in life-taken statues), the sun had four times altered his course; that the sea and the earth alternately changed into one another; that the beginning of the world is undetermined. Aristotle and Cicero both say the same; and some among us hold that the world has existed from all eternity, is mortal, and is renewed by various vicissitudes, calling Solomon and Isaiah as witnesses — to avoid the objections that God has once been a creator without a creature, that he had had nothing to do, that he got rid of that idleness by setting his hand to this work, and that he is therefore subject to change. In the most famous of the Greek schools, the world is taken for a god made by a greater god, composed of a body and a soul fixed at its centre and dilating outward to its circumference by musical proportions; divine, infinitely happy, infinitely great, infinitely wise, eternal. Inside him are other gods — the sea, the earth, the stars — who entertain one another with a harmonious perpetual agitation, a divine dance, sometimes meeting, sometimes drawing apart; concealing and revealing themselves; changing their order, now in front, now behind. Heraclitus was positive that the world was made of fire, and was destined by fate one day to be set ablaze and consumed, and then renewed again. And Apuleius says of men: _Sigillatim mortales, cunctim perpetui._ "In particular they are mortal; taken altogether, eternal." Alexander wrote to his mother an account drawn by an Egyptian priest from their monuments, testifying to the infinite antiquity of that nation and embracing the birth and progress of other countries. Cicero and Diodorus say that in their time the Chaldaeans kept a register of four hundred thousand years and more. Aristotle, Pliny, and others say that Zoroaster flourished six thousand years before Plato's time. Plato says the people of the city of Sais have written records going back eight thousand years, and that the city of Athens was built a thousand years before Sais. Epicurus, that at the same time things are here in the posture we see them, they are the same and arranged in the same way in several other worlds — which he would have asserted with even greater assurance had he seen the resemblance and concordance of the newly discovered world of the West Indies with ours, present and past, in so many odd particulars.

In truth, considering what has come to our knowledge of the workings of this earthly polity, I have often marvelled to see, across so vast a distance of places and times, such a coincidence of so great a number of popular and savage opinions, and of wild manners and beliefs, which by no means seem to come from our natural meditation. The human mind is a great worker of miracles! And this connection has, moreover, something extraordinary about it; it is found in names too, and in a thousand other things. For they have found nations there (which for all we know never heard of us) where circumcision was in use; where there were states and great civic governments maintained by women alone, without men; where our fasts and Lent were represented, with abstinence from women added to them; where our crosses were honoured in several ways — here, used to ornament their tombs; there, set up, particularly that of St Andrew, to protect themselves from nocturnal visions, and laid on the cradles of infants against spells. Elsewhere there was found a wooden cross of very great height, worshipped as the god of rain, and that a long way inland. There was seen an exact image of our penitents, the use of mitres, the celibacy of the priesthood, the art of divining by the entrails of sacrificed animals, abstinence from all sorts of flesh and fish, priests officiating in a particular language not the common one; and this fancy: that the first god was driven away by a second, his younger brother; that men were created with all sorts of necessities and conveniences, which have since been taken from them in part on account of their sins, that their territory was changed and their natural condition made worse; that they were once overwhelmed by an inundation of water from heaven; that only a few families escaped, who took refuge in caves on high mountains, whose mouths they stopped up so the waters could not get in, having shut up with themselves several sorts of animals; that when they noticed the rain had stopped they sent out dogs, and when these returned wet and clean they judged the water had not gone down much; afterwards they sent others, and seeing them return dirty, came out to repeople the world, which they found full of nothing but snakes. In one place we met with the belief of a day of judgment; so much so that they were extremely displeased at the Spaniards for disturbing the bones of the dead in plundering the tombs for treasure, saying that those bones, once jumbled, could not easily be put back together. Trade by exchange and no other way; fairs and markets for that purpose; dwarfs and deformed people to ornament the tables of princes; the use of falconry, according to the nature of their hawks; tyrannical taxes; nicety in gardens; dancing, acrobatic tumbling, instrumental music, coats of arms, tennis-courts, dice and lotteries — at which they sometimes grow so heated as to wager themselves and their freedom; medicine by nothing but charms; cipher writing; the belief in only one first man, the father of all nations; the adoration of one God who once lived as a man in perfect virginity, fasting, and penitence, preaching the laws of nature and the ceremonies of religion, and who vanished from the world without a natural death; the theory of giants; the custom of making themselves drunk on their drinks and drinking to the limit; religious ornaments painted with bones and dead men's skulls; surplices, holy water sprinkled; wives and servants who offer themselves in emulation to be burned or buried with the dead husband or master; a law by which the eldest inherits all the estate, no part being left to the younger but obedience; the custom that, on promotion to a certain office of great authority, the promoted person takes on a new name and leaves behind the one he had before; another, to strew lime on the knee of the newborn child with these words,

"From dust you came, and to dust you must return," as also the art of augury. The faint shadows of our religion observable in some of these examples are testimonies of its dignity and divinity. It has, in some manner, insinuated itself not only among the infidel nations on this side of the world by a certain imitation, but also among these barbarians, by what seems a common and supernatural inspiration. For there we find the belief of purgatory, but in a new form; what we assign to fire, they assign to cold, and imagine that souls are purged and punished by the rigour of extreme coldness. And this example reminds me of another pleasant variety: as some peoples there delighted in unmuffling the ends of their members and clipping the foreskin after the Mahometan and Jewish fashion, others made such a conscience of laying it bare that they carefully gathered it up with little strings to keep that end from peeping into the air. And another variety: whereas we, in honour of kings and feast-days, put on our best clothes, in some regions, to express their inferiority and submission to their king, the subjects come before him in their meanest garments, and on entering his palace throw some old tattered garment over their better dress, so that all the lustre and ornament should be in him alone. But to go on:

If nature encloses within the bounds of her ordinary course the beliefs, judgments, and opinions of men, as well as everything else; if they have their revolution, their season, their birth and death, like cabbage plants; if the heavens stir and rule them at their pleasure — what magisterial and lasting authority can we attribute to them? If we see by experience that the form of our being depends on the air, on the climate, and on the soil where we are born — and not only the colour, the stature, the complexion, and the features, but also the very faculties of the soul itself: _Et plaga cæli non solum ad robur corporum, sed etiam animorum facit_, "The climate has great influence not only on the strength of bodies but on that of souls too," says Vegetius — and that the goddess who founded the city of Athens chose to place it in a temperature of air fit to make men prudent, as the Egyptian priests told Solon: _Athenis tenue cælum; ex quo etiam acutiores putantur Attici; crassum Thebis; itaque pingues Thebani, et valentes_, "The air of Athens is thin and subtle, and so the Attic people are reputed more acute; at Thebes the air is thick, and so the Thebans are taken for heavy-witted and strong." In such a way that, as fruits and animals come out different, so men are also more or less warlike, just, temperate, and teachable — here given to wine, elsewhere to theft or lewdness; here inclined to superstition, elsewhere to unbelief; in one place to liberty, in another to servitude; capable of one science or one art, dull or quick-witted, obedient or rebellious, good or bad, according to the place where they live; and they take on a new complexion if moved, like trees. This is why Cyrus would not grant the Persians leave to leave their rough and craggy country for one more pleasant and even, saying that fertile, tender soils make men effeminate and soft. If we see now one art and one belief flourish, and at another time another, through some celestial influence; this age producing such-and-such natures, and inclining mankind to such-and-such propensities, the spirits of men one while gay and another grim, like our fields — what becomes of all those fine prerogatives we soothe ourselves with? Seeing that a wise man can be mistaken, and a hundred men and a hundred nations, and even human nature itself, as we believe, is for many ages wide of the mark on one thing or another — what assurance do we have that she will ever stop being mistaken, or that in this very age of ours she is not?

It seems to me that, among the other testimonies of our weakness, this one ought not to be forgotten: that man cannot, by his own wish and desire, find out what he wants; that not only in fruition but in imagination and wish, we cannot agree on what we would have to satisfy and content us. Let us leave it to our own thought to cut and tailor at pleasure; it cannot even desire what is good for it, and so satisfy itself:
Quid enim ratione timemus, Aut cupimus? Quid tam dextro pede concipis, ut te Conatus non poniteat, votique peracti?
["What do we fear or desire with reason? What do you ever conceive with so favourable a foot that you do not, in the end, regret the attempt and the wish fulfilled?"]

That is why Socrates only begged the gods to give him whatever they knew to be best for him; and the private and public prayer of the Lacedemonians was simply for things good and useful, leaving the choice and selection of them to the discretion of the Supreme Power:
Conjugium petimus, partumque uxoris; at illis Notum, qui pueri, qualisque futura sit uxor:
["We ask for marriage and for our wife's childbearing; but only the gods know what sort of boys, and what sort of wife, they will turn out to be."]

And Christians pray to God, "Thy will be done," so as not to fall into the trouble the poet imagines for King Midas. He prayed to the gods that everything he touched might be turned to gold; his prayer was answered. His wine was gold, his bread was gold, the feathers of his bed, his shirt, his clothes — all gold; so that he found himself overwhelmed by the fruition of his desire, endowed with an unbearable benefit, and had to unpray his prayers.
Attonitus novitate mali, divesque, miserque, Effugere optat opes, et, quæ modo voverat, odit.
["Astonished at the novelty of his evil, rich and wretched at once, he longs to escape his wealth, and hates what just before he had begged for."]

To take an example from myself: when I was young, I asked of fortune, above all things, the order of St Michael, which was then the highest distinction of honour among the French nobility, and very rare. She pleasantly gratified my longing — instead of raising me up and lifting me from my own place to attain it, she did me a much greater kindness, by bringing it so low and making it so cheap that it stooped down to my shoulders and below. Cleobis and Bito, Trophonius and Agamedes, having asked, the first pair of their goddess and the second pair of their god, a reward worthy of their piety, had death for a reward — so different from ours are heavenly opinions about what is fit for us. God might grant us riches, honours, life, even health, to our hurt; for not everything that is pleasing to us is good for us. If he sends us death or an increase of sickness instead of a cure — _Virga tua et baculus tuus ipsa me consolata sunt_, "Thy rod and thy staff have comforted me" — he does so by the rule of his providence, which discerns better and more certainly than we can what is suitable for us; and we ought to take it in good part as coming from a wise and most friendly hand.
Si consilium vis: Permittes ipsis expendere numinibus, quid Conveniat nobis, rebusque sit utile nostris... Carior est illis homo quam sibi;
["If you want advice, leave it to the gods themselves to weigh what is fitting for us and useful for our affairs... To them, man is dearer than he is to himself."]

For to ask of him honours and commands is to ask that he throw you into a battle, set you on a cast of the dice, or something of that sort, of which the outcome is unknown to you and the fruit doubtful.

There is no dispute so sharp and so violent among the philosophers as the one over the question of man's sovereign good — out of which, by Varro's count, two hundred and eighty-eight sects arose. _Qui autem de summo bono dissentit, de totâ philosophiæ ratione disputat._ "For whoever disagrees about the highest good is disputing about the whole reasoning of philosophy."
Tres mihi convivæ prope dissentire videntur, Poscentes vario multum diversa palato; Quid dem? Quid non dem? Renuis tu quod jubet alter; Quod petis, id sane est invisum acidumque duobus;

["I have three guests at table, and they all seem to disagree, each demanding very different things with very different palates. What shall I give? What shall I refuse? You turn down what the other asks for; what you call for is hateful and sour to the other two."]

Nature might say the same to their contests and debates. Some say our well-being lies in virtue; others, in pleasure; others, in submitting to nature; one, in knowledge; another, in being exempt from pain; another, in not letting ourselves be carried away by appearances — and this last fancy seems to have some relation to the one of the ancient Pythagoras,
Nil admirari, prope res est una, Numici, Solaque, quæ possit facere et servare beatum:
["To wonder at nothing is, Numicius, almost the one and only thing that can make a man happy and keep him so."]

which is the drift of the Pyrrhonian sect. Aristotle attributes wondering at nothing to magnanimity; and Arcesilaus said that constancy, and a right and inflexible state of judgment, were the true good, while consent and assent were the sin and the evil. There, by being so positive and establishing a definite axiom, he was abandoning Pyrrhonism — for the Pyrrhonians, when they say that ataraxy, which is the immobility of judgment, is the sovereign good, do not mean to say it affirmatively, but only that the same movement of soul that makes them avoid precipices and take shelter from the cold presents them with this fancy and makes them refuse another.

How I wish that, in my lifetime, either some other person or Justus Lipsius — the most learned man now living, of the most polished and judicious understanding, truly the equal of my Turnebus — had the will, the health, and the leisure to gather conscientiously into a register, sorted into their divisions and classes, as many as can be found of the opinions of the ancient philosophers concerning the subject of our being and of our conduct: their controversies, the succession and reputation of their sects, the application of the lives of the authors and their disciples to their own precepts, in memorable accidents and exemplary occasions. What a beautiful and useful work that would be!

For the rest, if we are to draw the rules of our conduct from ourselves, into what a tangle do we throw ourselves! For what our reason advises us, as the most likely course, is generally that each of us should obey the laws of his country — that was Socrates' advice, inspired, he says, by a divine counsel. And what does that say, except that our duty has no other rule than the accidental? Truth ought to have a like and universal face; if man could know equity and justice with a body and a true being, he would not tie it to the conditions of this country or that; it would not be from the whims of the Persians or the Indians that virtue would take its form. There is nothing more subject to perpetual agitation than the laws. Since I was born, I have known the English — our neighbours — change theirs three or four times, not only in matters of civil regimen (which is the one thing in which constancy may sometimes be dispensed with), but in the most important subject there can be, namely religion. I am the more troubled and ashamed at this because it is a nation with whom the people of my province formerly had such close familiarity and acquaintance that there are still in my house some traces of our ancient kindred. And here at home I have known a thing that was capital become lawful; and we who follow others may, by the chance of war, be one day found guilty of high treason, both divine and human, should the justice of our arms fall into the power of injustice and, after a few years' possession, take on a contrary character. How could that ancient god more clearly accuse the ignorance of human knowledge concerning the divine Being, and give men to understand that their religion was a thing of their own contrivance — useful as a bond for their society — than by declaring, as he did to those who came to his tripod for instruction, that every man's true worship was the one he found in use in the place where he happened to be? O God, what an infinite obligation we owe the bounty of our sovereign Creator, for having disabused our belief from these wandering and arbitrary devotions, and for having seated it on the eternal foundation of his holy word! But what then will the philosophers say to us in this necessity? "That we follow the laws of our country." That is to say, this floating sea of the opinions of a republic, or of a prince, that will paint justice for me in as many colours, and shape it in as many ways, as there are changes of passion in themselves. I cannot let my judgment be so flexible. What kind of virtue is it that I see in repute one day, and that tomorrow is in none, and that the crossing of a river makes a crime? What sort of truth is it that these mountains limit for us, and that becomes a lie to all the world beyond them?

But they are amusing when, to give some certainty to the laws, they say that there are some firm, perpetual, immovable ones, which they call natural, imprinted in mankind by the condition of its own being. Of these, some count three, some four, some more, some less — a sign that this is as doubtful a mark as the rest. Now they are so unlucky (for what else can I call it but bad luck that, out of an infinite number of laws, there is not one at least that fortune and the rashness of chance has allowed to be universally received with the consent of all nations?) — they are, I say, so unlucky that of these three or four select laws, there is not one that is not contradicted and disowned, not only by one nation but by many. Now the only likely sign by which they could argue or infer some natural laws is the universality of approval. For we would without doubt follow, with common consent, what nature had truly ordained for us; not only would every nation, but every private man, resent the violence done him by anyone who tried to push him to do something contrary to that law. But let them produce me one of that kind. Protagoras and Ariston gave no other essence to the justice of laws than the authority and opinion of the legislator, and said that, setting those aside, the honourable and the good lost their qualities and remained empty names of indifferent things. Thrasymachus, in Plato, holds that there is no other right but the convenience of the stronger. There is nothing in which the world varies so much as in laws and customs: what is abominable here is in honour elsewhere — as in Sparta dexterity in stealing was. Marriages between near relations are punishable by death among us; they are honoured elsewhere:
Gentes esse feruntur, In quibus et nato genitrix, et nata parenti Jungitur, et pietas geminato crescit amore;
["There are nations, it is said, where mother is joined to son and daughter to father, and family affection grows by the doubling of love."]

The killing of infants, the killing of fathers, community of wives, traffic in robberies, licence in every kind of sensual pleasure — in short, there is nothing so extreme that some nation's custom has not allowed it.

It is plausible that there are natural laws for us, as we see them in other creatures; but they are lost in us, this fine human reason everywhere thrusting itself in to govern and command, so as to muddle and confound the face of things according to its own vanity and inconstancy: _Nihil itaque amplius nostrum est; quod nostrum dico, artis est._ "So nothing of ours is any longer ours; what I call ours belongs to art." Subjects have various lights and various considerations, and it is from this that the diversity of opinions chiefly proceeds: one nation considers a subject in one light and stops there; another sees it from a different angle.

There is nothing more horrible to imagine than a man eating his father; and yet the people whose ancient custom this was looked on it as a testimony of piety and affection, seeking by it to give their forebears the most worthy and honourable burial — storing up in themselves, as it were in their own marrow, the bodies and relics of their fathers, and in a sense regenerating them by transmutation into their own living flesh, through the means of nourishment and digestion. It is easy to imagine what a cruelty and abomination it must have seemed to men possessed and steeped in this superstition to throw their fathers' remains to the corruption of the earth and to the food of beasts and worms.

Lycurgus considered the liveliness, diligence, boldness, and dexterity of stealing something from a neighbour, and the public benefit that resulted when each man looked more carefully to the preservation of his own; and he believed that, from this double exercise of attacking and defending, more advantage was to be drawn for military discipline (which was the chief science and virtue in which he wanted to train that nation) than the disorder and injustice of taking another man's goods were worth weighing against.

Dionysius the tyrant offered Plato a robe in the Persian fashion — long, damasked, perfumed. Plato refused it, saying that, having been born a man, he would not willingly dress himself in women's clothes. But Aristippus accepted it, with this answer: "No piece of clothing can corrupt a chaste courage." His friends reproached him with meanness of spirit for not taking more to heart that Dionysius had spat in his face: "Fishermen," he said, "let themselves be drenched in the sea from head to foot to catch a minnow." Diogenes was washing cabbages and, seeing him pass, called out: "If you knew how to live on cabbages, you wouldn't fawn on a tyrant." To which Aristippus replied: "And if you knew how to live among men, you wouldn't be washing cabbages." Thus reason finds appearances for opposite effects: it is a pot with two ears, and a man may take it by the right or the left:
Bellum, o terra hospita, portas: Bello armantur equi; bellum hæc armenta minantur. Sed tamen idem olim curru succedere sueti Quadrupedes, et frena jugo concordia ferre; Spes est pacis.

["War, O hospitable land, you bring us: the horses are armed for war; war these herds threaten. And yet these same four-footed creatures, once trained to draw the chariot and to wear the harmonious reins of the yoke, give hope of peace."]

Solon, urged by his friends not to shed powerless and useless tears for the death of his son, said: "It is for that very reason that I more justly shed them — because they are powerless and useless." Socrates' wife exacerbated her grief with this remark: "How unjustly these wicked judges are putting him to death!" "Why," he replied, "would you rather they had executed me justly?" We have our ears bored; the Greeks looked on that as a mark of slavery. We retire in private to enjoy our wives; the Indians do it in public. The Scythians sacrificed strangers in their temples; elsewhere temples were a refuge:
Inde furor vulgi, quod numina vicinorum Odit quisque locus, cum solos credat habendos Esse deos, quos ipse colit.
["Hence the fury of the crowd: each place hates the gods of its neighbours, believing that only the gods it itself worships are to be held divine."]

I have heard of a judge who, when he came across a sharp dispute between Bartolus and Aldus, and some point contested with many contradictions, wrote in the margin of his book, "a question for a friend" — meaning that the truth was so contested and disputed there that in a similar case he could favour whichever side he chose. It was only for want of wit that he did not write "a question for a friend" throughout. The advocates and judges of our time find enough slack in every case to fit it to whatever they themselves think best. In so infinite a science, depending on the authority of so many opinions, and so arbitrary a subject, an extreme confusion of judgments must necessarily arise. There is hardly any suit so clear that opinions on it do not greatly differ. What one court has decided one way, another decides the contrary, and itself contrary to that at another time. We see very frequent examples of this, thanks to the practice — admitted among us, and a marvellous blemish on the ceremonious authority and lustre of our justice — of not abiding by one sentence, but running from judge to judge and court to court to decide one and the same case.

As to the freedom of philosophical opinions concerning vice and virtue, we need not labour the point. There are found in them many opinions better hidden than published to weak minds. Arcesilaus said that in lechery it makes no difference where or with whom it is committed: _Et obscenas voluptates, si natura requirit, non genere, aut loco, aut ordine, sed formâ, ætate, figurâ, metiendas Epicurus putat... ne amores quidem sanctos a sapiente alienos esse arbitrantur... Quæramus, ad quam usque ætatem juvenes amandi sint._ "Epicurus thinks that obscene pleasures, if nature requires them, are to be measured neither by race, kind, place, or rank, but by age, shape, and beauty... They think that even sacred loves are not foreign to the wise man... Let us inquire up to what age young men are to be loved." These last two Stoic quotations, and the reproach Dicaearchus threw in Plato's own teeth on this score, show how much the soundest philosophy indulges licences and excesses very remote from common custom.

Laws derive their authority from possession and custom. It is dangerous to trace them back to their beginning; they grow great and ennoble themselves, like our rivers, as they run on; but follow them upstream to their source, and it is only a little spring, scarcely noticeable,

that swells in this way and fortifies itself by growing old. Just look into the ancient considerations that first set in motion this famous torrent so full of dignity, awe, and reverence — you will find them so light and weak that it is no wonder if these people, who weigh and reduce everything to reason, and who admit nothing on authority or on trust, have judgments often very remote from those of the public. It is no wonder if people who take their pattern from the first image of nature should in most of their opinions swerve from the common path. As for example, few of them would have approved the strict conditions of our marriages, and most of them have been for having wives in common, without obligation. They would refuse our ceremonies. Chrysippus said that a philosopher would do a dozen somersaults — yes, and without his breeches — for a dozen olives. That philosopher would hardly have advised Cleisthenes to refuse to give the fair Agarista, his daughter, to Hippoclides, for having seen him stand on his head on a table. Metrocles, somewhat indiscreetly, broke wind backwards while disputing in the presence of a great audience in his school, and hid in his own house for shame until Crates came to visit him and, adding to his arguments and consolations the example of his own liberty by setting himself to compete with him as to who could be louder, cured him of that scruple, and drew him into his own Stoic sect — freer than the more reserved Peripatetic one he had been in until then. What we call decency — not daring to do in public what it is decent enough to do in private — the Stoics call foppishness; and to mince matters, and to be so modest as to conceal and disown what nature, custom, and our desires publish and proclaim of our actions, they treated as a vice. The others thought it was to undervalue the mysteries of Venus to draw them out of their private chapel and expose them to public view, and that to bring them out from behind the curtain was to debase them. Modesty is a thing of weight; secrecy, reserve, and circumspection are part of esteem. Pleasure was wonderfully ingenious when, under the mask of virtue, she sought not to be prostituted in the open streets, trodden under foot, exposed to public view, lacking the dignity and convenience of her private rooms. Hence some say that to abolish public brothels is not only to scatter fornication into every place where it had been confined to one, but also, by the difficulty, to incite wild and idle people to this vice:
Mochus es Aufidiæ, qui vir, Scævine, fuisti: Rivalis fuerat qui tuus, ille vir est. Cur aliena placet tibi, quæ tua non placet uxor? Numquid securus non potes arrigere?
This phenomenon shows itself in a thousand examples:
Nullus in urbe fuit totâ, qui tangere vellet Uxorem gratis, Cæciliane, tuam, Dum licuit: sed nunc, positis custodibus, ingens Turba fututorum est. Ingeniosus homo es.
A philosopher caught in the very act, when asked what he was doing, coolly replied: "I am planting a man" — no more blushing to be so caught than if they had found him planting garlic.

It is, I suppose, out of tenderness and respect for the natural modesty of mankind that a great and religious author is of the opinion that this act is so necessarily bound to privacy and shame that he cannot persuade himself there could be any real performance in those shameless embraces of the Cynics — and that they contented themselves with merely miming lascivious gestures to keep up the impudent profession of their school; and that, to release what shame had withheld and restrained, it was afterward necessary for them to withdraw into the shade. But he had not thoroughly examined their debaucheries. For Diogenes, playing the beast with himself in public, wished, in the presence of all who saw him, that he could fill his belly by that exercise. When asked why he did not find a more convenient place to eat in than in the open street, he answered: "Because I am hungry in the open street." The women philosophers who mixed with their sect mixed also with their persons, in all places, without reserve. Hipparchia was only received into Crates' company on condition that she should in all things follow the practice and customs of his rule. These philosophers set a great price on virtue and renounce all other discipline but the moral; and yet, in all their actions, they ascribed sovereign authority to the choice of their sage, even above the laws, and gave no other curb to sensual pleasure than moderation and the preservation of others' liberty.

Heraclitus and Protagoras, since wine seemed bitter to the sick and pleasant to the well, the rudder crooked in the water and straight out of it, and other such contrary appearances found in subjects, argued from this that all subjects had in themselves the causes of these appearances; that there was some bitterness in the wine which had some sympathy with the sick man's taste, and the rudder some bending quality sympathising with whoever looked at it in the water — and so on. Which is to say that everything is in everything, and consequently, nothing in any one thing; for where everything is, there is nothing.

This opinion reminded me of our own experience that there is no sense or aspect of any thing — whether bitter or sweet, straight or crooked — that the human mind does not find in the writings it sets out to pore over. Into the cleanest, purest, most perfect words that can possibly be, how many lies and falsehoods have we read in! What heresy has not found in them ground and testimony sufficient to make itself embraced and defended? That is why the authors of such errors will never give up the proof of their interpretation of words. A person of dignity, who wanted to prove to me by authority his search for the philosopher's stone — in which he was head over ears engaged — recently cited to me at least five or six passages from the Bible on which, he said, he first founded his attempt, for the relief of his conscience (for he is a divine). And, in truth, the idea was not only entertaining but very well fitted to the defence of that fine science.

It is by this means that the reputation of fortune-telling fables is acquired. There is no soothsayer, if we grant him this authority, but, if a man will take the trouble to ruffle and turn the leaves of his words and peer narrowly into all their folds and glosses, can be made — like the Sibyls — to say whatever you want. There are so many ways of interpretation that it would be hard for a clever wit not to find some angle in any subject that will serve his purpose, either by an oblique or a direct line; that is why a cloudy and ambiguous style has been in such frequent and ancient use. Let the author once master that, and posterity will busy itself with his predictions, which not only his own qualities, but the accidental favour of the matter itself, may bring about for him. For the rest, let him express himself, foolishly or subtly, somewhat obscurely or contradictorily — it doesn't matter. A number of wits, shaking and sifting him, will bring out a great many different shapes, either according to his meaning, or collateral to it, or contrary to it — all of which will redound to his honour. He will see himself enriched by his disciples, like the regents of colleges by their pupils' yearly presents. This is what has given reputation to many things of no worth at all; it has brought several writings into vogue and given them the fame of containing any kind of matter you could desire — one and the same thing receiving a thousand thousand images and various considerations, as many as we please.

Is it possible that Homer could have meant to say all that we make him say, and that he intended so many and so varied figures, that divines, lawgivers, captains, philosophers, and all sorts of men who treat of sciences, however varied and opposed, quote him indifferently, and back their arguments with his authority, as the sovereign lord and master of all offices, works, and crafts, and counsellor-general of all enterprises? Whoever has had occasion for oracles and predictions has found enough in him to serve his turn. It is a wonder what wonderful and admirable correspondences an intelligent man, a particular friend of mine, has found in him in favour of our religion; and he cannot easily be put out of the conviction that it was Homer's design — though he is as well acquainted with that author as anyone of his time. And what he has found in Homer in favour of our religion, many in antiquity have found in favour of theirs. Just look at how Plato is tumbled and tossed about — everyone ennobling his own opinions by applying him to himself, and making him take whichever side they please. They drag him in and engage him in every new opinion the world receives, and make him, according to the changing course of things, differ from himself. Everyone makes him disavow, according to his own sense, the manners and customs lawful in his age but unlawful in ours; and all this with vivacity and force, according to the strength and liveliness of the wit of the interpreter. From the same foundation that Heraclitus had — that sentence of his that "all things have in them the forms we perceive" — Democritus drew an entirely contrary conclusion: that objects have nothing in them of what we perceive in them. And because honey is sweet to one and bitter to another, he argued from that that it was neither sweet nor bitter. The Pyrrhonians would say that they did not know whether it was sweet or bitter, or one or the other or both — for these always kept to the highest point of doubt. The Cyrenaics held that nothing was perceptible from without, and that only what touched us inwardly was — like pain and pleasure — acknowledging neither sound nor colour, but only certain affections we receive from them, and saying that man's judgment had no other seat. Protagoras believed that what seems true to each man is true to that man. The Epicureans lodged all judgment in the senses, and put the knowledge of things, and pleasure, there. Plato wanted the judgment of truth, and truth itself, derived from opinions and the senses, to belong to the wit and the thinking faculty.

This discussion has set me on the consideration of the senses, where the greatest foundation and proof of our ignorance lies. Whatever is known is, no doubt, known by the faculty of the knower; for since the judgment proceeds from the operation of the one who judges, it stands to reason that this operation is performed by his means and by his will, not by the constraint of another — as it would be if we knew things by their power, and according to the law of their essence. Now all knowledge is conveyed to us by the senses; they are our masters:
Via qua munita fidei Proxima fert humanum in pectus, templaque mentis;
["By that paved way which most directly leads belief into the human heart and into the temples of the mind."]

Science begins with them and resolves into them. After all, we should know no more than a stone if we did not know there is sound, smell, light, taste, measure, weight, softness, hardness, sharpness, colour, smoothness, breadth, and depth. These are the platforms and the principles of the whole structure of our knowledge; and, according to some, science is nothing else but sensation. Anyone who could make me contradict the senses would have me by the throat; he could not push me back any further. The senses are the beginning and the end of human knowledge:
Invenies primis ab sensibus esse creatam Notitiam veri; neque sensus posse refelli... Quid majore fide porro, quam sensus, haberi Debet?
["You will find that the notion of truth is first created from the senses, and that the senses cannot be refuted... Now what can be held in greater trust than the senses?"]

Grant them as little as we will, we must still grant them this, that all our instruction is conducted through their mediation. Cicero says that Chrysippus, having tried to weaken the force and authority of the senses, found himself faced with arguments and oppositions so vehement to the contrary that he could not satisfy himself in the attempt — whereupon Carneades, who took the contrary side, boasted that he would use Chrysippus's own words and arguments to counter and confute him, and so cried out against him: "Wretch! Your own force has destroyed you." There can be nothing more absurd than to maintain that fire does not warm, that light does not shine, that there is no weight or solidity in iron — which are things conveyed to us by the senses. There is no belief or knowledge in man that can be compared to that for certainty.

The first thought I have on the subject of the senses is this: I doubt whether man is equipped with all the natural senses. I see several animals living an entire and perfect life, some without sight, others without hearing. Who knows whether one, two, three, or many other senses may not be missing in us as well? For if any one is missing, our examination cannot detect the lack. It is the senses' privilege to be the outermost limit of our discovery; there is nothing beyond them that can help us in our exploration, not even one sense in the discovery of another:
An poterunt oculos aures reprehendere? an aures Tactus an hunc porro tactum sapor arguet oris? An confutabunt nares, oculive revincent?
["Can the ears correct the eyes, or touch the ears? Or shall taste in the mouth confute touch? Will the nostrils refute, or the eyes confound them in their own faculties?"]
They all make up the extreme limit of our ability:
Seorsum cuique potestas Divisa est, sua vis cuique est,
["To each its own power is allotted, separately; each has its own force."]

It is impossible to make a man naturally blind understand that he does not see; impossible to make him desire sight or regret its absence. So we should not draw any assurance from the fact that the soul is contented and satisfied with the senses we have — since the soul cannot feel its own infirmity and imperfection in this, if there is any. It is impossible to say anything to such a blind man — by reasoning, argument, or analogy — that could put into his imagination any notion of light, colour, or sight; there is nothing left for the senses to seize on to make it evident to him. Those born blind whom we hear wish they could see, it is not that they understand what they desire; they have learned from us that they are missing something, that there is something desirable that we have, which they can name and talk about its effects and consequences, but they have no idea what it is and do not grasp it at all.

I have known a gentleman of good family, born blind, or at least blind from such an early age that he has no idea what sight is — and yet he is so little sensible of his defect that he uses, as we do, the words proper to seeing, and applies them in a way wholly particular to himself. They brought him a child to which he was godfather; taking it in his arms, he said: "Good God, what a fine child! How beautiful to look at! What a pretty face!" He will say, like any of us: "This room has a fine view; it is clear weather; the sun shines bright." And moreover, since hunting, tennis, and shooting at the butts are our pastimes, and he has heard about them, he has taken a liking to them; he will ride out hunting and believes he has as good a share in the sport as we do; he will express himself as angry or as pleased as the best of us — and yet he knows nothing of it but by ear. Someone calls out to him, "Here's a hare!" when he is on some level plain where he can ride safely; and afterwards, when they tell him, "The hare is killed," he is as overjoyed and proud as the others who say they are. He will take a tennis-ball in his left hand and strike it away with the racket; he will fire a harquebus at random and is satisfied with what his people tell him — whether he overshot or missed wide.

Who knows whether all humankind doesn't commit a similar absurdity, for want of some sense, and whether through that defect the greatest part of the face of things isn't concealed from us? What do we know but that the difficulties we find in several works of nature come from this — and that several effects of animals which exceed our capacity are not produced by the faculty of some sense that we lack? And whether some of them may not, by this means, have a fuller and more entire life than ours? We grasp an apple with all our senses; we find in it redness, smoothness, fragrance, and sweetness — but it may have other properties besides these, like heating or binding, that no sense of ours has any reference to. Isn't it likely that there are sensitive faculties in nature fit to judge and discern what we call the occult properties of various things — as the loadstone's power to attract iron — and that the lack of such faculties is the reason we are ignorant of the true essence of such things? Perhaps some particular sense is what gives cocks to understand what hour it is at midnight, and when it begins to grow toward day, and makes them crow accordingly; that teaches chicks, before they have any experience of the matter, to fear a sparrowhawk and not a goose or a peacock — birds of a much larger size; that warns them against the hostile quality the cat has toward them, and makes them not fear the dog; to arm themselves against the mewing (a kind of flattering voice) of the one and not against the barking (a shrill and threatening voice) of the other; that teaches wasps, ants, and rats to fall on the best pear and the best cheese before having tasted them; and inspires the stag, the elephant, and the snake with the knowledge of a particular herb proper for their cure. There is no sense that has not a mighty dominion, and that does not by its power introduce an infinite number of pieces of knowledge. If we were defective in the perception of sounds, of harmony, and of the voice, it would bring an unimaginable confusion on all the rest of our science; for beyond what belongs to the proper effect of each sense, how many arguments, consequences, and conclusions do we draw about other things by comparing one sense with another? Let an intelligent man imagine human nature originally produced without the sense of sight, and consider what ignorance and trouble such a defect would bring on him, what darkness and blindness in the soul; he will then see how greatly important to the knowledge of truth the privation of another such sense, or of two or three of them, would be. We have formed a truth by the agreement and concurrence of our five senses; but perhaps we would need the consent and contribution of eight or ten to make a certain discovery of it in its essence.

The sects that contest the knowledge of man do it principally on the uncertainty and weakness of our senses; for since all knowledge is conveyed to us through their mediation, if they fail in their report, if they corrupt or alter what they bring us from outside, if the light that creeps into the soul by them is obscured along the way, we have nothing else to hold on to. From this extreme difficulty come all these fancies: "that every subject has in itself all that we find there"; "that it has in itself nothing of what we think we find there"; and the Epicureans' notion, "that the sun is no bigger than our sight judges it to be:"
Quidquid id est, nihilo fertur majore figura, Quam nostris oculis quam cernimus, esse videtur:
["Whatever it is, it is borne in no greater figure than that in which it appears to our eyes when we look on it."]
That the appearances which represent a body as large to the one near it and as smaller to the one farther away are both true:
Nec tamen hic oculos falli concedimus hilum... Proinde animi vitium hoc oculis adfingere noli:
["Yet we will not concede in the least that the eyes are deceived... Do not, therefore, blame the eyes for what is the fault of the mind."]

And, flatly, "that there is no deceit in the senses; that we are at their mercy, and must look elsewhere for reasons to excuse the differences and contradictions we find — even inventing lies and other fictions, if it comes to that, rather than accuse the senses." Timagoras swore that, by pressing or turning his eye, he could never make the light of the candle look double, and that the seeming so came from a defect of opinion, not of the instrument. The most absurd of all absurdities, with the Epicureans, is to deny the force and effect of the senses:

Proinde, quod in quoquo est his visum tempore, verum est. Et, si non potuit ratio dissolvere causam, Cur ea, quæ fuerint juxtim quadrata, procul sint Visa rotunda; tamen præstat rationis egentem Reddere mendose causas utriusque figuræ, Quam manibus manifesta suis emittere quæquam, Et violare fidem primam, et convellere tota Fundamenta, quibus nixatur vita salusque: Non modo enim ratio ruat omnis, vita quoque ipsa Concidat extemplo, nisi credere sensibus ausis, Præcipitesque locos vitare, et cætera, quæ sint In genere hoc fugienda.

["And so, whatever has been seen by the senses at any time is true. And if reason cannot resolve the cause why those things that close up were square seem round at a distance, still it is better, lacking a reason, to assign a wrong cause to either figure than to let go from one's own hands anything manifest, to violate first faith, and to tear up all the foundations on which life and safety rest. For not only would all reason fall, but life itself would collapse at once, unless you dared to trust the senses and to avoid sheer places and other things of that kind that must be shunned."]

This desperate and unphilosophical advice expresses only this: that human knowledge cannot sustain itself except by unreasonable, foolish, and mad reason; but that even so it is still better that man, to set a higher value on himself, make use of any other remedy, however fanciful, than confess his necessary ignorance — a truth so disadvantageous to him. He cannot avoid acknowledging that the senses are the sovereign lords of his knowledge; but they are uncertain and falsifiable in every circumstance. There he must fight it out to the last; and if his rightful forces fail him, as they do, to supply the gap with obstinacy, rashness, and impudence. If what the Epicureans say is true — that we have no knowledge if the appearances of the senses are false — and if what the Stoics say is also true — that the appearances of the senses are so false that they can give us no kind of knowledge — we shall conclude, to the disadvantage of these two great dogmatic sects, that there is no science at all.

As for the error and uncertainty of the operation of the senses, anyone may furnish himself with as many examples as he pleases — so ordinary are the faults and tricks they play on us. In the echo of a valley, the sound of a trumpet seems to come at us from a place behind us:

Exstantesque procul medio de gurgite montes, Classibus inter quos liber patet exitus, idem Apparent, et longe divolsi licet, ingens Insula conjunctis tamen ex his una videtur... Et fugere ad puppim colles campique videntur, Quos agimus præter navim, velisque volamus... Ubi in medio nobis equus acer obhæsit Flumine, equi corpus transversum ferre videtur Vis, et in adversum flumen contrudere raptim.

["Mountains standing far out from the middle of the deep, with a free passage open between for fleets, appear the same; and though they are far apart, they nevertheless seem one great island joined together... And the hills and fields seem to flee toward the stern as we drive past them in the ship and fly along under sail... And when in the middle of a swift river our spirited horse has stood firm, the force of the water seems to carry the body of the horse sideways, and to push him swiftly against the current."]

Take a musket-ball under the forefinger, with the middle finger crossed over it, and it feels so much like two that a man will have great trouble persuading himself there is only one — for the tip of each finger feels one at the same time. That the senses are very often masters of our reason, and force it to take impressions which it judges and knows to be false, is often seen. I set aside the sense of touch, which has its functions nearer, more lively, more substantial, and which so often, through the pains it brings the body, overthrows all those fine Stoic resolutions and forces him to cry out at his belly who has resolutely established this doctrine in his soul: "that the colic and all other pains and diseases are indifferent things, having no power to take anything from the sovereign felicity in which the wise man is seated by his virtue." There is no heart so effeminate that the rattle and sound of our drums and trumpets will not inflame it with courage; nor so sullen that the harmony of our music will not rouse and cheer it; nor a soul so stubborn that it will not feel itself struck with some reverence in considering the gloomy vastness of our churches, the variety of ornaments, and the order of our ceremonies, and in hearing the solemn music of our organs and the grave and devout harmony of our voices. Even those who come in with contempt feel a certain shivering in their hearts, and something of dread that makes them begin to doubt their opinions. For my part, I do not think myself strong enough to hear an ode of Horace or Catullus sung by a beautiful young mouth without being moved; and Zeno was right to say "that the voice is the flower of beauty." Someone once tried to make me believe that a certain person, whom all we French know, had imposed on me in reciting some verses he had made — that they were not the same on paper that they were in the air, and that my eyes would judge them differently from my ears: so great is the power of pronunciation to give shape and value to works that are left to the efficacy and modulation of the voice. That is why Philoxenus was not so much to blame, when he heard someone giving a poor accent to one of his compositions, for kicking and smashing certain earthen vessels of his, saying: "I break what is yours, because you corrupt what is mine." To what end did those men who, with firm resolve, killed themselves turn their faces away so as not to see the blow they themselves had appointed? And those who, for their health, ask and command incisions to be made on them and cauteries applied — why can they not endure the sight of the preparations, the instruments, and the operations of the surgeon, when the eye plays no part in the pain? Are not these proper examples to verify the authority the senses have over the imagination? It is to no purpose that we know these tresses were borrowed from a page or a lackey, that this rouge came from Spain and this pearl-powder from the Ocean Sea. Our sight will still compel us to confess the subject more agreeable and more lovely against all reason — for in that there is nothing of its own:
Auferimur cultu; gemmis, auroque teguntur Crimina; pars minima est ipsa puella sui. Sæpe, ubi sit quod ames, inter tam multa requiras: Decipit hac oculos ægide dives Amor.

["We are carried away by ornament; faults are hidden by gems and gold; the girl herself is the smallest part of herself. Often, amid so much, you may ask where what you love is: with this rich shield, Love deceives the eyes."]
What a strange power the poets attribute to the senses, when they make Narcissus so desperately in love with his own shadow,
Cunctaque miratur, quibus est mirabilis ipse; Se cupit imprudens, et, qui probat, ipse probatur; Dumque petit, petitur; pariterque accendit, et ardet:

["He admires everything for which he himself is admirable; he desires himself, unawares; and he who praises is himself praised; while he seeks, he is sought; the kindler is kindled and burns equally."]
And Pygmalion's judgment so troubled by the impression of seeing his ivory statue that he loves it and adores it as if it were a living woman!
Oscula dat, reddique putat: sequiturque, tenetque, Et credit tactis digitos insidere membris; Et metuit, pressos veniat ne livor in artus.

["He gives it kisses, and thinks they are returned; he follows it, embraces it, and believes that his fingers sink into the limbs he touches; and fears that bruises may appear on the parts where he has pressed."]

Put a philosopher into a cage of small, thin iron bars and hang him from the top of the high tower of Notre Dame in Paris. He will see, by clear reason, that he cannot possibly fall — and yet he will find (unless he is used to the slater's trade) that he cannot help being terrified and dazed by the sight of that excessive height. We have trouble enough holding our nerve in the galleries of our steeples, if they are made with open work, even when they are built of stone — and some people cannot bear even to think of it. Lay a beam across between two such towers, of breadth enough to walk on; there is no philosophical wisdom so firm that it can give us the courage to walk over it as we would along the ground. I have often tried this on our mountains in these parts, and though I am not one of the most easily frightened, I could not endure to look into that infinite depth without horror and trembling — though I stood at more than my own length from the edge of the precipice, and could not have fallen unless I chose to. I also observed there that, whatever height the precipice was, if there were some tree or some jutting rock to support and divide the sight, it eased our fear a little and gave more assurance — as if such things, in falling, might give us some support; but on sheer drops we cannot look without being giddy: _Ut despici sine vertigine simul oculorum animique non possit_, "that they cannot be looked down upon without dizziness of both eyes and mind." This is a manifest imposture of the sight. That is why that fine philosopher put out his own eyes, to free his soul from being diverted by them and to philosophise more freely; but by the same rule, he should have stopped up his ears, which Theophrastus says are the most dangerous instruments we have for receiving violent impressions to alter and disturb us; and finally he should have deprived himself of all his other senses — that is to say, of his life and being; for they all have power to command our soul and reason: _Fit etiam sæpe specie quâdam, sæpe vocum gravitate et cantibus, ut pellantur animi vehementius; sæpe etiam curâ et timore_, "For it often happens that minds are more violently struck by some sight, by the gravity and sound of voices, by singing; and often also by anxiety and fear." Doctors hold that there are certain complexions agitated to fury by the same sounds and instruments. I have seen some who could not bear to hear a bone gnawed under the table without losing patience; and there is hardly any man who is not disturbed by the sharp, shrill noise the file makes scraping iron — as also when they hear someone chewing close by, or anyone speaking who has an impediment in his throat or nose; some are moved by it to anger and hatred. What use was that piping prompter to Gracchus, who softened, raised, and modulated his master's voice as he declaimed at Rome, if the movements and quality of sound had no power to move and alter the judgments of his hearers? In truth, there is wonderful reason to make so much fuss about the firmness of this fine piece, which lets itself be twisted and turned by the motion and accidents of so light a wind.

The same cheat the senses play on our understanding, the understanding plays back on them in turn; the soul too sometimes has her revenge; they lie and quarrel over which shall most deceive the other. What we see and hear when we are carried away by passion, we neither see nor hear as it really is:
Et solem geminum, et duplices se ostendere Thebas.
["And the sun seems double, and two Thebes appear."]
The object we love appears more beautiful than it really is —
Multimodis igitur pravas turpesque videmus Esse in deliciis, summoque in honore vigere;
["And so in many ways we see crooked and ugly things treated as delights, and flourishing in the highest esteem."]

and the one we hate, uglier. To a discontented and afflicted man, the light of day seems dark and overcast. Our senses are not only depraved but very often stupefied by the passions of the soul. How many things do we see that we do not notice, if the mind is busy with other thoughts?
In rebus quoque apertis noscere possis, Si non advertas animum, proinde esse quasi omni Tempore semotæ fuerint, longeque remotæ:
["Even in plain matters, you may know that, unless you direct your mind to them, they are just as if they had been set apart at all times, and far removed."]
It would seem that the soul retires inward and uses up the powers of the senses. And so both the inside and the outside of man are full of weakness and falsehood.

Those who have compared our lives to a dream were, perhaps, more right than they realised. When we dream, the soul lives, works, and exercises all its faculties, neither more nor less than when awake — but more largely and more obscurely; and yet not so much that the difference is as great as that between night and the noon brightness of the sun, but rather as that between night and shade: there she sleeps, here she only slumbers — but more or less, it is still dark, still Cimmerian darkness. We wake sleeping and sleep waking. I do not see so clearly in my sleep; but as for being awake, I never found it clear enough or free from clouds. Moreover, sleep, when it is deep, sometimes rocks even dreams themselves to sleep; but our waking is never so lively that it properly purges and dissipates those whimsies, which are waking dreams, and worse than dreams. Our reason and soul receive these fancies and opinions that come in dreams, and authorise the actions we do in dreams with the same approval as those of the day. So why do we not doubt whether our thought, our action, is not another sort of dreaming, and our waking a certain kind of sleep?

If the senses are our first judges, it is not only ours that we are to consult; for in this faculty the beasts have as great a share as we, or greater. Certainly some of them have keener hearing than man, others keener sight, others a keener sense of smell, others of touch and taste. Democritus said that the gods and brutes had the sensory faculties more perfect than man. But between the effects of their senses and ours, the difference is extreme. Our spittle cleans and dries up our wounds; it kills the snake:
Tantaque in his rebus distantia differitasque est, Ut quod aliis cibus est, aliis fuat acre venenum. Sæpe etenim serpens, hominis contacta saliva, Disperit, ac sese mandendo conficit ipsa:

["And so great is the distance and difference among these things that what is food to some is bitter poison to others. For often a snake, touched with human spittle, perishes, and destroys itself by gnawing at itself."]
What quality shall we attribute to our spittle? As it affects us, or as it affects the snake? By which of the two senses shall we prove the true essence we are looking for?

Pliny says there are certain sea-hares in the Indies that are poison to us, and we to them — so much so that we kill them with the slightest touch. Which is truly the poison, the man or the fish? Which shall we believe — the fish of the man, or the man of the fish? One quality of the air infects a man and does the ox no harm; another infects the ox but does not hurt the man. Which of the two is truly and by nature the pestilent quality? To people with jaundice, all things look yellow and paler than they do to us:
Lurida præterea fiunt, quæcunque tuentur Arquati.
["Whatever the jaundiced look at, moreover, looks pale and yellow too."]

Those troubled with the disease the doctors call hyposphagma — a suffusion of blood under the skin — see everything red and bloody. What do we know but that these humours, which alter the operations of sight, predominate in beasts and are normal with them? For we see some whose eyes are yellow, like us when we have jaundice, and others of a bloody colour; it is likely the colours of objects look different to them from what they look like to us. Which of the two will make a right judgment? For it is not said that the essence of things has a relation to man only. Hardness, whiteness, depth, and sharpness have reference to the service and knowledge of animals as well as ours, and nature has equally designed them for their use. When we press down on the eye, the body we look at appears longer and more drawn out — many animals have their eyes so pressed down; this length, then, may be the true form of that body, and not the one our eyes give it in their usual state. If we close the lower part of the eye, things appear double:
Bina lucernarum florentia lumina flammis... Et duplices hominum facies, et corpora bina.
["The lights of the lamps blossom in twin flames... and men appear with double faces and two bodies."]

If our ears are blocked, or the passage stopped with something, we receive sound quite otherwise than we usually do; animals whose ears are hairy, or have only a tiny hole instead of an ear, do not hear as we do but receive another kind of sound. We see at festivals and theatres that if a painted glass of a certain colour is set against the light of the torches, everything in the place appears green, yellow, or violet:

Et vulgo faciunt id lutea russaque vela, Et ferruginea, cum, magnis intenta theatris, Per malos vulgata trabesque, trementia pendent; Namque ibi consessum caveæ subter, et omnem Scenæ speciem, patrum, matrumque, deorumque Inficiunt, coguntque suo volitare colore:

["And yellow and red and dark-iron curtains commonly do this, when, stretched over the great theatres, spread on poles and beams, they hang trembling; for there they tinge the assembly below in the bowl and all the look of the stage — the fathers, mothers, and gods — and make them flit about in their own colour."]
It is likely that the eyes of animals — which we see are of various colours — produce the appearance of bodies in accord with those colours.

To make a right judgment, then, of the differences between the senses, we should first be agreed with the beasts, and second among ourselves — which we are not in the least, but enter into dispute every time one person hears, sees, or tastes something otherwise than another does, and we argue, as much as about anything else, about the diversity of the images the senses present to us. A child, by the ordinary course of nature, hears, sees, and speaks differently than a man of thirty; and he than one of sixty. The senses are duller and dimmer in some people, more open and quick in others. We receive things variously, depending on what we are and on how they appear to us. Those rings cut in the shape of feathers, called "endless feathers," no eye can take the measure of, nor keep from being deceived: on one side they seem to widen, on the other to narrow to a point, even as the ring is turned on the finger; yet by feel, they all seem of equal size.
