Now since our perception is so uncertain and contested, it is no wonder we are told that we may declare that snow appears white to us; but to affirm that it is in its own essence really so is more than we are able to justify. And this foundation once shaken, all the knowledge in the world must necessarily fall to ruin. What! Do our senses themselves hinder one another? A picture seems raised and embossed to the sight; in the handling it feels flat to the touch. Shall we say that musk, which delights the smell and offends the taste, is pleasant or not? There are herbs and unguents proper for one part of the body that are harmful to another; honey is pleasant to the taste but offensive to the sight. Those who, to assist their lust, used in ancient times to set magnifying-glasses in front of the members they were going to employ, so as to please themselves the more by that ocular swelling — to which of their senses did they give the prize? Was it the sight, which represented the parts as large and great as they could wish, or the touch, which represented them small and contemptible? Are they our senses that supply the subject with these different qualities, while the subjects themselves have only one? As we see in the bread we eat: it is nothing but bread, but by being eaten it becomes bones, blood, flesh, hair, and nails:
Ut cibus in membra atque artus cum diditur omnes, Disperit, atque aliam naturam sufficit ex se;
["As food, when it is distributed through all the limbs and joints, loses its former state and out of itself supplies a different nature."]

The moisture sucked up by the root of a tree becomes trunk, leaf, and fruit; and the air, being but one, is modulated in a trumpet into a thousand sorts of sounds. Are they our senses, I would like to know, that in the same way form these subjects into so many different qualities — or do the subjects really have them in themselves? And on this doubt, what can we determine about their true essence? Moreover, since the accidents of disease, of raving, or of sleep make things appear otherwise to us than they do to the healthful, the wise, and the awake, is it not likely that our right posture of health and understanding, and our natural humours, also have the means to give a being to things relative to their own condition, and accommodate things to themselves, just as the disordered states do? Is health any less capable of giving them an aspect than sickness is? Why does not the temperate man have his own form of objects, just as the intemperate does — and why may he not as well stamp them with his own character as the other does? The man whose mouth is out of taste says the wine is flat; the healthy man commends its flavour; the thirsty man, its briskness. Now since our condition always accommodates things to itself and transforms them according to its own posture, we cannot know what things truly are in themselves — since nothing comes to us but what is falsified and altered by the senses. Where the compass, the square, and the rule are crooked, all propositions drawn from them, and all buildings erected on those guides, must necessarily be defective too. The uncertainty of our senses makes uncertain everything they produce:

Denique ut in fabricâ, si prava est regula prima, Normaque si fallax rectis regionibus exit, Et libella aliquâ si ex parte claudicat hilum; Omnia mendose fieri, atque obstipa necessum est, Prava, cubantia, prona, supina, atque absona tecta; Jam ruere ut quædam videantur velle, ruantque Prodita judiciis fallacibus omnia primis; Sic igitur ratio tibi rerum prava necesse est, Falsaque sit, falsis quæcunque ab sensibus orta est.

["And so as in building, if the first measure is crooked, if the square is false in the right angles, and if the level limps in any part, everything must come out faulty, lopsided, leaning, sloping, sagging, and out of line — roofs that look like they want to fall, and do fall, all betrayed by faulty first judgments. Just so your reasoning about things must necessarily be crooked and false, if it has arisen from false senses."]

As to the rest, who can be fit to judge and to determine those differences? As we say in controversies of religion that we must have a judge inclined to neither side, free from all choice and affection — which cannot be among Christians — so it falls out here. For if he is old, he cannot judge of the sense of old age, being himself a party in the case; if young, the same exception applies; if healthy, sick, asleep, or awake, he is still the same incompetent judge. We would need someone exempt from all these states, as from things indifferent to him; and by this rule we would need a judge who never existed.

To judge of the appearances we receive of subjects, we ought to have a deciding instrument; to verify this instrument, we must have demonstration; to verify this demonstration, an instrument. And here we are back on the same wheel, no further along. Since the senses cannot settle our dispute, being themselves full of uncertainty, then reason must do it. But no reason can be set up except on the basis of another reason, and so we run back to infinity. Our fancy does not apply itself to things outside us, but only conceives them through the senses; and the senses do not comprehend a foreign subject, but only their own affections; so that fancy and appearance are not parts of the subject, but only of the passion and suffering of the sense — and this passion and the subject are different things. Therefore whoever judges by appearances is judging by something other than the subject. And to say that the passions of the senses convey to the soul the quality of foreign subjects by resemblance — how can the soul and the understanding be sure of this resemblance, having of itself no commerce with foreign subjects? Just as those who never knew Socrates cannot, when they see his portrait, say it is like him. Now whoever wants nevertheless to judge by appearances: if by all of them, that is impossible, because they hinder one another by their contrarieties and discrepancies, as we see by experience. Shall some select appearances govern the rest? You must verify this select group by another select group, the second by a third, and so it will never come to an end. Finally, there is no constant existence either of the objects' being or of our own: we, our judgments, and all mortal things are unceasingly running and rolling. And consequently nothing certain can be established from the one to the other, both the judging and the judged being in continual motion and change.

We have no communication with being, because all human nature is always in the middle, between being born and dying, giving only an obscure appearance and shadow, a weak and uncertain opinion of itself. And if perhaps you fix your thought on trying to apprehend your own being, it will be like grasping water — for the harder you clench your hand to squeeze and hold what is by its own nature flowing, the more you lose of what you would grasp and hold. So, since all things are subject to pass from one change to another, reason — which looks there for a real substance — finds itself deceived, unable to lay hold of anything that subsists and remains; for everything is either entering into being and has not yet arrived there, or is beginning to die before it is born. Plato said that bodies never had any existence, only birth — conceiving that Homer had made Ocean and Tethys father and mother of the gods, to show us that all things are in perpetual fluctuation, motion, and variation; the opinion, as he says, of all the philosophers before his time, except Parmenides alone, who would not allow things to have motion, and on whose power he sets a great value. Pythagoras held that all matter was flowing and unstable; the Stoics, that there is no present time, and that what we call so is nothing but the juncture and meeting of the future and the past; Heraclitus, that no man ever entered twice into the same river; Epicharmus, that he who borrowed money an hour ago no longer owes it now; and that he who was invited last night to come to dinner today comes nevertheless uninvited, since they are no longer the same men, but have become others; and that no mortal substance could be found twice in the same condition — for by the suddenness and quickness of the change, it disperses one moment and reunites the next; it comes and goes in such a way that what begins to be born never arrives at the perfection of being, since that birth is never finished and never stops, as being at an end, but is always shifting and changing from one seed to another. As human seed is first made, in the mother's womb, into a formless embryo; then delivered as a suckling infant; then becomes a boy, then a youth, then a man, and finally a decrepit old man — so that each successive age and generation is always destroying and spoiling the one before:
Mutat enim mundi naturam totius ætas, Ex alioque alius status excipere omnia debet; Nec manet ulla sui similis res; omnia migrant, Omnia commutat natura, et vertere cogit.

["For time changes the nature of the whole world, and one state of things must take over from another; nor does any thing remain like itself; all things migrate, nature transforms everything and forces it to change."]

"And yet we foolishly fear one kind of death, when we have already passed, and pass every day, so many others. For not only, as Heraclitus said, is the death of fire the generation of air, and the death of air the generation of water; but, more manifestly still, we can see it in ourselves: manhood dies and passes away when old age comes on; youth ends in the flower of a grown man's prime; infancy in youth; and our first age dies in infancy. Yesterday died in today, and today will die in tomorrow; nothing remains in the same state or is always the same thing. And that it is so, let this be the proof: if we are always one and the same, how does it come about that we are pleased with one thing now, and with another by and by? How is it that we love or hate contrary things, that we praise or condemn them? How is it that we have different affections, no longer holding the same feeling in the same thought? For it is not likely that, without change, we should take on other passions; and what undergoes change does not remain the same — and if it is not the same, it is not at all; rather, along with itself, being also unknowingly changes and alters, becoming always another thing from another. And consequently the natural senses cheat and deceive themselves, taking what only seems to be for what is, for want of really knowing what that-which-is is. But what is it then that truly is? That which is eternal — that is to say, that never had a beginning, nor ever shall have an ending, and to which time can bring no change. For time is a movable thing, and shows itself as if in a shadow, with a substance ever flowing and running, never standing stable and permanent; to which belong the words _before_ and _after_, _has been_ or _shall be_ — which at first sight clearly show that it is not a thing that is. For it would be a great folly and a manifest falsity to say that that _is_ which is not yet, or which has already ceased to be. And as for those words _present_, _instant_, _now_, on which it seems we chiefly support and ground our understanding of time — when reason looks closely at them, it immediately destroys them; for it divides and splits the now into _future_ and _past_, having of necessity to consider it divided in two. The same happens to nature, which is measured, as to time, which measures it; for she has nothing more subsisting and permanent than time does, but all things are either being born, bearing, or dying. So that it would be impious to say of God — who alone _is_ — that he _was_, or that he _shall be_; for those are terms of declension, transmutation, and vicissitude, of what cannot continue or remain in being. So we must conclude that God alone _is_ — not according to any measure of time, but according to an immutable and immovable eternity, not measured by time, not subject to any decline; before whom nothing was, and after whom nothing shall be, either newer or more recent; but a real being, who with one sole _now_ fills the for-ever; and that there is nothing that truly is but he alone — without our being able to say that he _has been_ or _shall be_; without beginning and without end." To this so religious conclusion of a pagan, I will only add this testimony from one of his own condition, to close this long and tedious discourse, which would supply me with endless matter: "What a vile and abject thing is man," says he, "if he does not raise himself above humanity!" It is a good word, and a profitable desire — but absurd all the same. For to make the handle bigger than the hand, the cubit longer than the arm, and to hope to stride further than our legs can reach, is both impossible and monstrous; just as it is for a man to rise above himself and his humanity. For he can see only with his eyes, and grasp only with his grip. He shall be exalted, if God will lend him an extraordinary hand; he shall exalt himself, by abandoning and renouncing his own proper means, and by allowing himself to be raised and elevated by means purely celestial. It belongs to our Christian faith, and not to Stoic virtue, to lay claim to that divine and miraculous metamorphosis.
